World.title: The shipping industry profits from conflict and looks East
World.content:
This past May and June, while the Strait of Hormuz crisis was at its peak and a fifth of the world’s traded oil was looking for a way around the blockage, researchers from Kapa Research were interviewing the businesses that move the cargo. We spoke with 314 shipowners and C-suite executives ​from​​​ the world’s leading shipping groups and asked them how they see the years ahead. ​ ​​The responses reveal a level of confidence that exceeded expectations. An overwhelming 94​​​ percent​​​​​​​ express optimism about their company’s prospects​, and 70​ percent​​​ believe global shipping is in better shape today than it was five years ago.

The Global Shipping Outlook 2026 is Kapa Research’s quantitative study of the industry’s leadership, with respondents across every major shipping region, from Europe’s main maritime cent​er​​​s to the United States and Asia. Because fieldwork ran at the height of the crisis, the survey is a rare real-time record of how shipping leaders think under pressure.

Geopolitical crises in Ukraine, the Red Sea and the Middle East are named the most serious problem​s​ for shipping today by 76​ percent​​​ of respondents, the top concern in every region we surveyed. Yet when we asked what the Hormuz crisis means for their own company, 40​ percent​​​ said it creates new opportunities and only 23​ percent​​​ see significant obstacles. ​ ​​Nearly half of the industry’s leadership regards turmoil as good for business​​.​ The logic is pragmatic. Conflict pushes ships onto longer routes, longer routes absorb vessel supply​​ and freight rates rise while demand for goods persists. Shipping moves against the cycle. When instability rises, so do revenues.

The responses reveal a level of confidence that exceeded expectations. An overwhelming 94​​​ percent​​​​​​​ express optimism about their company’s prospects.

​​The industry also treats this as a lasting reset rather than a temporary challenge. 76​ percent​​​ expect the effects of the Hormuz crisis on global shipping to outlast six months, and opinion splits almost in half on whether this is the sector’s most serious crisis of the past 50 years, ​which covers​​​ the oil shocks, the tanker war, the global financial crisis and C​ovid​​​-19. One phrase from our interviews captures the mindset behind optimism: ​“​​​​Shipping keeps working even when the world stops.​​”​​​​

We therefore asked the uncomfortable question directly. Does global shipping today want peace​​ or does it benefit from turmoil? The peace camp wins, but only just: 54​ percent​​​ to 46​ percent​​​. Even among those who say the crisis hurts their own company, a third concede that the industry gains. Such cando​​r is rare in any sector, and it tempers any expectation that shipping will lobby hard for de-escalation. Markets gaining on volatility do not vote against it.

Confidence, however, does not mean that the influence equilibrium stays the same. Asked which power will affect developments in global shipping the most in the years ahead, 76​ percent​​​ of our respondents point to the East, meaning China and India, while 17​ percent​​​ choose the West. China is rated the leading shipbuilding nation by 69​ percent​​​, the operator of the most competitive fleet by 62​ percent​​​ and a near-universal 96​ percent​​​ ​​call its role important for ​​strengthening ​​global shipping. Trust, though, has not moved East with the tonnage. Only 17​ percent​​​ rate Chinese ship management highly, while traditional maritime powers such as Greece, Norway​​ and Germany continue to be recognized as the industry’s superior managers.

The same shift appears when executives rate the world’s leaders. Xi Jinping​, the president of China,​ stands alone at the top with a net favourability (percent of positive minus percent of negative views) of ​​+44, ahead of Narendra Modi​, the prime minister of India,​ at +24, while the bottom of the ranking is crowded with political leaders at the cent​er​​​ of today’s wars and confrontations. For an industry that plans in decades, predictability seems to weigh more than political alignment, and maritime leaders reward the global actors who ensure a more predictable environment.

Nearly half of the industry’s leadership regards turmoil as good for business​​.​

The study’s technology section shows where the next edge will be decided. Shipping’s digital core has advanced from its experimentation phase. Remote monitoring and voyage optimi​z​​​ation are standard equipment, used by over seven in ten companies, while a second wave, predictive maintenance and ​Internet of Things ​​​sensors, is scaling, and a third, ​artificial intelligence (​AI​)​ analytics and digital twins, is only emerging. Each wave reaches roughly half the companies of the one before it. Tradition survives alongside the sensors, since 70​ percent​​​ still track fleet performance with the noon report (a holdover from the age of sail). ​AI​​​ is the divide to watch​:​​​ 65​ percent​​​ of companies already use or pilot AI, yet only 7​ percent​​​ use it extensively​​ and adoption splits along tonnage lines. Among fleets above one million deadweight ​​tonnes, 79​ percent​​​ work with AI, against 50​ percent​​​ in the mid-sized tier. Scale buys data, teams and budgets, the returns compound, and command of AI and cybersecurity will help set the new shipping hierarchy. As one shipowner told us, “Better positioning produces better data, which produces better positioning.”

No such technology will replace shipping crews. The shortage of skilled personnel remains the third most serious problem in the ranking, at 37​ percent​​​, and companies respond with high safety standards, competitive pay, internet access on board and training. Two findings point to a deeper change​:​​​ 72​ percent​​​ of companies intend to employ more women at sea​​ and 74​ percent​​​ now call ESG​ (environment, social, governance)​ performance important to their overall business strategy.

Shipping keeps working even when the world stops.​ One response from the interviews

Shipping carries about four​-​​​fifths of world trade, so the way its leaders think matters far beyond the industry. What they told us at the peak of a crisis is that volatility is now structural, that the cent​er​​​ of maritime gravity is shifting East, and that they plan to keep moving through whatever comes. Governments, corporations and international organi​z​​​ations facing the same instability have lessons to draw from ​their​​​ resilience.

​​The full Global Shipping Outlook 2026 report is available ​here​​.

​​A special thanks to LAROS by Prisma Electronics SA for their insights and support in this year’s study.​

World.title: Britain told EU citizens to trust its settled status system. Then it mixed up identical twins.
World.content:
The eVisa database keeps a record of a person’s full name, date of birth, nationality, and a facial photograph. But these traits are by definition often a very close match for identical twins, including Webb, whose name is similar to that of her sister.

Many such cases

Monique Hawkins, acting CEO of the3million, which campaigns for the rights of EU citizens living in the U.K., said problems with the eVisa system sometimes left people unable to prove their identity when they needed it most.

“We have seen many cases where someone else’s immigration status is entangled with another person’s eVisa account. We had hoped, after repeatedly raising this issue, that the Home Office had taken more steps to prevent it happening. It just shows how, despite claims that the eVisa system is highly resilient, it can fail people at the critical moments they need it to work,” she said.

Hawkins said it was “crucial that people have a genuinely stable means by which to prove their status” and described the digital-only system as “rushed,” adding: “We regularly see people not only denied boarding, but also compensation, as carriers and the Home Office play a blame game shifting responsibility between each other.”

While a Home Office spokesperson did not dispute Webb’s account, they defended the eVisa system, arguing it had worked for many people.

“Over 10 million people have already successfully used eVisas to prove their immigration status,” the spokesperson said. “As we expand our digital system, we are committed to data accuracy and ensuring that the safeguards in place to support eVisa users are accessible to anyone reliant on the digital system. In the rare cases where errors are identified, the majority of cases are resolved within 24 hours.”

World.title: Ukraine widens its targets — and its tolerance for causing civilian casualties
World.content:
The numbers help illustrate the change. In 2025, Ukrainian attacks inside Russia killed 253 civilians, according to the United Nations, which says it was not able to independently verify the numbers. This year, in the month of July alone, Russian authorities reported that 79 civilians were killed and 601 injured, a marked increase in the casualty rate.

Zelenskyy has said that Wildberries is a legitimate target because it has been “used by the aggressor to ensure the supply of sanctioned components for the production of drones and navigation equipment.” Russian soldiers supplement their equipment by purchasing items from Wildberries.

Maryana Bezuhla, a Ukrainian lawmaker and one of the most outspoken critics of Zelenskyy and Ukraine’s military leadership, is unapologetic about the increased risk to civilians. “Russia’s logistics system is used to wage the war of aggression against Ukraine,” she told POLITICO. “Russia has been targeting Ukrainian civilians all the years of the war.”

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has denied accusations from Ukraine that Wildberries handles military supplies but conceded to journalists that “the situation is indeed difficult” for the company.

Dmitry Peskov attends a meeting at the Kremlin in Moscow on June 3, 2026. | Pool photo by Ramil Sitdikov via AFP/Getty Images

There is no indication that Ukraine is deliberately targeting civilians — even as Russia continues to hit apartment buildings, hospitals, schools and other civilian infrastructure with ballistic missiles and drones. And yet, there is no indication that the rising civilian toll in Russia is causing Kyiv to reconsider its approach.

“It is a very important thing to stress from the outset, that any civilian casualties resulting from Ukrainian attacks are collateral damage,” said Jaroslava Barbieri, Ukraine expert at Britain’s Chatham House. “No Ukrainian strikes have deliberately targeted civilian districts.”

World.title: Germany’s establishment has a plan to contain the far right. Sort of.
World.content:
As premier, one of Siegmund’s earliest duties would be to take over the annually rotating chair position of the regular conferences of Germany’s 16 state premiers. The role usually comes with a visit to Berlin and a joint appearance with the chancellor before the press.

Calling this uncharted territory would be an understatement. “The AfD is questioning the fundamental decisions made by the Federal Republic of Germany since 1949,” Merz once said.

The chancellor is not alone in his concern. All other major parties, and large parts of the German media, see the AfD as a threat to the country’s liberal postwar order. Yet, if the party takes power in a state for the first time, the political establishment will no longer be able to keep it at arm’s length. While normal relations may be out of the question, at least for the foreseeable future, Germany’s federal system requires a minimum of cooperation and mutual support.

So how would the German establishment deal with a state governed by the AfD?

POLITICO put this question to officials in the federal government and several state governments. The reluctance to answer was striking, especially among Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union and their Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union. Senior party figures and state ministers either refused to comment or would not be quoted by name.

The hesitation is understandable. The CDU and the CSU once owned the political space to the right of center. Today, the AfD is eating into it. State ministers from both the Social Democrats and the Greens were more prepared to discuss strategy on the record.

World.title: The UK assisted dying bill is coming back. Its Labour champion is looking to Australia for inspiration
World.content:
Though Edwards argues her own legislation is “preferable and has stronger safeguards” than the Australian model — unbearable suffering is not a criterion for eligibility in her bill — she found it helpful to see how assisted dying has worked in practice the last time British MPs tackled this issue.

It’s an experience from which many in Labour still bear the scars — and on which new Prime Minister Andy Burnham already appears to have drawn a line in the sand.

Stepping forward

MPs passed fellow Labour backbencher Kim Leadbeater’s Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill last year by 314 votes to 291. But it failed to become law after delays in the U.K.’s House of Lords.

Now Edwards is reintroducing the bill — and is adamant that the groundbreaking social change can succeed this time around.

It means that next month, the House of Commons will once again be thrust into a divisive vote on a matter of conscience, deciding whether to legalize assisted dying in England and Wales for terminally ill adults judged as having fewer than six months left to live.

“When Kim’s bill came up, I did have conversations with my dad about how things have gone in Australia,” Edwards says. The situation reassured her compared to “more extreme examples” like Canada, where a terminal condition is not required for patients to be eligible, but instead an irreversible, “advanced state of decline” and “unbearable physical or mental suffering.”

World.title: Zelenskyy: Elections would ‘tear Ukraine apart’
World.content:
His remarks come after former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov — ousted from his government role in July following a controversial reshuffle — called for elections earlier this week.

“If our partners offer us specific conditions under which elections can be held … safely, legitimately and democratically,” with the participation of soldiers on the front line and citizens who fled to other countries to escape the war, “then let’s discuss it,” Zelenskyy continued. But “it is impossible under the conditions we have right now, when Putin refuses to agree to any form of ceasefire,” he argued.

Fedorov has emerged as a rival to the current president. In a video address Tuesday, he argued that “people cannot endlessly live in a state where they do not understand why certain decisions are made.”

But his appeal has been criticized by both Zelenskyy allies and opposition members: Elections — which are suspended under Ukraine’s martial law, in place since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022 — would only strengthen the Kremlin’s position and sow division. “I have genuinely had, and continue to have, a very positive attitude toward Mykhailo,” the president said of Fedorov. “We have been through a lot together. “But I believe that he is either going himself – or is being pushed – toward the wrong things.”

Fedorov seems undeterred and doubled down in comments to the BBC on Sunday, saying he has a “moral right” to raise the topic of elections. “If I cannot share my ideas and be open about them with my own society, then what are we fighting for?”

World.title: Owner of Swiss bar in deadly New year blaze held for domestic abuse, media say
World.content:
The owner of the Swiss bar ravaged by a deadly New Year fire is in pre-trial detention, accused of domestic abuse against his wife and co-owner of the establishment, media reported on Sunday.

 

French couple Jacques and Jessica Moretti have been the focus of intense scrutiny since the fire ripped though their bar Le Constellation, in the Crans-Montana ski resort in the early hours of 1 January.

The blaze killed 41 people, most of them teenagers, injuring 115 other people.

The Morettis are among 16 people facing criminal investigation in the case. They face charges including manslaughter by negligence and arson by negligence over the fire.

Jacques Moretti has now been arrested and detained following alleged violence against his wife earlier this month, local Geneva broadcaster Léman Bleu reported.

People light candles and place floral tributes outside the sealed off Le Constellation bar in Crans-Montana, 3 January, 2026 AP Photo

The incident reportedly happened on the night of 11 August at the couple's home in Switzerland's southwestern Wallis canton and was so serious that Jessica Moretti had to be hospitalised.

Neither the public prosecutor's office nor the couple's lawyers responded immediately to requests for comment.

However, the Moretti's lawyers released a statement on Sunday evening referring to the report, stressing that the alleged events were being investigated in a separate case pertaining "exclusively to their private life."

"They should not be confused with the Constellation tragedy," the lawyers said in the statement.

They added though that the reported events "nevertheless fall within a context that cannot be ignored: that of a particularly intense ordeal that the Morettis have been trying to face together since 1 January."

World.title: Can the EU fight underwater threats? Ask the Euronews AI chatbot
World.content:
Water Matters

Europe's water is under increasing pressure. Pollution, droughts, floods are taking their toll on our drinking water, lakes, rivers and coastlines. Join us on a journey around Europe to see why protecting ecosystems matters, how our wastewater can be better managed, and to discover some of the best water solutions. Video reports, an animated explainer series and live debate - find out why Water Matters, from Euronews.

World.title: Iceland's moment of reckoning: What the referendum means for the EU
World.content:
Icelanders have been called to vote on whether to resume negotiations to join the European Union, or shelve the prospect of full membership for the foreseeable future.

 

The August 29 vote has been framed by the Icelandic government as a "now or never" opportunity to embrace the prospect of EU membership, or maintain the country's status quo in the European Economic Area, a position that guarantees Reykjavík access to the European single market but not a seat at Brussels' table.

Crucially, the referendum will only decide whether Iceland resumes talks with Brussels. Any decision to formally join the EU could require a second referendum, potentially as early as 2028.

"It is quite clear that this vote is about getting a mandate to negotiate," Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir said in the national parliament in May. "I do not think we should be getting hung up on rhetoric here. We are going to conclude a good agreement. The people will have the first say in this and they will have the last say in this."

Euronews breaks down what happens in both scenarios.

Why now?

Iceland's relationship with the EU has been far from linear. The island country applied to join the bloc in 2009, following a deep financial crisis. Accession negotiations were eventually suspended when a Eurosceptic coalition came to power in 2013.

By then, Iceland's economy had recovered strongly, removing one of the main incentives for joining, and public support for EU membership had faded as negotiations got stuck on the sensitive issue of fisheries.

As a result, in 2015 the Icelandic government told Brussels it had no intention of resuming the accession talks, and that Iceland was no longer to be regarded as a candidate country.

The reversal came in 2024, when a pro-EU coalition government took office. Its coalition agreement included a commitment to hold a referendum on whether to resume the accession talks before 2027.

Since then, major geopolitical developments have reshaped the international landscape, with US President Donald Trump threatening to seize Greenland — at times mistaking it for Iceland — and the Arctic becoming a hotspot for rare earth minerals and new trade routes.

In a report published earlier this year, Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir wrote that "the international system we have lived with since the end of the Second World War is shaking," adding that deeper cooperation with the EU was "a key variable" in safeguarding Iceland's interests.

Still, the decision to hold a referendum was made before these shifts in international politics, and considerations regarding Iceland's defence alliances and security have yet to make their way into a campaign that remains largely focused on economic issues.

How is the referendum campaign going?

Opinion polls suggest the vote could go down to the wire.

A July poll by Maskína put support for "Yes" at 53% and "No" at 47%, suggesting that turnout could be pivotal in determining the outcome.

Another poll by Gallup earlier this month found that 46% of voters supported 'Yes', 46% supported 'No' and 8% were undecided.

While the vote has been framed as crucial against the backdrop of a shifting geopolitical landscape, bread-and-butter issues such as farming and fishing have emerged as voters' top concerns.

Fishing has become a central and sensitive part of the debate, not only for economic reasons — fish and marine products account for around 40% of Iceland’s exports — but also because control over the country’s territorial waters is deeply tied to national sovereignty and identity.

The main sticking point in any future negotiations would likely be Iceland's relationship with the EU's Common Fisheries Policy (CFP), which sets catch limits and fishing quotas among EU member states.

Iceland's main fishing industry federation, SFS, has said that EU membership would leave Iceland without "the power to act as an independent coastal state".

Icelandic government figures have acknowledged that the chapters covering agriculture and fisheries are likely to be the most difficult to close. The accession process was suspended in 2013 before a formal negotiating position on fisheries had been adopted.

An Icelandic government report on the matter points to "issues such as formal authority over marine resources, limitations to investments and advocacy at international level."

The dispute was particularly acute over mackerel, the so-called "mackerel wars," because Iceland had adopted a unilateral position on mackerel quotas that the EU considered excessive, while Iceland objected to arrangements reached between the EU, Norway and the Faroe Islands.

What happens if 'Yes' wins?

Crucially, a "Yes" vote would not mean Iceland joins the bloc; it would jump-start intense negotiations with Brussels on the conditions under which the Nordic country would become a new member state.

In practice, that would require the European Commission to establish a task force similar to the one already in place for the current frontrunner in EU accession talks, Montenegro, putting further pressure on an already strained enlargement machinery.

"Should Icelanders choose to pursue EU membership, Iceland would certainly be a frontrunner in this process," EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said, commenting on the referendum.

Iceland has already closed 11 of the 33 chapters that make up the accession negotiations, with Brussels expecting the process to conclude within one or two years since the country is already deeply integrated in the European single market.

Still, the main sticking point — fisheries — is bound to remain.

"Accession negotiations always reflect the specific realities of each candidate country," European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos wrote on Bluesky, suggesting Brussels might be open to finding common ground on the sensitive issue.

Reykjavik is highly likely to seek special arrangements or exemptions from the CFP, which Brussels may be forced to contemplate in the negotiations. Yet this could also open a Pandora's box, with Irish fishing organisations now calling for the same exemptions for its industry as any granted to Iceland under future accession talks.

The Commission has made enlargement a top political priority. Iceland's formal decision to resume accession talks would give the enlargement agenda welcome momentum, adding geographical and economic balance to the roster of prospective members — and possibly making the ratification process easier to swallow for the most sceptical member states.

What happens if 'No' wins?

A “no” vote would be a setback for the EU’s expansion drive, which has gathered momentum over the past four years following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the Trump administration's erratic foreign policy agenda that projected Brussels as an anchor of stability.

EU officials reined back public commentary on the referendum in order to avoid appearing to interfere in Reykjavík's affairs. But privately, there is acknowledgement that a green light to negotiations would be a major boost to its policy of enlargement.

A "No" vote would also suggest that the prospect of EU membership remains insufficiently attractive to wealthier, northern states, especially as a coalition of Nordic countries is seeking to reduce Brussels' budget as part of intense negotiations.

Unlike Iceland, the EU’s other candidate countries are poorer than the bloc’s existing members, with markedly lower GDP per capita levels.

Iceland itself has also framed the vote as a pivotal decision, meaning a “no” vote would silence the debate around the country’s prospective EU membership for years or even decades, as PM Frostadóttir and the ruling pro-European parties would suffer a major defeat, whilst anti-EU forces would be bolstered.

A negative response would be particularly burning, since voters would not reject EU membership, but even to find out what a membership deal would look like.

For Brussels, it would mean a major setback in its enlargement momentum and also close off a strategic opportunity to expand its positioning in the North Atlantic and Arctic region for generations.

A "No" vote would also raise fresh questions about how Reykjavík can use the current frameworks to deepen cooperation with the EU on issues like security and defence in a shifting geopolitical landscape.

World.title: Dog Stars and Dark Matter: The best things to do, hear, see or watch in Europe this week
World.content:
As we near the end of August, a new season approaches — but don't go ordering any pumpkin spiced lattes just yet.

 

The remains of summer are still lingering, and bring with them more unusual exhibitions, mind-bending TV series, and blockbuster action.

From Apple TV+'s second season of the multiverse thriller Dark Matter, to the release of Interpol's hauntingly introspective new studio album, this week's releases give us something to get stuck into as the summer sun slowly begins to wane.

In case you missed it, there's also our list of the best exhibitions to see in Europe — some of which end soon, so make haste! And for the contrarian music lovers out there, our ranking of the most overrated albums is not so much a recommendation, but might inspire some re-listening.

Until next time, here are your upcoming highlights.

Exhibitions and events

Asta Nørregaard: Truth and Beauty

Asta Nørregaard, "Maggie ready to travel", 1881 Photo: National Museum / Jacques Lathion

When: Until 18 October

Where: National Museum (Oslo, Norway)

In the late 19th century, Asta Nørregaard became one of Norway's most famous portrait artists. After studying in Germany, she went on to paint everyone from her fellow artist Edvard Much, to Norwegian monarch King Hakoon VII; each subject depicted with delicate detail and pastel-hued personality. These form the crux of The National Museum's exhibition, which also highlights Nørregaard's keen eye for fashion and lesser-appreciated religious works. For both fans and the uninitiated, it's an opportunity to experience the breadth of a previously overlooked artist's career — and reappraise its impact. Find out more here.

Jürgen Addiers: I Have No Idea What I Am Doing

When: 27 August - 20 September 2026

Where: M HKA Museum of Contemporary Art (Antwerp, Belgium)

The title of Belgian artist Jürgen Addiers' new exhibition is impossible to forget. Not only does it sit inside a sculpture of metal spheres that hang from the museum's ceiling — it's also a sentence we have all, at some point, felt.

But as Addiers also articulates, that's not such a bad thing. The unknown is a freedom of sorts; a place where experimentation is most possible and imagination can grow. Through his mixed media, absurd collages and abstract installations, a blend of humour and doubt emerge that, together, acknowledge the strange juxtapositions of existence. Find out more here.

Bonus highlight: Fans of Monet and Renoir should visit the National Gallery's 'Painting Side by Side' exhibition in London, which ends 15 September.

Movies

The Dog Stars

Where: Cinemas

When: 28 August

After a virus wipes out most of humanity, a pilot named Hig (Jacob Elordi) sets up fort in an abandoned airport hangar with his dog and weapon-wielding friend, Brangley (Josh Brolin). Amidst avoiding violent scavengers and grappling with trauma, a mysterious radio message brings hope — setting Hig on a treacherous journey into the unknown. Based on a post-apocalyptic book of the same name by Peter Heller, Ridley Scott steers this action-packed film adaptation that also stars Margaret Qualley, Guy Pearce and Allison Janney.

Bonus highlight: Gregg Araki's I Want Your Sex, a bombastic ode to exploring pleasure, is released in UK and Ireland cinemas

TV series

Dark Matter (season 2)

Where: Apple TV+

When: 28 August

Based on the bestselling 2016 book by Blake Crouch, Dark Matter follows a physicist named Jason Dessen (Joel Edgerton), whose entire life is suddenly upended when he's abducted into an alternate reality. A contemplation on existence, identity, and the veil between our choices and life paths, this compelling series makes the multiverse a metaphor for confronting deeper psychological fears. Season 2 sees its characters venture stray from the original source material — and cements Apple TV+ as the current kings of sci-fi TV.

Bonus highlight: The fifth and final season of teen mystery series Outer Banks is out now on Netflix.

Music

Interpol: This Mirror Weighs a Ton

When: 28 August

American post-punk band Interpol return with their eighth studio album, a follow up to 2022's 'The Other Side of Make-Believe'. Layered with intricate instrumentals, wandering harmonies and low-fi laments, it's a frequently haunting collection of tracks that feels ambient and calm — like slipping into a gentle abyss. It's also one of the band's most experimental efforts yet.

Bonus highlights: The darkwave sounds of American artists Boy Harsher return with their fourth album, ‘Get Mean’, released on 28 August. For a different, rockier vibe, Alabama Shakes' 'I Must Be Dreaming' is out the same day.

World.title: DR Congo and M23 fighters agree to roadmap for peace talks, Switzerland says
World.content:
The Democratic Republic of Congo and the Rwanda-backed M23 armed group have agreed to a roadmap for peace talks, according to a joint statement published on Sunday.

 

"The Parties developed a roadmap setting out sequenced steps and timelines for negotiations under the Doha Framework Agreement and committed to flexibility and creativity within the existing structure," the statement published by Switzerland, which had hosted the negotations, said.

"They reaffirmed their commitment to pursue negotiations towards comprehensive peace and conflict resolution through the implementation of the Framework Agreement," it added.

The two sides signed a US-brokered framework agreement last year in the Qatari capital Doha, but fighting has continued since, prompting both to gather in Switzerland last week for a new round of talks.

ormer members of the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of Congo (FARDC) and police officers who allegedly surrendered to M23 rebels arrive in Goma, 23 February, 2025 AP Photo

The closed-door talks took place from 17-21 August, bringing together representatives from the United States, Qatar, Switzerland, the African Union Commission and Togo, which served as African Union mediator.

The two sides said they had "agreed on the importance of a standardised method for reporting allegations of ceasefire violations," with a first ceasefire verification mission due in Minembwa in DRC's South Kivu Provnce on Monday.

Both also agreed to create a "mechanism tasked with reviewing progress and addressing challenges in implementation of obligations and commitments under the Doha Framework Agreement."

Multiple armed groups have fought over territories in Eastern DRC, which are rich in minerals critical to much of the world’s technology, including the Rwandan-backed M23, which seized large swathes of the region last year.

World.title: Indian police used excessive force during protests, Amnesty International says
World.content:
Indian police used excessive force, including electric shock devices and pellet guns, against youth-led protests that forced the education minister to resign last month, Amnesty International said on Monday.

 

A report from the rights' group clashes with the police account that force was used only after protesters turned violent, and comes after India's Supreme Court set up a panel on Thursday to investigate violence by both police and demonstrators.

Demonstrations in the capital New Delhi, triggered by the leak of the national medical entrance test, turned violent on 20 July when thousands of protesters attempted to march towards parliament.

Amnesty said witness testimony and visual evidence it had verified confirmed the use of "pellet-firing shotguns, tear gas launchers, grenades, batons and electric shock devices against protesters" in Delhi and the eastern state of Bihar.

Amnesty said it had also verified two instances of a police officer "unlawfully using lethal force against a crowd" in Bihar's Siwan district. No one was killed.

Protesters chant slogans during a demonstration demanding educational reforms in New Delhi, 24 July, 2026 AP Photo

"The weapons were deployed in a manner that breached international law and standards and domestic policing guidelines," it added.

Amnesty said that there were "isolated incidents of protesters throwing stones," but that the "heavy-handed response was state-sanctioned violence masked as crowd control."

Delhi Police said in a Supreme Court hearing last week they had used force only after protesters "resorted to violence."

They said anti-social elements "masquerading as aggrieved students" caused "grievous injuries" to security forces.

On Friday, opposition leader Rahul Gandhi staged a sit-in outside a Delhi police station with a 19-year-old protester who said he was injured by pellets during the July demonstration.

Gandhi demanded a police investigation into the shooting and officers later registered a case over the complaint.

Led by the online Cockroach Janta Party, the protests broadened from anger over exam irregularities into a wider movement over unemployment, opportunities for young people and what critics describe as Prime Minister Narendra Modi's increasingly authoritarian rule.

The protests proved to be the biggest challenge that Modi has faced after winning a third term in 2024.

World.title: ‘Nature makes every colour in the world’: Meet the company brewing an end to toxic chemical dyes
World.content:
The fashion industry is among the most polluting on the planet, and dyeing fabric a big reason why. The process consumes huge volumes of water, energy and chemicals, leaving a lasting mark on the environment.

 

"The industry uses upward of 70 highly toxic chemicals in the dyeing process," Orr Yarkoni, CEO and co-founder of Colorifix, tells Euronews Earth.

He explains that this figure covers not just the dyes themselves but the additional chemicals needed to help colour bond to fabric. "Over 30 of them are irretrievable, meaning no matter what you do to the water after you use them, they stay in the water, so they'll end up in the ocean."

According to Yarkoni, the industry's reliance on synthetic dyes dates back to the 19th century, when manufacturers shifted away from natural alternatives.

"The industry moved to using cheap, effective chemistry that unfortunately proves to be quite toxic for life in general, including humans," he says. Moving away from these chemicals has proven slow, largely due to a lack of viable alternatives that can operate at scale.

Colorifix creates dyes using biology instead of chemistry The Earthshot Prize

Brewing colour like beer

Colorifix's approach borrows directly from nature's own methods of producing pigment, without extracting it from plants or animals. "We borrow the information of how the pigment or dye stuff is made in nature," Yarkoni tells Euronews Earth.

The company inserts that genetic code into bacteria, which are then grown in fermentation tanks. "Very similar to how you make beer, but instead of alcohol, we're brewing the colour," he explains.

Once harvested, the biological dye – along with the biomass used to help it bond to fabric – replaces the synthetic chemicals typically used in the dyeing process.

Yarkoni says this delivers significant environmental savings, citing figures specific to polycotton: "We're seeing upward of 77 per cent savings in water, 51 per cent savings in energy, and 31 per cent savings in emissions by doing things biologically."

He is careful to stress that natural origin does not automatically mean a product is safe. "Natural does not mean non-toxic," he says, noting that Colorifix tests every dye it produces for cytotoxicity, skin irritation and allergenicity, going beyond standard testing required for synthetic dyes.

"We don't want to repeat the mistakes of the past of pushing with something that looks good and causes serious problems down the line."

Producing dyes that meet the performance demands of the textile industry has also been a challenge. Colours must resist fading in sunlight, survive repeated washing and not rub off onto skin.

"We developed hundreds of colours," Yarkoni says, adding that Colorifix now offers a full colour range for synthetic fibres such as polyester, with a more limited but growing palette for cotton and other cellulosic fabrics.

Bacteria can produce a wide range of colours The Earthshot Prize

From lab to industry

Colorifix has moved beyond research and into commercial use, with major fashion brands adopting the technology, according to Yarkoni. The company has also begun shipping its dyes as ready-to-use concentrates, rather than requiring manufacturers to install fermentation equipment on site.

"We're releasing these products now as concentrates... that means we can ship the product ready to use in the dye machine without having to do any additional processing on site," he says.

Yarkoni credits Colorifix's recognition as an Earthshot Prize finalist with raising the company's profile among manufacturers and brands. "It's helped really highlight our solution to the problem and bring more awareness to brands and manufacturers," he says. "We've had outreach from all over the world following the exposure."

Looking ahead, Yarkoni argues that petrochemicals should be reserved for uses where no natural alternative exists, rather than applied broadly across industries such as fashion: "Colour is one of the worst things to make out of petrochemicals because nature makes every colour in the world, and rivers still run clean".

World.title: LAX, JFK, DXB: Everything you need to know about airport codes
World.content:
While airport codes used to be something you’d only see on your boarding pass and luggage tags, nowadays, the three letters are absolutely everywhere. You can rep your home city with phone cases, décor, t-shirts… I’ve even seen airport code shoelaces.

 

But have you ever stopped to wonder how those three letters were chosen, or why we need them in the first place?

With airport codes hitting the headlines as Palm Beach International Airport changes to DJT following its renaming after current president Donald J. Trump, we thought it was time for a deep dive…

What is an airport code, and what is it used for?

An airport code is a unique three-letter geocode that corresponds to a single airport around the globe.

The geocodes are assigned by the International Air Transport Association (IATA), and there are around 11,300 in the IATA Airline Coding Directory. These codes aren't just assigned to airports, either – they can also be used for heliports, rail stations and bus stations.

Introduced in the 1930s, airport codes were originally just two letters but became three in the 1940s as the number of airports grew.

“These universal codes are essential to the functioning of the aviation and travel industries, ensuring that systems involved in reservations, scheduling, ticketing, cargo documentation, and other operations speak the same language,” the IATA notes on its website.

How are airport codes chosen?

Around 40 to 50 codes are newly assigned annually.

The standard procedure is to use the first three letters of the location’s name, but if that is already taken, the airport will need to choose an unassigned combination that preferably starts with the first letter of the location’s name.

For example, Amsterdam Airport Schiphol’s IATA airport code is AMS, Frankfurt International Airport’s is FRA, and Dublin Airport’s is DUB, while Dubai International Airport is DXB, because DUB was already taken.

It worked out in Dubai’s favour, though, as the airport is commonly known by its code, much like JFK in New York or LAX.

Some airport codes instead come from the airport’s name, as is the case with Paris Charles de Gaulle Airport (CDG) or Stockholm Arlanda Airport (ARN).

Exceptions to the rule

Notable exceptions to the rule include Canadian airports, where the code for most major airports starts with Y.

This is because when deciding the three-letter codes, it was decided to use the two letter code from before alongside a Y at the front if the area had a weather station.

That’s how we’ve ended up with codes like YOW for Ottawa and YVR for Vancouver.

Why do airport codes change?

While the IATA notes that airport codes “are considered permanent and are almost never changed”, over the past 12 months, some 750 changes have been made.

Some examples of airports that have changed code include Don Mueang International Airport, which was originally known as Bangkok International Airport and had the code BKK. Its code is now DMK, while Suvarnabhumi Airport, the busier airport serving the Thai capital which opened in 2006, is now BKK.

John F. Kennedy International Airport was originally known as Idlewild Airport, and had the code IDL. It adopted the code JFK when it was renamed after the late president in 1963.

You can browse all of the world’s airport codes on the IATA website.

World.title: Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan strengthen ties as Israel tensions rise
World.content:
Tensions between Turkey and Israel have intensified after an Israeli airstrike targeted a Syrian military airbase near the Turkish border. The strike came days after Turkey’s new military pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.

Advertising

Ankara swiftly condemned Tuesday's Israeli airstrike on Syria’s Abu Duhur military airbase, 70 kilometres from its border, calling it illegal and a breach of Syrian sovereignty.

Ankara is a key ally of Syria's new authorities. Israel justified its actions, accusing Turkey of seeking to expand its military footprint in Syria, which it sees as a serious threat.

“Israel is uneasy about the Turkish presence in Syria, and Turkish ambitions to play a major role in Syria’s future are unsettling from an Israeli perspective,” explains Turkey expert Gallia Lindenstrauss of Israel's Institute for National Security Studies.

“There's concern that Turkey will establish its own bases in Syria,” she added.

Israeli-Turkish tensions have risen over Israel’s war in Gaza and Lebanon, and Ankara’s support of Hamas, evolving into a broader regional rivalry.

“In general, there's uneasiness [in Israel] about Turkey's assertiveness, both in Syria and in the Mediterranean and other parts of the Middle East and the greater regional arena," said Lindenstrauss.

Landmark agreement

Earlier this month, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan made headlines by signing a landmark military accord in the Saudi city of Mecca. Known as the Mecca Accord, this alliance pledges mutual defence if any member is attacked, akin to NATO’s Article 5.

Turkish international relations expert Soli Ozel claims the impetus for the agreement is uncertainty around Washington’s willingness or ability to protect its regional allies amid ongoing tensions involving Iran.

“Undoubtedly, the United States is proving to be an increasingly unreliable partner. Countries worldwide, especially in the larger Middle East region, are looking for other ways to provide security for themselves,” said Ozel.

Iran says ‘Muslim Nato’ pact reflects retreat from US security umbrella

The Mecca Accord members view each other as bringing complementary strengths to deal with shared concerns.

"Pakistan brings military capabilities and is a nuclear power. The Saudis have the money. Turkey has a budding defence industry and a large army. It claims not to be against any country, but I think those three parties agree that Iran is a destabilising actor, as is Israel,” explained Ozel.

The Mecca Accord is set to boost defence and intelligence ties, with Saudi Arabia expected to bolster Turkey’s expanding defence sector.

But many analysts see Iran and Israel as the accord’s principal focus.

“The deal is meant to signal both to Iran and Israel that they will be isolated in the region if they continue with assertive, belligerent policies,” said Asli Aydintasbas of the United States-based Brookings Institution.

Turkey steps up as Europe's indispensable and uncomfortable defence partner

'Two axes in the Middle East'

Despite Iran’s recent attacks on Saudi Arabia, Aydintasbas argues that while the Mecca Accord has a mutual defence clause – meaning an attack on one member is an attack on all – Turkey and Pakistan will not be drawn into a conflict with Iran.

“We know that they have no desire to get involved. But it does mean there will be greater military cooperation,” said Aydintasbas.

Countering Houthi rebel attacks in the Red Sea on Saudi tankers could be the first real test of the alliance.

But Aydintasbas cautions that the Mecca Accord will not replace the US as the “ultimate security provider” for the region. Instead, it's more about burden sharing, a move that fits well with Washington’s wider agenda.

Washington has given its blessing to the accord, and expansion talks are already under way.

European Union slams 'inflammatory' Houthi Red Sea tanker attack

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan hinted that Egypt could be the next member, with Turkish media reporting that Egypt’s foreign minister will join his Saudi, Turkish and Pakistani counterparts for a meeting in Istanbul later this month.

“Developments in Egypt are of major concern to Israel,” said Lindenstrauss. But she believes the Mecca Accord is an opportunity for Israel, given there are mutual concerns among its allies over the Accord.

“Israel already has very close relations with Greece, Cyprus, the United Arab Emirates and India,” she noted. "And I do envision a deepening of this relationship. And so we have the formation of two loose axes in the Greater Middle East."

World.content:

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council President Antonio Costa have arrived in Kyiv.

World.title: New Zealand proposes social media ban for under-16s
World.content:
The government is set to follow Australia's lead and introduce a bill banning children from social media. But the plan already faces opposition from within the ruling coalition.

New Zealand's government is set to introduce legislation Monday banning children under the age of 16 from social media, following the lead of several countries across the world, including neighbor Australia.

What does New Zealand's social media ban entail?

The Online Safety Bill would require platforms like Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and Facebook to verify users are 16 or older using tools such as facial age estimation and digital ID, with fines of up to 10% of global revenue for non-compliance.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said the harm to children is too great to ignore.

"We simply cannot accept the harm being done to a generation of New Zealand children," he said, citing effects on mental health, sleep and education. Education Minister Erica Stanford said penalties would apply only to platforms, not families.

When will the bill be introduced?

The bill's future is uncertain, as coalition partners NZ First and ACT have both voiced opposition, questioning the law's effectiveness. Australia's similar ban took effect last year, though a June study found little evidence it reduced teen social media use, AFP reported.

World.title: US: Wildfire forces mass evacuations near Reno, Nevada
World.content:
A wind-driven wildfire has forced roughly 42,000 people to evacuate and destroyed homes as fire crews continue to battle extreme conditions.

A fast-moving, wind-driven wildfire forced tens of thousands of people to evacuate their homes near Reno in the US state of Nevada over the weekend.

An unknown number of homes have been destroyed and at least six people have been injured.

Officials have expanded the "GO NOW" zone to include almost 90,000 residents as conditions make the fire unpredicatable.

What do we know about the Hawk Fire in Nevada?

The fire started Saturday morning off Hawk Meadow Trail and spread rapidly through the Peavine Peak area northwest of the city, growing to between roughly 13,000 and 15,000 acres by Sunday.

About 42,000 residents were ordered to evacuate, with another 45,000 told to be ready to leave, officials said. The evacuation zone stretched to the edge of the University of Nevada in northwest Reno, a city of more than 280,000 people near the California border.

At least six people were injured — three first responders and three civilians — local authorities said. Officials said the fire was human-caused but have not released further details.

"The Hawk Fire is a very dynamic incident for us as it's being driven by the winds. The wind-driven fires move very rapidly into our residential areas," fire chief Richard Edwards told AFP.

Officials say the Hawk Fire was human-caused Image: Trevor Bexon/Getty Images/AFP

Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo declared a state of emergency in Washoe County and mobilized the National Guard, deploying two helicopters and 60 troops to assist firefighting and security efforts. "This is an active and rapidly evolving situation, and I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain vigilant and follow the direction of local officials," he said, according to Reuters.

Human cost of the wildfire

The fire has already destroyed homes. Cari Kieffer told AP her family fled with only minutes to spare, grabbing clothes, a Bible, her wedding photos and her mother's ashes, but leaving behind birth certificates and childhood photos.

"I kept looking outside and the flames just kept getting closer and closer every time I looked," she said. "I was like, we gotta go like now."

"We lost all our stuff. Everything we own is gone."

Can Germany teach Europe how to prevent wildfires? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Nearly 10,000 customers remained without power in Washoe County on Sunday, down from about 60,000 the day before, AP reported. Parts of US Route 395 were closed, two hospitals evacuated patients, and officials monitored whether the county jail would need to be evacuated. The Reno-Tahoe airport remained outside the evacuation zone, with flights operating normally.

The blaze adds to a wave of fire activity across the drought-stricken Western United States this year. Fifteen new fires broke out across Nevada on Saturday alone.

World.title: Norway: King Harald's health has 'deteriorated,' palace says
World.content:
The 89-year-old King of Norway is Europe's oldest reigning monarch. He has been suffering from a blood condition.

The health of Norway's King Harald has "deteriorated" while in the hospital this weekend, the royal household said in a statement on Sunday.

Harald, 89, is being treated for haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by the rapid destruction of red blood cells.

The disorder causes fatigue, weakness, shortness of breath and paleness.

"His Majesty the King's health deteriorated ​over the weekend. The King is ⁠receiving ​antibiotics for ​a bacterial infection in his ​blood, and ‌has responded to this ​treatment," the ⁠palace said. His condition was stable, the statement added.

What else do we know about the health of Norway's king?

Harald was admitted on Monday to Oslo University Hospital because of fluid retention related to cortisone treatment he has been receiving. He was placed on sick leave for two weeks.

The king has also canceled a visit to the Trondelag region in central Norway on September 1 and 2, which fall after the two-week sick leave period.

Members of Harald's family visited the monarch in the hospital [FILE: August 2024] Image: Cornelius Poppe/NTB/POOL/AFP via Getty Images

Several relatives have visited him in hospital on Sunday, including his wife, Queen Sonja, their son Crown Prince Haakon, Haakon's wife Crown Princess Mette-Marit and the king's sister, according to the Verdens Gang newspaper.

Haakon has been acting as regent in his father's absence.

Harald's history of health issues

Harald, who ascended the throne in 1991, is the oldest reigning monarch in Europe.

The king has suffered from numerous health issues in recent years. He has had a pacemaker fitted and has been forced to scale back his official activities and responsibilities.

He was hospitalized with an infection and dehydration in February this year during a private trip with Queen Sonja in Tenerife.

Despite his health issues, he has said he will not abdicate, as he took a lifelong oath before parliament.

Mette-Marit's son's rape trial has dented the royal family's reputation in Norway [FILE: June 2022] Image: Lise Aserud/NTB/AP Photo/picture alliance

Norwegian royals' difficult year

Harald's health is the latest concern for the Norwegian royals, who have been marred by scandal this year.

His son Haakon's wife, Mette-Marit, has been in the headlines for her close ties with late US financier and convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Her son from a previous marriage, Marius Borg Hoiby, was sentenced in June to four years in prison on two counts of rape.

Hoiby has appealed the verdict.

World.title: Kazakhstan parliamentary vote cements president's power
World.content:
Candidates from seven state-approved parties took part in the election, while opposition parties were banned. As Central Asia's largest nation, Kazakhstan maintains a delicate balance between Russia and the West.

Kazakhstan's ruling party comforably won an election for the country's new, single-chamber parliament on Sunday, according to exit polls.

State television shared three exit polls giving the Adilet party between 70% and 72% of the vote.

The vote comes after a new constitution approved in March did away with the Senate to create a new unicameral Kurultai — a reference to the medieval councils of the region's nomadic past.

Backers of the new body say it will give parliament more say in decision making, critics argue it will only cement the power of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.

The 73-year-old took the reins from authoritarian Nursultan Nazarbayev — who himself ruled the country for 30 years after the collapse of the Soviet Union — in 2019.

The constitutional reform also opens the door for President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev to stay in power Image: Turar Kazangapov/REUTERS

The pro-presidential Adilet party was expected to win an overwhelming majority in Sunday's vote, while exit polls showed four smaller parties loyal to Tokayev also won seats in the new parliament.

Seven state-approved parties have been allowed to field candidates for the 145-seat parliament while genuine opposition parties have been banned.

The election took place amid soaring inflation (which is hovering around 10.2%) and rising taxes, fueling concerns for the government — and particularly Tokayev — of a repeat of January 2022 cost of living unrest that left 238 protesters and police dead.

Inequality, corruption led to Kazakhstan unrest To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Press crackdown and financial strain color Kazakhstan's election

Beyond financial strain, Sunday's vote also took place against the background of crackdowns on press freedom, with numerous reporters under house arrest and official criminal cases being brought against 10 independent journalists and bloggers.

Tokayev, a former Soviet official and Kazakh diplomat who worked at the UN, touted his reforms and justified the many changes he has initiated — including the introduction of the new constitution — as necessary in a fast-changing world.

"Without a doubt, these elections will be remembered as perhaps the most interesting in our country's history," said Tokayev on Friday.

"Amid unprecedented geopolitical tensions and mounting global challenges, we must firmly and consistently implement our strategy to transform Kazakhstan into a truly developed state," he added.

Tokayev has sought to maintain a delicate balance between Moscow — with their shared Soviet ties — and the West since sanctions were imposed on Russia over its invasion of Ukraine. Resource-rich and strategically located Kazakhstan also has ties to China and the European Union.

Although Tokayev has said that he has no plans of staying in power beyond his current term, the constitutional reform that 87% of voters backed this March effectively reset term limits for the office — making him eligible to run for another seven-year stint in 2029 should he change his mind.

World.title: Zelenskyy repeats Ukraine not behind Nord Stream attack
World.content:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine was assisting German authorities with their investigation into the Nord Stream explosions. A second Ukrainian national was arrested in connection with the blasts.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy reiterated on Sunday that Ukraine was not involved in the 2022 attack on the Nord Stream underwater gas pipelines.

"Ukraine has never officially taken part in any operation related to the blowing up of Nord Stream," Zelenskyy told reporters on Sunday in response to a question about the ongoing investigation.

He said that Germany was "well aware that Ukraine did not stand behind the execution or the very conception of this operation."

Germany seeks extradition of Nord Stream 2 bombing suspect To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Zelenskyy hopes 'not to lose trust'

German authorities alleged last month that the attack had been ordered by the Ukrainian state, while a second Ukrainian national was also detained over the blasts this week.

Zelenskyy said Ukraine was assisting German authorities with their investigation.

"It is very important for us not to lose our partnership, not to lose the trust of European countries that have been helping Ukraine since the very beginning of this war," he said.

German authorities implicate Ukraine

The Nord Stream 1 pipeline ran under the Baltic Sea and delivered gas from Russia to Germany and other countries in Europe. A second pipeline called Nord Stream 2 was constructed but never went into use.

In September 2022, both pipelines were sabotaged with undersea explosions. No group claimed responsibility for the attack.

Nord Stream: Germany's thwarted dream of energy security To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In early 2026, German authorities detained the first suspect, a Ukrainian national Serhii K., and alleged that he and six accomplices had acted "on the orders of state authorities in Ukraine."

Prosecutors said the plan was to "destroy the Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 pipelines" with the objective of "permanently halting gas supplies via the pipelines and preventing Russia from using the revenue from natural gas trade to finance its war efforts."

World.title: Greece: Migrants clash with police at detention center
World.content:
Clashes broke out between police and people at a migrant detention center in northern Greece, with 35 having escaped the facility before half of them were detained again.

Migrants clashed with police at a detention center in northern Greece, with 35 having escaped the premises after cutting through a perimeter fence before police detained about half of them again, authorities said on Sunday.

Greece is a major point of entry for migrants to Europe, and the country's conservative prime minister has introduced tough rules to deport those who've been denied asylum in the country.

Greece, along with other European Union countries, for example, is in talks with African countries about establishing centers for failed asylum-seekers, a move that has drawn criticism from international rights groups.

Crete fears more migrant arrivals could hurt tourism To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Police deploy flashbangs during clashes

Police said they called for reinforcement to the detention center in Sintiki, a few kilometers from the Bulgarian border, after migrants threw rocks at police.

Authorities used flash-bang grenades against people during those clashes, which they said lasted until the early hours of Sunday morning.

At least five migrants were injured and taken to the hospital. Police recaptured 17 of those who escaped and the search continued for 18 others.

The temporary accommodation center houses about 450 people while their applications are processed, a protracted procedure that can take a long time.

World.title: Guinea: Garbage collapse at landfill kills dozens
World.content:
Heavy seasonal rains caused a mound of garbage to collapse, burying dozens of people and nearby homes before the break of dawn.

At least 30 people have died after a landfill collapsed in Guinea's capital, Conakry, officials said on Sunday.

Heavy rains overnight caused a large mound of rubbish to collapse at the Dar Es Salam landfill, burying nearby homes before dawn.

At least six other people were seriously injured.

Guinea's minister for territorial administration, Djenabou Toure, visited the site, where workers used excavators to search for more bodies.

Workers used earthmovers for as part of the search-and-rescue operation Image: AFP

Landfill was slated for closure

The government had recently ordered the expulsion of nearby residents in informal housing due to a fear of collapses.

Balde Mamadou Bailo, the sanitation officer for the Military Engineering Battalion, said the Dar Es Salam site had been slated for closure on Sunday.

Heavy seasonal rains have been known to trigger collapses at landfills in some countries, with Uganda and Ethiopia suffering similar tragedies in recent years.
