World.title: Exit Polls Put Adilet Party Near 72% in Kazakhstan’s First Kurultai Election
World.content:
ASTANA – The Adilet party was projected to receive around 72% of the vote in Kazakhstan’s inaugural election to the Kurultai on Aug. 23, according to three exit polls released at midnight on Aug. 24. Exit polls, which were announced during a live election night broadcast, also showed four other parties narrowly clearing the threshold for representation in the country’s new unicameral Parliament.

The seven parties contesting the election were Adilet, Respublica, the Auyl People’s Democratic Patriotic Party, the People’s Party of Kazakhstan, the Aq Jol Democratic Party, the Baytaq Green Party and the Nationwide Social Democratic Party.

The three surveys put Adilet’s support between 70.7% and 72.3%, positioning the party for a commanding majority in the new 145-member unicameral Parliament. The figures are preliminary and do not constitute official election results.

According to the Institute of Public Policy, Adilet is expected to get 72.3% of the vote, followed by the Auyl party with 6.2%, Respublica with 5.2%, the Aq Jol Democratic Party with 5.1% and the Nationwide Social Democratic Party (NSDP) with 5%.

The People’s Party of Kazakhstan received 2.8%, while the Baytaq Green Party received 0.9%. Another 2.5% of respondents selected the “against all” option.

A separate exit poll by the Institute of Eurasian Integration put Adilet at 71.8%, Auyl at 6.4%, Respublica at 5.4%, NSDP at 5.2% and Aq Jol at 5.1%. The People’s Party received 3%, Baytaq 1% and “against all” 2.1%.

The Institute for Comprehensive Social Research-Astana, known as SOCIS-A, projected 70.7% for Adilet, 6.4% for Auyl, 5.5% for Respublica, 5.4% for Aq Jol and 5% for NSDP. It put the People’s Party at 3.2%, Baytaq at 1.2% and “against all” at 2.6%.

All three exit polls suggested that five of the seven competing parties had reached the 5% electoral threshold. The People’s Party and Baytaq remained below the threshold in all three polls.

The Central Election Commission (CEC) is expected to announce preliminary results after ballots have been counted. Exit polls survey voters after they leave polling stations and serve only as an early indication of the outcome.

Preliminary CEC figures showed voter turnout at 74.19% when polling stations across Kazakhstan closed at 8 p.m. Sunday. More than 12.6 million citizens were registered to vote at more than 10,000 polling stations nationwide and abroad. The final overseas voting process will conclude at the polling station at Kazakhstan’s Consulate General in San Francisco at 8 a.m. Astana time on Aug. 24.

Sunday’s vote was the first parliamentary election held under the new constitutional system. The election determines the composition of the 145-member Kurultai, which replaced Kazakhstan’s former bicameral Parliament under the new Constitution that took effect July 1. All seats are allocated proportionally through party lists in a single nationwide constituency. Parties must receive at least 5% of the vote to qualify for seats. A total of 545 candidates representing seven political parties contested the election.

Overall, 777 foreign observers from 42 countries and 13 international organizations have been accredited to monitor Kazakhstan’s election.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s First Kurultai Election Concludes With Preliminary Voter Turnout at 74.19%
World.content:
ASTANA – Voting in Kazakhstan’s first elections to the Kurultai concluded at all polling stations across the country at 8 p.m. on Aug. 23, with 9,352,151 voters, or 74.19% of those registered, having received ballots, according to preliminary voter turnout data from the Central Election Commission (CEC).

Polling stations have now closed nationwide, and precinct election commissions have begun counting the ballots. Under Kazakhstan’s election legislation, the vote-counting process may not exceed 12 hours from the start of counting. Territorial election commissions will transmit preliminary voting and counting results to the CEC through electronic channels.

The highest turnout was recorded in the Turkistan Region at 92.16%, followed by the Zhetisu Region at 91.19% and the Kyzylorda Region at 90.75%. Turnout in the Aktobe Region reached 88.30%, while the East Kazakhstan Region recorded 87.50% and the Zhambyl Region 85.18%.

Turnout stood at 82.69% in the Akmola Region, 81.41% in the Abai Region, 77.31% in the North Kazakhstan Region, 76.47% in the Kostanai Region and 76.28% in the Karagandy Region.

Among the cities of national significance, Shymkent recorded 75.42% turnout, Astana 51.67% and Almaty 43.23%.

Other regional figures included 73.38% in West Kazakhstan, 71.38% in the Mangystau Region, 71.20% in the Pavlodar Region, 71.17% in the Almaty Region, 70.74% in the Atyrau Region and 70.72% in the Ulytau Region.

Voting continues at overseas polling stations

Voting abroad is continuing in accordance with local time zones. As of 7 p.m. Astana time, all 79 polling stations established at Kazakhstan’s diplomatic missions and consular offices in 61 countries had opened. Voting had concluded in 11 countries, with 6,007 of the 11,402 registered voters abroad having cast their ballots.

Polling stations in Washington, New York, San Francisco, Ottawa and Brasilia continued operating as of the latest update. Seventy-four overseas polling stations were expected to complete voting by midnight Astana time.

The final overseas voting process will conclude at the polling station at Kazakhstan’s Consulate General in San Francisco at 8 a.m. Astana time on Aug. 24.

Protocols from overseas precinct election commissions will be transmitted to the CEC for inclusion in the overall election results.

Observers assess new parliamentary system

International observers said the election represents more than a change in the structure of Kazakhstan’s legislature. They noted that the new political system, established under the Constitution adopted in 2026, will ultimately be assessed by its ability to strengthen accountability, ensure institutional stability and create a predictable environment for citizens and investors.

The election marks the first vote for Kazakhstan’s new unicameral Kurultai, which will comprise 145 deputies elected through proportional representation in a single nationwide constituency.

The CEC will announce preliminary election results at a dedicated briefing, with the time to be communicated separately.

World.title: Observers See Unicameral Parliament as Boost for Stability and Investment
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s transition to a unicameral parliament and the implementation of its new constitutional framework were among the key issues raised by foreign observers during the parliamentary vote taking place on Aug. 23. The country’s prospects for attracting international investment were also a major focus of their discussions.

For international observers, the election to Kurultai, a new unicameral parliament, established under the Constitution adopted in 2026, represents more than a change in the structure of Kazakhstan’s legislature. They said the new political system will ultimately be judged by its ability to strengthen accountability, ensure institutional stability and create a predictable environment for citizens and investors.

Indonesian Ambassador to Kazakhstan Rachman Mohamad Fadjroel said the country’s Constitution provides the foundation for its ongoing political reforms.

“I believe the most important point in Kazakhstan is its Constitution, because this is the vision for the future of the country. Article 1 defines Kazakhstan as a democratic, secular, social and law-based state,” Fadjroel told The Astana Times.

He said the reforms underway are guided by these constitutional principles and demonstrate Kazakhstan’s commitment to democratic development.

“Today’s Kurultai election is an opportunity to demonstrate how democracy works in Kazakhstan in practice,” he said, adding that the country’s election has sent a positive message to the international community.

Unicameral parliament as a new political chapter

Domenico Palmieri, secretary general of the Italian Institute of Asia, described the election as a milestone for Kazakhstan, calling it the first major step in implementing the country’s new constitutional framework.

In an interview with The Astana Times, he said the transition to a unicameral parliament could streamline the legislative process and facilitate political reforms.

“From my point of view, a unicameral system is better. It is easier to work smartly and efficiently,” Palmieri said, adding that its effectiveness will ultimately depend on the performance of the new parliament and government.

“Only the future, starting from today, with the new parliament and government, can show whether this was the right decision taken by the Kazakh people,” he said.

He also noted that five Italian parliamentarians were observing the election in the Almaty Region.

“This shows the interest and attention of Italy toward the Kazakh nation,” Palmieri said.

He added that the new constitutional arrangements should now be translated into practical policies that contribute to social stability and economic development.

Clearer institutions could support investment

Nicolas Butylin, head of geopolitics at Berliner Zeitung, Germany’s daily newspaper, spoke about the implications of the new political system for foreign investors. He said a streamlined institutional structure could make it easier to understand where decisions are made and how checks and balances operate.

He described the Kurultai as another step in the country’s institutional development, stressing that the country should be assessed against its own progress rather than measured solely against Western democracies.

“I would not compare Kazakhstan to Western European democracies. I don’t think this is the benchmark. The more useful question, from my perspective, is to compare Kazakhstan with the state of Kazakhstan 10 years ago. To see if, with the new Kurultai, the system is more open, more accountable and more competitive,” Butylin said.

He noted that for Western businesses considering investment in Kazakhstan, institutional evolution and predictability would remain key factors.

Butylin also emphasized Kazakhstan’s growing importance to Germany and Europe through the Middle Corridor, particularly amid disruptions to established trade routes.

“From this perspective, especially in the economic part with natural resources, Kazakhstan will play a crucial role for the future of Germany as well,” he said.

Glenn Agung Hole, professor at the University of Southeast Norway and an expert in economics and international relations, noted that the parliament’s ability to provide legislative stability would be critical for business.

“From an economic perspective, the new Kurultai is important because they need to make stable laws. And business, finance and the stock exchange need to see that taxes and laws are followed through,” Hole said.

He emphasized that international investors need confidence that the rules governing their investments will remain predictable over time.

“We have to see stability over time. At least three to five years, international investors need to see that they can put their investment here and that it will be safe for the next three to five years and longer,” he said.

Kazakhstan’s strategic role in China-West trade

Ken Moriyasu, a senior researcher at the Washington D.C.-based Hudson Institute, placed Kazakhstan’s political reforms within a broader geopolitical and investment context.

“When it comes to investment, it’s important to understand the players involved here. China clearly is the biggest investor,” Moriyasu said.

He described Kazakhstan as a key partner for China as Beijing is seeking to reduce its reliance on maritime routes and expand overland connections.

“Political stability is very important,” he said, noting that Kazakhstan’s vast territory and strategic location make it an important component of these routes.

Moriyasu also emphasized that the development of overland corridors through Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan and Türkiye does not necessarily conflict with U.S. interests.

“It is very beneficial for the United States that China creates these land transport corridors, but the countries that these corridors pass through remain friends with America,” he said.

The Kurultai vote continues in Kazakhstan with 10,423 polling stations operating across the country. The Kurultai will have 145 seats elected for five-year term. A total of 777 foreign observers from 42 countries and 13 international organizations have been accredited to monitor Kazakhstan’s election.

World.title: Tokayev Says Vice President Appointment Expected Within 10 Days
World.content:
ASTANA – President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said the new Vice President is expected to be appointed within the next week or 10 days, speaking to media representatives after casting his ballot in the country’s first elections to the Kurultai on Aug. 23.

Responding to questions about the reforms and the changes expected after the Kurultai and the Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi (People’s Council) begin their work, Tokayev described the newly established Vice President position as a significant and necessary institutional change.

“We deliberately established this new position in the Constitution. I would not be mistaken in saying that it is extremely necessary. In the current difficult times, such a position is particularly needed by our country,” Tokayev said.

He said the name of the person who will take the position is expected to become known within the next seven to 10 days, adding that it would be premature to disclose the candidate’s name during the voting process.

“I think this will be a well-known person whom you all know very well,” he said.

Tokayev also highlighted the planned launch of the Kazakhstan Khalyk Kenesi, a new state body that he said would build on the work previously carried out by the Assembly of the People of Kazakhstan. According to him, the new institution will serve as a multifunctional political mechanism as part of the country’s broader reforms.

Tokayev on 2029 presidential election

Asked whether he intends to use his constitutional right to seek another presidential term in 2029, Tokayev said the Constitutional Court’s recent decision confirming his eligibility is lawful, but that discussing his future candidacy would be premature.

“The Constitutional Court made this decision. It is lawful, and I have the legal right to be re-elected. But as for the upcoming elections or, as you put it, whether I will run or not, and in which year, it is premature to speculate on this,” he said.

Tokayev said the government has many tasks to complete before it can address such questions. He also said the government’s composition would change, while stressing that there are currently no grounds for concern about its work.

“Personnel changes are always inevitable because they give the government new strength,” Tokayev said, adding that such changes should be aimed at providing a serious impetus to the government’s work rather than dismissals for their own sake.

Voter turnout exceeds 65.37%

Meanwhile, voter turnout in Kazakhstan’s first elections to the Kurultai reached 65.37% by 4 p.m. on Aug. 23, with 8,240,336 voters having received ballots, according to the Central Election Commission (CEC).

The Kyzylorda Region recorded the highest turnout at 81.38%, followed by East Kazakhstan at 79.33%, Zhetisu Region at 77.03%, and Turkistan Region at 76.73%.

Turnout in the Aktobe Region stood at 75.63%, Akmola Region at 73.69%, Abai Region at 71.18%, Karagandy Region at 70.91% and Kostanai Region at 70.09%.

Among the cities of national significance, turnout reached 67.92% in Shymkent, 46.38% in Astana and 36.65% in Almaty.

Other regional figures were 67.23% in the Almaty Region, 67.06% in Pavlodar Region, 65.86% in Mangystau Region, 64.29% in Ulytau Region, 63.94% in North Kazakhstan, 63.37% in Atyrau Region, 61.81% in West Kazakhstan and 69.11% in the Zhambyl Region.

The CEC will provide the next update on voter turnout at 6 p.m.

World.title: International Observers Deliver Assessment of Kazakhstan’s First Kurultai Vote
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s transition to a single-chamber legislature entered a new stage Aug. 23 as voters went to the polls to elect the country’s first Kurultai, with international observers monitoring the process.

The election is part of a broader effort to modernize Kazakhstan’s political institutions and strengthen their ability to respond to the country’s changing social and economic landscape, Deputy Foreign Minister Arman Issetov said during an Aug. 22 briefing with foreign media.

He noted that Kazakhstan is pursuing political reform not because it is facing a crisis, but because the country is developing and its institutions should be prepared for the next stage of that development.

“We expect that the new political system will help maintain stability and continuity while ensuring the further development of state institutions. It should also provide more effective representation of public interests and improve the quality of decision-making,” Issetov said.

He also linked the reforms to the country’s economic development, saying a more complex economy requires more effective state institutions, predictable legislation and high-quality public administration.

“The more diverse society becomes, the more important it is to have mechanisms that allow for the various public interests to be taken into account. This is one of the main reasons behind the current constitutional reform,” Issetov said.

“It is not aimed at changing for the sake of change. Its objective is to bring political institutions in line with modern Kazakhstan and prepare them for the next stage of the country’s development,” he said.

The election has drawn international attention, with observers from foreign countries and organizations monitoring the electoral process, visiting polling stations and meeting with election officials and political parties. Their assessments offer an international perspective on how the new political system is taking shape in practice.

Shanghai Cooperation Organization

According to SCO Deputy Secretary-General T.R. Midhun, voting was well organized and polling stations were fully prepared.

“We went to the polling stations when they opened. We saw the procedures and the queues of people who were willing to participate in the election. It was early morning, and people were still very keen to start as early as possible,” he said.

Midhun noted that the mission’s task was to observe all stages of the electoral process and form an objective assessment based on direct observation and factual information. The mission will also monitor the closing of polling stations and procedures required under Kazakhstan’s legislation.

The SCO’s final assessment will be presented at a press conference on Aug. 24, he said.

In an interview with The Astana Times, Midhun said Kazakhstan’s political and economic reforms marked a profound transformation for the country.

“I think and hope that after these reforms Kazakhstan will strengthen its position and potential in the international arena. This, of course, will contribute to the SCO,” he said.

Midhun highlighted Kazakhstan’s role as a founding member of the SCO and praised its contributions in transport, logistics, political relations and cultural cooperation.

He also pointed to the country’s initiative to convene a meeting of heads of ports and logistics centers, calling it a “very constructive” contribution to the organization.

According to Midhun, SCO member states and dialogue partners account for around 40% of the world’s population and approximately one-quarter of global GDP.

“As one of the largest regional organizations, we have always paid special attention to the development of relations between countries in the fields of security, political relations, energy, and transport. When the world is changing, the role of the SCO is, of course, growing,” he said.

Parliamentary Assembly of Turkic Speaking Countries (TURKPA)

Osman Mesten, a Turkish lawmaker who chairs TURKPA’s Commission on Legal Affairs and International Relations, called the election a historic milestone.

“Following the referendum and the transition to a single-chamber legislature, the elections are the first held under the new system,” Mesten said.

Parliamentarians from Azerbaijan, the Kyrgyz Republic and Türkiye are participating in election observation missions.

Mesten noted that the delegation had met with the Central Election Commission chairman and representatives of political parties participating in the election.

“We observed that each party had been able to prepare for the elections and conduct outreach among voters to encourage participation and the exercise of their democratic rights,” he said.

He also highlighted women’s representation among candidates, noting that women account for around 43% of all candidates.

Mesten said Kazakhstan’s transition to a unicameral parliament could streamline the legislative process and improve its efficiency.

“A single-chamber legislature is certainly important from the perspective of democratic representation and for ensuring that the legislative process functions in a more orderly, efficient and effective manner,” he told The Astana Times.

Mesten noted that Türkiye had previously a bicameral legislature but transitioned to a unicameral parliamentary system following constitutional reforms.

“I believe that a single chamber enables decisions to be made more effectively, more quickly and more efficiently. It also eliminates some of the disadvantages associated with a dual-chamber system,” he said.

He also welcomed Kazakhstan’s decision to name the new legislature the Kurultai, describing the term as a reference to the country’s historical roots and shared heritage across the Turkic world.

“By choosing this name, Kazakhstan is referring to its deep historical roots. It also conveys the message that the country seeks to build a strong nation and a strong state by drawing strength from its heritage,” Mesten said.

“The name Kurultai is meaningful not only for Kazakhstan. It reflects our shared history and common roots. For this reason, it has inspired pride and enthusiasm throughout the Turkic world, including in Türkiye,” he said.

A total of 777 foreign observers from 42 countries and 13 international organizations have been accredited to monitor Kazakhstan’s Kurultai election.

World.title: “When the state serves an oligarch, villages and cities empty out.” Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”
World.content:
Video podcast “Protests in Georgia”

The traditional pro-European “Saturday march” in Tbilisi on August 22 was dedicated to Georgian citizens who have left the country in search of work and better opportunities.

Participants said the growing emigration is driven by the policies of the ruling Georgian Dream party, which they say have pushed the country away from the European integration path enshrined in the Constitution.

Many blame the party’s founder and honorary chairman, oligarch Bidzina Ivanishvili, personally.

“Villages and cities are emptying out when the state serves Ivanishvili” — this was the central message of the march, reflected in the slogans and statements by speakers.

Organisers announced that throughout September, the traditional “Saturday marches” will be held in support of Georgian emigrants.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

News in Georgia

World.title: Armenia’s new parliament: balance of power, tools of government and opposition’s dead end
World.content:
Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

The parliamentary election results in Armenia have confirmed the continuity of the country’s political system while exposing deep structural contradictions. Political competition has shifted decisively towards intense polarisation. The National Assembly risks turning into little more than a platform for mutual accusations resembling a television talk show, rather than the country’s highest legislative body.

Political analyst Alexander Iskandaryan’s assessment

Continuity of the system, limits of influence and a fragmented opposition

“The new National Assembly has retained the key feature of its predecessor. The Constitution allows the ruling Civil Contract party to make almost any decision on its own, except on issues that require a constitutional majority. The two opposition factions — former president Robert Kocharyan’s Armenia Alliance and businessman Samvel Karapetyan’s Strong Armenia — have access to the media and the parliamentary platform, and can openly express their views and criticise the government. However, they have no real leverage over current policy.

The opposition forces have undergone a reshuffle. In the eighth National Assembly, Kocharyan’s faction held the largest number of seats. In the new parliament, however, it is the smaller of the two opposition factions. They are also unlikely to build a stable coalition or an “umbrella” structure. Because of their different origins and the lack of a practical basis for cooperation, even if they unite, they will not secure 50% of the seats needed to take the initiative. A long-term alliance is impossible. In 35 years of the Third Republic, the opposition has never managed to produce a successful example of unity. The minority is therefore left with little more than keeping the protest movement alive.”

Legitimacy, voters and the government’s narratives

“The ruling party has significant external legitimacy. This includes recognition of the election results by the US, EU, Turkey and Azerbaijan, as well as Russia’s refusal to withhold recognition from Nikol Pashinyan. The ruling force also relies on support from the bureaucracy. In fact, bureaucratic legitimacy has grown stronger. Civil servants clearly understand their ties to the political leadership and recognise the risks that a change of elites could bring.

At the same time, the government’s social legitimacy remains low. Kocharyan won 10% despite his high negative rating, while Karapetyan’s party, hastily assembled over six months with its leader under arrest, won a quarter of the vote despite high turnout. This is a serious signal of the level of public dissatisfaction.

Realising that its support will not grow, the government abandoned any real ideology. Political strategists pragmatically discarded the “high-minded Yerevan intelligentsia”, which would not have voted for the government anyway and would not have gone to the polls. Instead, they focused on their target audience: residents of small towns and villages with lower levels of education, young people and older generations.

To maintain control, the government uses several narratives:

“Peace versus war” — portraying opponents as the “party of war” and frightening voters with the prospect that an opposition victory would lead to a new war in September.

“Democrats versus oligarchs” — selectively labelling businesses. Wealthy entrepreneurs who support the government are simply called “businessmen”, while any affluent opponents are automatically branded “oligarchs”.

“Europe versus Russia” — systematically linking the entire opposition to Moscow. Karapetyan is portrayed this way because he came from Russia, Gagik Tsarukyan because of his ties to Belarus, and Kocharyan as Putin’s personal friend.

Accusing voters of supporting the opposition solely for money. This new level of polarisation has emerged in official statements by the authorities.”

The government’s geopolitical narrative and the opposition’s dead end

“The government’s anti-Russian discourse found fertile ground. These sentiments had been developing for years, and the events of 2020 and 2023 — the war in Karabakh, followed by the exodus of the entire Armenian population from Nagorno-Karabakh — only strengthened them.

At the same time, people across the post-Soviet space have traditionally associated the word “European” with quality and development: European healthcare, European education, European cars and so on. The government has effectively exploited this perception. Direct public support for Pashinyan from senior US officials, up to and including the US president, also played an important role.

The opposition has found itself in a strategic dead end. It cannot openly say “we are pro-Russian” or “we are not pro-Russian”. Unable to reject the geopolitical trend that enjoys broad public support, opposition parties have had to adapt and repeat that they are “also in favour of cooperation with Europe, but for a more carefully calibrated policy”.

Personal attacks instead of alternative programmes

“Instead of substantive work, the opposition is sliding into negative rhetoric and personal attacks: who is corrupt, who got their wife a job, who owns which flat and who once “didn’t even have a washing machine”. Armenian society knows perfectly well how the bureaucratic hierarchy works, so such “exposés” do not work. All these scandals only play into the government’s hands, allowing it to say: “Look who we have to work with in parliament.”

A constructive alternative would be to develop concrete programmes in different areas — healthcare, pensions, the economy, the army and so on. Even if the ruling majority rejects, say, 15 such professional programmes in a row, a systematic effort to offer solutions will eventually resonate with society. For now, trolling has replaced politics.”

Real state priorities: security, energy and meritocracy

“While parliament is busy trolling, the country’s key problems remain unresolved. One of them is security.

It is wrong to call the situation with Azerbaijan peace. You can see what real peace looks like on the border with Georgia, for example: people can cross freely using an ID card, while there are no transport corridors, European observers, military guards or concrete walls, even though 30% of the border remains undelimited. With Baku, however, there is only a state of “no war”. That is far from peace. At the same time, Azerbaijan is rapidly expanding its military capabilities in every sphere, including its air force.

Armenia needs to make foreign policy decisions and find ways to overcome the energy crisis.

Relations with all four neighbours — Russia, Turkey, Azerbaijan and Iran — are in crisis. Meanwhile, the Armenian-American TRIPP “Trump Route” project — a transit route through Armenia — remains little more than a political narrative. At the same time, launching new facilities, such as an AI data centre in Hrazdan, could create an acute electricity shortage that talk of American small modular nuclear reactors alone cannot solve.

In the Armenian city of Hrazdan, Firebird AI’s artificial intelligence factory has begun operations. The facility is the largest AI data centre in the region. The first phase of the project, worth more than $500 million, uses advanced NVIDIA accelerators and server equipment from leading global manufacturers. Some experts believe the factory’s launch could put additional pressure on the country’s energy system. (firebird.ai)

The state needs a competent administration to overcome these challenges.

The country needs to embrace meritocracy, appointing people based on competence rather than loyalty.

Finally, the country’s leadership needs to reconsider its attitude towards citizens.

Nikol Pashinyan is the prime minister of all Armenians, not just the voters of Civil Contract. The claim that people could only have voted against the government in exchange for money is false and toxic. The government now faces a vast array of real problems. Its first task is to recognise the scale of those challenges and start addressing them.

Balance of power in Armenia’s new parliament

World.title: Anea the raccoon’s favourite activity at Tbilisi Zoo – video
World.content:
Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

Raccoons love water. You can often see them swimming, wetting their fur or carefully washing their paws. Anea, a resident of Tbilisi Zoo, is no exception.

On hot days, Anea particularly enjoys dipping her paws in water and having a cool shower. So her keepers set up an improvised shower in her enclosure, which, as you can see in the video below, delighted her.

There is a metal container in her enclosure for drinking water, but who says she cannot take a bath in it too? Despite its small size, Anea fits perfectly inside, happily splashes around in the water and uses it to escape the summer heat. After noticing the raccoon’s love of bathing, her keepers have already ordered a bigger “bath”.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status.



The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo.



We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Anea the raccoon at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Opinion: ‘Moscow’s main fear is that Armenia will choose European Union’
World.content:
Opinion on Russia’s demand for a referendum in Armenia

In recent days, Russia‘s demand for Armenia to hold a referendum on whether the country should remain in the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) or choose the European Union has increasingly been seen as a threat. Experts from the “Armenian Council” think tank made the assessment in an article.

Russia has long demanded such a referendum, including at the highest level. But there are now threats to initiate proceedings concerning Armenia’s membership of the EAEU. Decisions within the bloc require consensus, and Yerevan has the right to veto them.

“Russia’s main phobia is that the situation will deteriorate over time, leading the Armenian people to choose the European Union,” the authors argue.

They stress that this is not only Russia’s “main phobia”, but also its “main misconception”. The analysts believe that even the “economic pressure and blackmail” that Russia began applying to Armenia in May, during the pre-election period, have not changed Armenian public opinion. They cite the results of the parliamentary election on 7 June as evidence: Armenia’s ruling party won, rather than pro-Russian forces.

Ahead of Armenia’s parliamentary election, Russia imposed restrictions on imports of Armenian agricultural products. It also banned imports of flowers, Jermuk mineral water, certain alcoholic drinks and fish products. The authorities justified the measures by citing failures to meet required quality standards. However, Armenian experts and officials viewed the issue in the context of the election campaign. They therefore expected the pressure to end after the election. But that did not happen. Moreover, Russia introduced new restrictions after the election. At the same time, in early June, four EAEU member states called on Armenian authorities to hold a referendum as soon as possible on choosing between the Eurasian bloc and the EU. Yerevan responded that there were currently no grounds for such a vote because Armenia’s European integration process had not yet reached the stage at which citizens could make a choice. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has repeatedly said that Armenia should first obtain EU candidate status or, at the very least, put the issue on the agenda. However, Moscow continues to insist. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin said the EAEU expects Armenia to hold a referendum by December. Otherwise, the bloc’s leaders would “take this fact into account when determining appropriate further joint steps”. He said a report on the possible consequences of suspending the EAEU Treaty in relation to Armenia would be discussed at the December meeting of the Supreme Eurasian Economic Council.

Armenia’s prime minister spoke about a referendum on EU membership

“No one in Armenia has ever talked about holding a referendum on EAEU membership or an alternative in the form of the EU.

On 9 January 2025, when the Armenian government discussed and approved a bill to launch the EU accession process, Prime Minister Pashinyan said:

“Armenia can begin the process of joining the EU only if a certain number of referendum participants vote ‘yes’ in accordance with the procedure established by the Constitution.”

Senior Armenian officials later repeated this point on various occasions.

The key point is that Armenia will hold a referendum on joining the European Union, not on whether to remain in or leave the EAEU.

This fundamental difference significantly changes the forecasts for the expected outcome. However, if Armenia votes to join the EU, it will inevitably leave the EAEU at some stage of the subsequent process.”

Russia is pushing for a referendum on a different question

“Armenia’s willingness to hold a referendum on EU membership is fundamentally different from what Moscow wants to impose.

Russia is clearly manipulating the situation by demanding a referendum on the EAEU now, when Armenia is at least a decade away from joining the EU.

We need to understand the real reason for this urgency.

The Kremlin understands that if EU membership becomes a genuine possibility, no rational society could vote against it.

Therefore, to keep Armenia in the EAEU and have a chance of stopping its move towards the EU, a referendum must take place as soon as possible, while the prospect of EU membership remains unclear and uncertain.”

Moscow is trying to “beat” Europe by exploiting Armenian businesses’ dependence

“The EAEU mechanisms currently work in favour of Armenian businesses, creating influence and dependence.

At the same time, Armenia is steadily diversifying its economy, reducing that influence and dependence.

The question of whether to remain in the EAEU directly affects many companies with specific interests in Russia. By contrast, EU membership remains a more abstract issue for them for now.

Moscow does not expect to “beat” Europe in economic competition over the next few years or even decades and offer Armenia more attractive conditions. It therefore believes it still has an opportunity to influence the situation now. That is why it is in such a hurry.”

Opinion on Russia’s demand for a referendum in Armenia

World.title: Armenia-Azerbaijan exports could begin ‘soon’: Pledges, figures and remaining barriers
World.content:
Exports from Armenia to Azerbaijan

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan told journalists that “exports from Armenia to Azerbaijan could begin in the near future”. He also said that bilateral trade was already on the agenda. According to Pashinyan, Azerbaijani specialists visited Armenia in September 2025 and January 2026 to discuss infrastructure issues, including power lines, railways and pipelines.

The statement comes against the backdrop of tangible but still highly asymmetrical trade relations between the two countries, which began to take shape following the signing of the declaration in Washington in August 2025.

Official data and figures

According to Azerbaijan’s State Customs Committee, Azerbaijan exported around $17.4m worth of goods to Armenia between January and July 2026. The shipments consisted mainly of petroleum products, particularly diesel and petrol. Over the same period, Azerbaijan’s indirect imports from Armenia amounted to just $960. This figure was recorded in March, with imports falling to zero in subsequent months.

Following the lifting of transit restrictions in October 2025 and the start of the first fuel deliveries in December, Azerbaijan has facilitated both direct exports to Armenia and the transit of goods from Russia and Kazakhstan, including grain, fertilisers and other products. Volumes remain small, but the direction of travel has changed: borders that had been closed for decades have effectively begun to open.

There has yet to be any official commercial export from Armenia. In January 2026, Armenian Economy Minister Gevorg Papoyan said the two sides had exchanged lists of potential goods for bilateral trade. These included aluminium foil and raw materials for its production, ferromolybdenum, textiles, flowers, greenhouse produce including tomatoes and peppers, raw materials for brandy production, and other goods.

The specific contents of the lists and the expected volumes of shipments have not yet been officially published. Further development of trade will depend on agreements between companies.

What could be traded, and why?

Azerbaijani experts note that, at the initial stage, developing trade in industrial goods and raw materials appears more realistic than focusing primarily on food products. Vugar Bayramov, an MP and member of the Milli Majlis Committee on Economic Policy, citing preliminary estimates, puts the potential annual trade turnover for 38 categories of goods at up to $300m. These include food and industrial products as well as raw materials. In his view, mutual supplies of goods other than fuel could begin between the two countries in the near future.

Economist Natig Jafarli says the process is developing gradually. According to him, Azerbaijan has an advantage in energy resources, while potential Armenian exports could include agricultural products, fish, fruit and iron ore. However, Azerbaijan is not yet importing goods from Armenia, while the necessary infrastructure, including bank transfers, insurance and contractual mechanisms, has yet to be fully established.

Akif Nasirli, chairman of the Centre for Liberal Economists, believes food products could also be viable export candidates, including fruit and vegetables such as apricots, peaches, cherries, tomatoes and peppers, as well as fish, mineral water and wine. In his view, restrictions on the Russian market are forcing Yerevan to seek alternative export markets.

Former Finance Minister Fikret Yusifov has previously argued that, if trade relations are restored, a trade deficit for Armenia would be inevitable, but that these economic ties should nevertheless be developed for the sake of peace.

There is also a widespread view among experts that food and beverages are psychologically more sensitive categories of goods. Construction materials, cable and electrical products, industrial raw materials, chemicals and light-industry goods, by contrast, may be perceived considerably more favourably.

Psychological barrier

This is one of the deepest and most sensitive aspects of the issue. Expert assessments published by Caliber note that memories of the 44-day war remain fresh. The appearance of products labelled Made in Armenia on shop shelves could initially provoke mixed reactions, ranging from curiosity to social media campaigns. Trust in food and beverages, including wine and brandy, is particularly important, as some consumers may have irrational concerns about their safety. With industrial goods and construction materials, by contrast, the country of origin is less visible to consumers and purchasing decisions tend to be more pragmatic.

During a transitional period, neutral packaging in English or Russian, or rebranding, could potentially be used. The appearance of Azerbaijani fuel on the Armenian market has already created a precedent for a kind of “economic truce”. A similarly pragmatic approach could work in the opposite direction, although this will not happen automatically.

In both societies, support for peace does not yet necessarily translate into an equally positive attitude towards goods from the neighbouring country. Traders from border areas who wished to remain anonymous, as well as entrepreneurs with experience of informal “re-exports” through Georgia using channels that have existed since the 1990s, say that price and quality could eventually become the decisive factors. However, this process could take years.

Practical obstacles and possible timeframes

Issues surrounding certification, phytosanitary controls, customs procedures, bank transfers and insurance have yet to be fully resolved.

Logistics currently operate mainly through Georgia. Direct rail links and the TRIPP corridor are still at the infrastructure development stage. Competition also remains high, with suppliers from Turkey, Russia and Iran already present in the market alongside domestic producers. The competitiveness of Armenian goods will therefore depend on their price, quality and logistics costs.

Under an optimistic scenario, small-scale shipments of industrial goods and raw materials could begin within several months to a year. A more realistic scenario would see trade gradually expand over one to three years, while under a pessimistic scenario, political fluctuations and public reaction could delay the process considerably.

What to watch next

Key indicators could include the first genuine commercial shipments from Armenia appearing in customs statistics, the introduction of banking mechanisms for cross-border payments, official approval of a list of potential goods for trade, and changes in the procurement policies of retailers such as Bravo, Araz and others.

Independent polling and sociological research in both countries will also be needed to assess public attitudes towards goods labelled “Made in …”. Without such data, statements about future trade will remain largely expressions of intent.

World.title: ‘From crisis management to stability’: Pashinyan unveils new government programme
World.content:
Armenia’s 2026–2031 government programme

The Armenian government has approved its programme for 2026-2031. Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said it marked a shift from crisis management to stability. Looking back on his eight years as prime minister, he said the coronavirus pandemic, followed by the war and the post-war situation, had forced the government to operate in crisis-management mode. Now that Armenia and Azerbaijan have established peace, the government can “return to the unfinished part of the agenda of the 2018 Velvet Revolution”.

The new programme focuses on stability, he said. Pashinyan stressed that it rests entirely on the concept of “Real Armenia” and the principles underpinning the establishment of the Fourth Republic.

In 2025, the ruling Civil Contract party announced a new strategic goal: establishing the Fourth Republic of Armenia. The party congress unanimously adopted a declaration to this effect. According to the document, the Fourth Republic “will be based on the concept of preserving the internationally recognised sovereign territory of the Republic of Armenia, covering 29,743 sq km, in accordance with the 1991 Alma-Ata Declaration”. The declaration says the party reached this decision after analysing the history of the Third Republic. The Third Republic refers to the present-day Republic of Armenia, which declared independence following a nationwide referendum in 1991. The First Republic refers to the republic proclaimed on 28 May 1918. Accordingly, Soviet Armenia is considered the Second Republic.

“Following the 7 June 2026 election, the ideology of ‘Real Armenia’ won. This means it has become the official ideology. Armenia is therefore entering the stage of its history that we call the Fourth Republic. We must continue and give new momentum to democratic, anti-corruption, economic and public administration reforms,” the prime minister stressed.

Government plans for the next five years

According to the new programme, the Armenian government will pursue the following goals in 2026-2031:

strengthening and further institutionalising the peace established between Armenia and Azerbaijan;

maintaining and further developing a favourable security environment around Armenia, in particular by normalising and developing relations with countries in the region and deepening existing partnerships beyond it;

unblocking Armenia through the Crossroads of Peace project and the “Trump Route” (TRIPP) transit programme;

liberalising the visa regime with the EU for Armenian citizens;

deepening democratic, anti-corruption, economic and public administration reforms.

With whom does Yerevan plan to deepen partnerships under its “balanced foreign policy”?

In 2026-2031, the Armenian government will pursue a “balanced and proportionate” foreign policy.

“It has proved effective in stabilising Armenia’s external environment. Regionalisation plays a key role in foreign policy, whose goal is to ensure conditions in which Armenia can not only live without external support, but do so comfortably,” the document says.

Based on this approach, the government places particular importance on further developing relations with Georgia, Iran, Turkey and Azerbaijan. The government has outlined the following steps for each neighbouring country:

Georgia

Yerevan will continue implementing the measures set out in the Declaration on Establishing a Strategic Partnership between Armenia and Georgia. This will create new mutually beneficial opportunities for political, trade, economic, energy and transport cooperation, as well as regional and joint infrastructure projects.

Iran

Armenia will continue energy cooperation with Iran, develop cross-border infrastructure and expand transport routes through Iran, including North-South and Persian Gulf-Black Sea corridors.

Turkey

The Armenian government will continue efforts to establish diplomatic relations with Turkey, open the Armenian-Turkish border and put at least two modern border crossing points into operation. It also plans to restore and expand transport, energy and digital infrastructure, as well as bilateral and multilateral trade.

Azerbaijan

The government plans to continue efforts to sign and ratify a peace agreement and carry out work on the delimitation and demarcation of the state border. Contacts between civil society and business communities in the two countries will continue, helping to establish bilateral trade.

The foreign policy priorities specifically include deepening strategic partnerships with the European Union, the US, France and China. With Russia, Armenia plans to “transform and deepen its partnership”.

Against the backdrop of tensions over the ban on Armenian food and other exports to Russia and the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), which Russia leads, the programme says:

“Work will continue to ensure the full and uninterrupted exercise of the EAEU’s fundamental freedoms — the free movement of labour, services, goods and capital — as well as to develop relations with member and observer states.”

Regarding relations with the European Union, the programme stresses that Armenia will continue working to meet standards in democracy and the rule of law, as well as in the economic, financial and other spheres.

Armenia intends to deepen its partnership with the United States further. Cooperation will continue based on the principles set out in the Strategic Partnership Charter and bilateral memorandums of understanding.

“The TRIPP project, the ‘Trump Route’, will be implemented, at least in terms of operating energy and railway infrastructure, while integrating Armenia into major regional infrastructure projects,” the programme says.

Armenia’s 2026–2031 government programme

World.title: Parrots Rocky and Kiki: Tbilisi Zoo’s brightest residents – video
World.content:
Macaws at Tbilisi Zoo

Tbilisi Zoo is home to two species of macaws: scarlet macaws (Ara macao) named Rocky and Kiki, and blue-and-yellow macaws (Ara ararauna) named Chico and Paco. Their bright plumage catches visitors’ attention at first sight.

The macaws at Tbilisi Zoo are currently in the middle of their breeding season. Chico and Paco are expecting chicks. They usually incubate their eggs for 24–28 days. During this period, both parents actively protect and care for their future offspring.

Rocky and Kiki have become particularly cautious during this period. They often hide from people and rarely leave their enclosure. If you are planning to visit them at the zoo, keep in mind that they may be difficult to spot at the moment.

Macaws are known for their strong bonds. Pairs almost always stay together: they preen each other’s feathers, look for food together and protect each other when danger threatens.

With proper care, macaws can live for 50–60 years, and sometimes even longer — more than 70 years. Rocky’s exact age is unknown, but he is the oldest parrot at Tbilisi Zoo. Despite his advanced age, Rocky still has the same short-tempered and grumpy nature he has always had.

Once, when a keeper was a little late with a treat — a nut — Rocky immediately made his “protest” known by biting him on the finger. Because of their powerful beaks, macaw bites can be very painful and may cause serious injuries.

Macaws are incredibly intelligent birds. They have excellent memories, and some can even imitate human voices and words.

Although macaws are often kept as pets, caring for them is no easy task. They need plenty of space, daily attention, mental stimulation and constant variety in their surroundings.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Macaws at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Opinion from Abkhazia: ‘Nika Gvaramia said nothing new about resolving Georgian-Abkhaz conflict’
World.content:
An interview with Nika Gvaramia, one of the leaders of the Georgian opposition, about ways to resolve the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict attracted considerable attention in Georgia. In Abkhazia, however, it attracted almost no attention.

In his blog, Inal Khashig, editor of the Abkhaz newspaper Chegemskaya Pravda, offered his view on why. He believes the lack of interest among Abkhaz people is mainly because Gvaramia said nothing new in the interview and offered none of the things Abkhaz people would want to hear.

Inal Khashig: “From my strictly Abkhaz perspective, Gvaramia did not say anything radically new. If anything, he simply revived the old idea of resolving the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict through Georgia’s integration into the European Union, which would serve as an attractive incentive for Abkhaz people.

Georgian politicians have periodically put forward this idea since the presidency of Mikheil Saakashvili. The most recent was Georgia’s current prime minister, Irakli Kobakhidze, who in 2024 even set a specific deadline for achieving the goal. ‘Georgia will join the European Union together with our Abkhaz and Ossetian brothers by 2030,’ he declared at the time from a high-profile podium. In short, the EU idea has already been discussed many times.”

From Gvaramia’s interview, I also understood that Georgia cannot resolve the conflict through military means at present because it lacks the resources needed to guarantee the desired outcome. In this context, economic development and shared security interests should form the basis for resolving the conflict.

The only “new” idea proposed by the opposition politician is that Georgia needs to overcome the trauma it suffered after the Georgian-Abkhaz war of the 1990s because these memories “prevent it from moving forward and hold back development”. And on this point, I completely agree with Nika Gvaramia.

In my view, Georgia’s constant insistence on the need to regain Abkhazia is actually a heavy burden that prevents the country from achieving its full potential.

It is like a man who devotes all his energy and the rest of his life to trying to win back a wife who left him long ago. You can consider his life wasted.

I am convinced that if Mikheil Saakashvili had not abandoned his reform agenda in favour of “restoring territorial integrity” during his presidency, Georgia would almost certainly have made much greater progress in building its statehood.

I can well imagine that when Nika Gvaramia speaks about the need to overcome the trauma, he actually means giving up once and for all on claims to the lost territories. But as a politician, he understands the consequences of making such an admission openly.

As for the idea of restoring trust between Abkhaz people and Georgians, Gvaramia talks about this as well. But his understanding of “trust” is not very different from that of other Georgian politicians: essentially, “we will open up the world to you and shower you with benefits, but first come back to us”. In other words, it is a kind of bargain, with no guarantee that the other side is not bluffing.

But genuine trust looks very different.

In my view, a tangible step towards beginning the process of rebuilding trust between Abkhaz people and Georgians would be for Tbilisi to abolish the discriminatory Law on Occupied Territories, which does little short of preventing Abkhazia and South Ossetia from breathing freely without Georgia’s permission. But Nika Gvaramia did not mention this law even once. Perhaps that is why his interview went unnoticed in Abkhazia.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.



Nika Gvaramia interview

World.title: Russia's election commission praises Kurultai vote, citing transparency and inclusivity
World.content:
ASTANA, Kazakhstan, August 24. "We highly appreciate the preparation and conduct of the election of Kurultai deputies."

Trend's special correspondent in Astana reports that Alena Bulgakova, a member of Russia's Central Election Commission, made the remarks in an interview with journalists.

"Every voter had the opportunity to express their will and make an informed choice. In this regard, the measures taken to organize the electoral process were implemented in accordance with the laws of the Republic and international electoral standards," she said.

Bulgakova also highlighted the openness, transparency and publicity of the electoral process.

"It is important to note the degree of openness, transparency and publicity of the electoral process, which was also maintained, because both party observers and independent observers were present at all polling stations," she said.

She emphasized that the election process met all standards and was also highly rated by international observers.

"The turnout that the Central Election Commission of the Republic has already presented today speaks for itself, because voters trust the process, voters are making an informed choice to ensure a достойное future for themselves and their children and the prosperity of the republic," Bulgakova said.

Bulgakova also noted the use of inclusive practices, saying that all polling stations provided opportunities for people with disabilities to exercise their right to vote.

World.title: ADB launches AI infrastructure resilience project with Azerbaijan, other member states
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 24. The Asian Development Bank (ADB) has launched a project focused on using artificial intelligence (AI) to strengthen infrastructure resilience and support adaptation, with Azerbaijan among the participating countries.

The project involves ADB member countries, including Azerbaijan, Afghanistan, Armenia, Bangladesh, Bhutan, Georgia, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, China, Pakistan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Türkiye, Uzbekistan and other countries across the Asia-Pacific region.

According to the ADB, the project has been allocated $800,000 in funding from the Technical Assistance Special Fund.

The project is also aimed at strengthening the capacity of ADB developing member countries to identify, assess and reduce disaster-related risks. Its implementation is expected to indirectly help protect poor and vulnerable populations, which are disproportionately affected by the consequences of natural and other disasters.

The initiative will use AI capabilities to strengthen infrastructure resilience and improve approaches to risk adaptation, the bank said.

According to ADB data, Azerbaijan received $2.53 billion in sovereign financing for 10 projects from 2015 to 2024. Of this amount, 51% was allocated to regional cooperation and integration projects, one of the highest shares among countries in the relevant group. Another 39% went toward private-sector development, 18% toward climate financing and 10% toward digital technology initiatives.

From 2015 to 2024, the bank approved nine nonsovereign projects totaling $963.9 million, with 100% of the financing directed toward private-sector development. Notably, 78% of total commitments were related to regional cooperation and integration, the highest share among comparable upper-middle-income countries reviewed by the ADB.

According to the Central Bank of Azerbaijan, ADB's direct investment in Azerbaijan's economy amounted to $2.075 million in the first quarter of this year. The figure was $455,000, or 28.1%, higher than in the same period last year.

World.title: Uzbekistan Central Bank to launch fintech innovation hub, venture fund, CBDC white paper
World.content:
TASHKENT, Uzbekistan, August 24. The Central Bank of Uzbekistan is launching a number of new initiatives to develop the country’s fintech ecosystem, including a Fintech Innovation Hub, a dedicated venture fund and a program to train 5,000 young people, Governor of the Central Bank Timur Ishmetov said, Trend’s special correspondent reports from Tashkent.

He made the remark while speaking at the Silk Road Finance & Technology Forum.

According to Ishmetov, the Fintech Innovation Hub will begin accepting its first cohort of residents in the fourth quarter of 2026. The hub will provide a pathway for fintech startups through incubation and acceleration, regulatory guidance and pilot testing to assess market readiness. “We have established a dedicated venture fund. We are discussing with experienced international fund managers while building a direct pipeline from the Innovation Hub to international scaling, with the aim of providing larger ticket sizes and attracting international co-investments,” Ishmetov said.

He noted that the Central Bank will also take its policies on payments, payment systems, open banking and operational resilience to the next level. The core framework, governance model and technical architecture are already in place, according to the governor. “This policy enhancement will make the financial system future-proof,” he said.

Another initiative will be a program to train 5,000 young people in fintech by 2028. The first cohort will begin training by the end of this year under a program being developed with the participation of universities in Singapore and GFTA, combining academic foundations with practical fintech skills.

Ishmetov also announced that Uzbekistan will publish a white paper on a central bank digital currency (CBDC) as part of its broader fintech framework. “The paper will address the assessment of potential use cases, design options, key trade-offs, and implications for the financial system,” he said.

The Central Bank governor stressed that the initiatives form part of a unified strategy focused on innovation, appropriate regulation, modern financial infrastructure, access to talent and capital, and positioning Uzbekistan as a gateway for fintech growth across Central Asia.

World.title: Kazakhstan's Adilet party leads Kurultai election with 71.17% of vote
Uzbekistan maintains annual GDP growth at 6–7% — Deputy PM
World.content:
TASHKENT, Uzbekistan, August 24. Uzbekistan’s average annual GDP growth has remained at around 6–7%, while the size of the country’s economy has tripled from around $60 billion to $180 billion, Uzbek Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Economy and Finance Jamshid Kuchkarov said, Trend’s special correspondent reports from Tashkent.

He made the remark while speaking at the Silk Road Finance & Technology Forum.

According to Kuchkarov, GDP per capita has also increased significantly, from approximately 4,600, bringing Uzbekistan into the group of upper-middle-income countries.

The deputy prime minister noted that Uzbekistan has also made significant progress in reducing inflation. After remaining in double digits several years ago, inflation has now declined to single-digit levels. “Inflation is expected to be around 6.5% this year, with the aim of reaching the 5% target next year,” he said.

Kuchkarov said that Uzbekistan has maintained external public debt at around 27% of GDP, while budget deficits have remained below 3% of GDP in recent years.

He also highlighted improving external assessments of Uzbekistan’s economy, noting that the country’s credit ratings have been upgraded by Fitch and other rating agencies, while foreign direct investment inflows have increased annually. “Going forward, we will take all necessary measures to bring inflation down to the target level, maintain fiscal discipline, and ensure prudent and sustainable public debt,” Kuchkarov said.

He stressed that the Uzbek government would take all necessary steps to ensure that Uzbekistan maintains a favorable and predictable environment for investors and market participants over the next decade. “We will work to achieve an investment-grade sovereign credit rating, complete Uzbekistan’s accession to the World Trade Organization, further reduce the state’s presence in the economy, and continue market-oriented reforms,” Kuchkarov said.

World.title: Uzbekistan, Tajikistan accelerate joint agricultural projects
World.content:
Photo: the Ministry of Agriculture of Uzbekistan

BAKU, Azerbaijan, August 24. Uzbekistan and Tajikistan are expanding agricultural cooperation through practical projects in cotton and grain production, food processing, agrologistics and exports.

This was reflected in a statement by the Ministry of Agriculture of Uzbekistan, following the participation of Uzbekistan’s Deputy Agriculture Minister, J. Abduzuhurov, in the Food Industry Forum and the UPAK EXPO-2026 international exhibition in Tajikistan.

At the forum’s opening ceremony and plenary session, Abduzuhurov outlined Uzbekistan’s efforts to develop agricultural processing, modern agrologistics and packaging infrastructure, as well as attract investment to the sector.

The discussions focused on processing and exporting agricultural products, ensuring food security and expanding international cooperation.

As part of the visit, Abduzuhurov met with Bahromjon Rajab Ahmadzoda, Tajikistan’s deputy agriculture minister, to review the progress of joint projects in cotton production, grain farming and other agricultural areas.

The sides agreed to accelerate the implementation of existing projects, improve coordination and strengthen direct working contacts between relevant organizations in the two countries.

“Strengthening direct working contacts between the responsible organizations will help accelerate the implementation of joint agricultural projects and improve coordination between the two sides,” the Uzbek Agriculture Ministry said.

Abduzuhurov also visited UPAK EXPO-2026, where Uzbek companies including CITRIC.UZ, EUROSNAB, PLAST TECH SOLUTION (FOOD PACK), ASIA PACK and STAR CUP presented their products.

The visit is expected to support the expansion of Uzbekistan-Tajikistan cooperation in agriculture, food processing, agricultural exports and related industries, with a focus on practical projects and closer business ties.

World.title: Silk Road Finance & Technology Forum kicks off in Tashkent (PHOTO)
World.content:
TASHKENT, Uzbekistan, August 24. The Silk Road Finance & Technology Forum has opened in Tashkent, focusing on the development of financial technologies, digital transformation, and capital market integration across the Great Silk Road region, Trend's special correspondent reports from Tashkent.

The event brings together heads of central banks, representatives of relevant ministries and agencies from Central Asia, the Caucasus, the Middle East, and Eastern Europe, as well as key global fintech industry players and leading international experts.

Among the participants are heads of major regional banks, top executives from international payment systems, venture fund managers, and representatives from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank.

In addition, developers of innovative artificial intelligence solutions for banking, cybersecurity specialists, investors, and representatives of startup ecosystems are attending the forum.

Forum participants are discussing strategies to accelerate banking sector digitalization, introduce Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs), expand cross-border payment systems, and broaden access to financial services for small and medium-sized enterprises.

Special attention is being paid to developing unified standards for regulating digital assets and strengthening regional cooperation in cybersecurity and data protection.

Furthermore, participants are focusing on attracting foreign direct investment into the region's technology sector, establishing favorable regulatory sandboxes for fintech startups, and driving joint initiatives for IT and finance talent development.
