World.title: Trump's 300,000 tonne beef import plan cops backlash
World.content:
The National Cattlemen's Beef Association (NCBA) in the United States has slammed President Donald Trump's plan to import more beef, saying it would "flood the market" and "undermine American producers".

On late Friday, Mr Trump shared on social media he had "concluded a deal to substantially lower the price of ground beef for working American families".

"As we work to rebuild [the US cattle] herd and help our ranchers, for the next 90 days, the United States will allow up to 300,000 metric tons of ground beef to be imported with no out-of-quota tariff," Mr Trump wrote.

" We have a commitment that this beef will be sold at 25 per cent below current market prices. "

The announcement has received plenty of backlash from the US cattle sector, including the industry's peak lobby group the NCBA.

In a statement to its members, the group urged them to "act now" against the proposal and said no cow-calf producer in America was asking for increased imports.

It said the proposal would risk "undercutting American farmers and ranchers".

"It threatens to undermine the very market conditions that are encouraging cattle producers to rebuild the American herd," NCBA said.

"After years of drought, high input costs, and shrinking inventories, strong demand for high-quality American beef is sending the right market signals for producers to reinvest and expand.

"Flooding the market with discounted foreign beef sends exactly the opposite signal.

"Government intervention designed to force down prices will create long-term harm to family farms and ranches, domestic beef production, and the stability of the US cattle industry."

The price of ground beef in the Unites States is at record highs. (ABC Landline)

After years of drought, the US cattle herd is at its lowest level since the 1950s and ABC Landline has been told that 55 per cent of US cattle country remains in drought.

R-Calf USA chief executive Bill Bullard said in a statement increasing beef imports made no sense.

"Beef imports have already risen to record levels, while retail beef prices continue climbing and the US cattle herd continues shrinking," he said.

"Most importantly, this policy undermines the producer confidence necessary to rebuild the US cattle herd. Herd expansion takes years. Producers deciding whether to retain heifers today must have confidence that future cattle prices will justify that investment."

In the year to date, the US has imported more than 1.2 million tonnes of beef from various nations. (ABC Landline)

Brazil perhaps the only winner

Global Agritrends analyst Simon Quilty said Brazil was perhaps "the only winner" from Mr Trump's announcement.

"Brazil is currently paying a 26.4 per cent duty, but it's questionable how much [extra beef] they could put into the United States [under this policy]," he said.

"There's really no upside for Australia, which is sending beef to the US tariff free and at about 75 per cent of our [annual quota] allocation.

" The concern is this could lower the overall price within the US market, which therefore lowers Australia's beef export prices due to a saturation of that lean meat market in America. "

Mr Quilty said a lot of details were lacking on how the US would enforce the commitment that imported beef would be sold at a 25 per cent discount to current market prices.

Simon Quilty says Brazil could be the "only winner" from this proposal by Donald Trump. (ABC Wodonga: Ashlee Charlton)

Australian prices 'likely to be negatively impacted'

In its latest report for Meat and Livestock Australia, the Steiner Consulting Group said year to date the United States had imported more than 1.2 million tonnes of beef from various nations, which was up 14.5 per cent on last year.

It said Australia had been the biggest supplier, exporting more than 300,000 tonnes.

It said imported beef prices had already been slipping and it expected Australian lean beef prices were "likely to be negatively impacted" as the removal of tariffs would give "South American suppliers more flexibility to offer discounts and compete for business".

The report concluded the push to "ship as much beef as possible to the US" would "significantly distort the market", and that US beef producers would be on the "losing side".

Watch ABC TV's Landline at 12:30pm on Sunday or on ABC iview.

World.title: AI costs are rising for Australian businesses. Does it compute?
World.content:
Australian businesses paying to use AI are weighing up what value they are getting from the disruptive technology.

"It's actually only really a relatively new thing that we have started to speak about," Anna Volkova, the head of people and culture at HR software company HiBob, told ABC News.

The platform has seen wins from using artificial intelligence, but it has been difficult to judge that against the mounting cost.

With AI capabilities changing so quickly, Ms Volkova said the business can "never catch up" with the need to redesign how it works to get the most out of it.

This has made it hard to work out precisely if the money is being spent effectively.

"We'll probably start to see impact to our bottom line in maybe two or three years, and I think most businesses are in that boat."

Despite the cost of AI tokens tumbling, businesses are spending more than ever. (ABC News graphic)

Jeremy Pell, whose firm Elastic helps companies to manage the cost of AI, agreed with that estimate.

"We're in a really interesting time at the moment," he said.

" Businesses are forced to pay this additional investment into AI, but they haven't yet reaped the 'bottom-line' benefits of the cost savings yet. "

Jeremy Pell says companies have not yet reaped the bottom-line benefits. (ABC News: Berge Breiland)

Last week, Assistant Minister for Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton described the value flowing out of Australia via AI as a "distant sucking sound".

In a speech at the ANU Crawford School of Public Policy, he said Australians were already spending $5-8 billion each year on artificial intelligence.

" With the overwhelming majority of those payments flowing offshore, in effect, we are creating a new import bill. An import bill for intelligence. "

That is just the start, with the government estimating local spending on AI could "plausibly" reach $20 billion to $40 billion annually within a decade.

Tokens adding up to billions

Even a few years ago, AI was not a line item companies had in annual budgets.

Now, in the current reporting season for ASX-listed companies, you can measure it in billions.

The technology spend at Australia's biggest bank, the Commonwealth Bank, increased from $2.3 billion in the 2025 financial year to $2.4 billion in this most recent financial year. It lists savings too.

"Measured gross benefits from AI use cases, including reinvested capacity, were [around] $200 million in FY26," its results presentation noted.

" Gross benefits from AI use cases are expected to double in FY27, and to exceed investment. "

On Wall Street, investors are asking whether the billions invested by US tech giants in AI will ever be justified by returns, creating concern about an AI-fuelled stock market bubble.

Stu Scotis, AI leader for consulting firm Deloitte, said the equation of how to spend an IT budget is getting tougher.

Stu Scotis says there are more uses of AI for increasingly complex tasks. (ABC News: Patrick Rocca)

Clients are weighing up long-term information technology costs — like storage and refreshing laptops — with a new, runaway expense.

"What we used to plan for as a static activity is now somewhat variable," he said.

Mr Scotis said current conversations are around "tokens": units of data processed by AI, or essentially the amount of grunt used to compute tasks.

Complex requests use more tokens, simple ones fewer.

The cost of tokens has plummeted in recent years, with increased competition, more efficient chips and more supply.

An unprecedented amount of data centre construction has increased the computing power available in the world.

Adding in more energy-efficient microchips, increased competition and the technology improving how much it can compute per token, it is now cheaper than ever.

As the below chart from research institute Epoch shows, the cost of the most powerful models has fallen the fastest.

Epoch used the "Massive Multitask Language Understanding" benchmark to rank AI large language models.

The price for large language models GPT-4 Turbo level or better (the most powerful, shown by the blue line) fell from $US15 ($20.90) for one million tokens in November 2023, to 17.5 US cents (24.4 cents) per million in February last year.

Research institute Epoch found the cost of the most high-powered tokens has fallen the fastest. (Supplied: Epoch)

Despite this trend, what companies are spending on AI is rising.

That is because firms are finding new tasks for AI to take on, leading to increasingly difficult computations, requiring more tokens per request.

AI not necessarily cheaper than workers

Mr Scotis put it another way: Human workers are paid in dollars, digital workers — or AI models — are paid in tokens.

"You want to get value for the digital workers and their output," he explained.

That means companies investing in AI need to examine the "value, outcome or growth" that comes from the tasks they complete, just as companies evaluate the work of human employees.

China throws spanner into tech boom Elon Musk's latest venture sent global stock markets to dizzying heights, but its performance since does not augur well for the company or the future of the AI boom.

" You start to get pretty clear, measurable outcomes that mean your investment in AI dollars or AI tokens actually pay a return. "

He said the human workers should not be too worried about being replaced.

"The cost of a digital worker doesn't necessarily mean it's cheaper than a human," he said.

"The complexity of the task, the length of time which a digital worker runs can, in some instances, be more expensive than a person."

Mr Scotis said firms needed to make a judgement "as to where you want to invest that type of work in your organisation, and does it make sense to do so".

It is a question being weighed in boardrooms right now.

How do companies pay for AI?

There are multiple ways that companies pay for artificial intelligence.

Some use "seats", paying per employee that accesses the technology.

This model is often used with platforms like Microsoft's Copilot, where AI abilities can be unlocked in existing programs, like writing documents in Word or juggling numbers in Excel spreadsheets.

The most common way to pay is by tokens.

The frequency with which employees are using AI models and the amount of tokens used in the queries is a new and increasing cost for businesses — which many of them will not have been paying for in even last financial year's report.

"That's the cost metric these businesses are grappling with," said Elastic's Jeremy Pell.

Different model, different prices

Another variable is that some of the cutting-edge or "frontier" AI models use more tokens.

That has led to companies using different models for different tasks, to avoid paying top dollar for tasks a more basic model can handle.

AI spending by major US firms is raising alam bells for some investors. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Some firms have also become more deliberate about the use of AI, sometimes capping the amount of tokens employees can use in a certain time frame.

"Businesses can no longer do AI for AI's sake," Mr Pell said.

"It's a matter of making sure that you are driving the business forward and these initiatives are driven and tied to the business's return on investment … It's working out which bits are useful."

'Scattergun' AI approach

AI expert Jon Whittle has warned the "scattergun" approach business has taken to using AI means the cost calculations are becoming more difficult, even as the price of tokens falls.

"I don't think companies are being very strategic right now about their AI use cases," he told The Business.

"They're just trying to find any place where they can use it, and that's why they're having costs increase so much."

Jon Whittle says the cost of tokens has come down dramatically. (ABC News: Simon Winter)

Professor Whittle, a former technical lead at NASA, director of CSIRO's AI capability and founder of Australia's National AI Centre, said a particular issue was that AI itself did a poor job at estimating the amount of tokens required.

Research has shown estimates can differ "by a factor of 30" running the same request on the same technology.

"I think that's the number one thing keeping [chief financial officers] up at night right now," Professor Whittle said.

"It turns out that even the AI itself is not very good at predicting the cost that a particular AI task will take."

Speed increases as AI crunches data faster

From her Sydney office, Anna Volkova says the major advantage her firm currently gets from AI is speed.

Anna Volkova says decisions around AI are essentially choices to spend in the hope it will be worth it. (ABC News: Daniel Irvine)

By connecting artificial intelligence to the software tools the company already uses, staff have been able to do more, at greater pace.

But the bill is mounting.

ABC Business Daily The podcast that helps you unpack the latest business and finance news.

She said, eventually, the business would likely need to evaluate usage "by need", not "limiting responsible experimentation" but looking for uses that maximise what staff get out of using AI as a tool.

"I think the things that we're looking for in terms of really seeing the return for our people … is it making their work better, easier?" she asks.

" Is it helping our leaders make decisions faster? "

It turns out the questions business leaders are asking about AI are very human.

World.title: Ex-radio host says Alan Jones had arm around man who alleges indecent assault
World.content:
Media figure Jason Morrison has told the trial of broadcaster Alan Jones that he did not see anything worrying at a lunch where a junior colleague has accused Mr Jones of touching his crotch.

Mr Morrison, who said he had known Alan Jones for more than 25 years, is giving evidence in his former colleague's criminal trial, where he has pleaded not guilty to 22 counts of indecent assault and sexual touching of six men.

The former 2GB host and producer is giving evidence in the NSW Local Court about a lunch Mr Jones hosted in 2008, where he allegedly touched a young colleague, Complainant C, on the crotch and upper thigh under the table.

Why Complainant C felt he 'couldn’t say no' to Alan Jones In The Case Of reporter Isobel Roe explains Complainant C's sometimes emotional testimony, the power dynamic between the two, as well as the cross-examination's focus on "uncomfortable" texts C sent Mr Jones.

Complainant C told the trial last week he believed other guests were looking at him from across the table, and said he believed they saw Mr Jones's outstretched arm going towards his lap.

He said after the lunch, some unnamed attendees at the lunch made a comment that he was "copping a feel" from Mr Jones under the table, a remark he said made him feel "deeply embarrassed".

On Friday the court heard from another lunch attendee, who said he recalled Mr Morrison and another man looking over at Complainant C at the table, and said the two men appeared "startled" and "amused" at Mr Jones swirling his wine with one hand while his other hand was under the table.

The witness said they could not see what was happening under the table.

That witness described Complainant C as appearing "distraught".

'Nothing that worried me'

Mr Morrison has so far told the trial Complainant C was "stuck with" Mr Jones at the "adult end" of the table, while attendees at the "fun end" were making jokes about the young man having to sit next to his "boss".

Asked by the crown prosecutor what Complainant C's demeanour was at the table, Mr Morrison said it was nothing that worried him.

"Smiling … nothing that worried me, put it that way," he said.

"People worked weird hours with a tough job, and they let off steam.

"Nothing stands out, if that's what you're asking."

Media figure Jason Morrison says a comment by another lunch guest that the pair looked like a "great couple" was "banter".

Mr Morrison was asked several times if anyone made any comments to Complainant C about Mr Jones after the lunch, or during the lunch.

He gave evidence that he could only remember general conversation and jokes about Complainant C being seated away from his friends at the table.

"Some people joked about how they kind of looked like a 'great couple'," he said.

"It wasn't really anything else other than banter."

Mr Morrison said at one point, Mr Jones had his arm around Complainant C while speaking to another guest, "in the manner somebody does when they're talking about somebody".

He said he worked with Mr Jones at 2GB in the early 2000s, and at various other times during his career.

Mr Jones denies any of the alleged assaults took place (ABC News: Jamie McKinnell)

Mr Morrison's has concluded for the day amid legal argument.

Complainant C has alleged Mr Jones indecently assaulted him eight times by touching him or kissing him in his Circular Quay apartment lifts, the lifts at work, or in a car.

Mr Jones denies any of the assaults happened.

World.title: Elder 'distressed' over racist graffiti on beloved timber bridge
World.content:
The racist and profane vandalism of a historic timber bridge has sparked outrage on the New South Wales Far South Coast.

Cuttagee Bridge was built in 1892 and is part of a route used by tourists travelling south from Bermagui to Tathra.

Barraga Bay resident and Restoration of Cuttagee Bridge group spokesman Phillip Coates said the explicit graffiti was noticed by members of the public on Sunday.

He described the language used as "sickening".

Barragga Bay resident Phil Coates described the language used in the graffiti as "sickening" (ABC South East NSW: Adriane Reardon)

“It's language that you wouldn't and shouldn't use today, but someone has taken their stride and put it up for public vigil," Mr Coates said.

" It's extremely shameful and very racist. "

The graffiti on Cuttagee Bridge was spotted by members of the public on Sunday. (Supplied: Philip Coates)

The message is believed to refer to Djiringanj man and traditional elder Uncle Gary Campbell.

Mr Campbell said his family have been left distressed by the words.

“They've really got sick minds, whoever went out and did that," he said.

" I'm just a little bit distressed about it because my name's mentioned on there. "

Gary Campbell believes the vandalism was aimed at him. (ABC South East NSW: Floss Adams)

Bega Valley Shire Council chief executive Anthony McMahon condemned the act and confirmed that the graffiti was removed this morning.

"Any act of racism is disgusting and has no place in our community," the statement reads.

"It serves only to offend, hurt and create division. In this instance the graffiti was also a personal attack on a member of our community as well as an act of criminal vandalism that creates a safety risk for road users."

NSW Police are urging anyone with information to contact Bega Police or Crime Stoppers.

Bridge backstory

Cuttagee Bridge is a single-lane timber structure that has been at the centre of community and political debate for years.

Last year Bega Valley Shire Council voted to turn the aging structure into a two-lane concrete bridge, despite many residents calling for it to be restored instead.

This year a decision was made to progress with a two-lane hybrid bridge featuring concrete and decorative timber elements, along with a shared pathway and handrails.

Council accepted $15 million from the NSW government to support the upgrade and a further $15 million commitment was announced in July.

Cuttagee Bridge is well-known feature of the area. (ABC News)

Mr Campbell, who has publicly shared his opinion about the restoration of the bridge, said the graffiti was "tied to my views about the bridge".

"When they build this new bridge, they're going to disturb everything around that, like there's artefacts, there's burial sites there," he said.

"The old fellas used to spot fish on the point, and they're going to have all their big equipment up on that point where it's crumbling."

Mr Coates also believes the location of the graffiti was chosen deliberately and "related to the bridge saga".

World.title: Woman dead after car crashes into lunchtime diners in Melbourne
World.content:
A woman is dead after a car crashed into lunchtime diners at a shopping centre in Melbourne's east.

The woman was sitting outside a restaurant at Westfield Knox, in Wantirna South, about 12.45pm when the car crashed into the building.

Police said the woman died at the scene.

She is yet to be formally identified.

The vehicle's driver and a passenger were taken to hospital with non-life threatening injuries.

The restaurant, Martini and Co, is closed until further notice. (Facebook: Westfield Knox/File)

An Ambulance Victoria spokesperson said they were both in stable conditions.

A second cafe customer was checked by paramedics at the scene.

"Major Collision Investigation Unit detectives will attend to investigate the circumstances surrounding the crash," a Victoria Police spokesperson said.

" Police do not believe the incident was an intentional act. "

In a social media post, the restaurant, Martini and Co, was declared closed until further notice.

"We apologise for any inconvenience and appreciate your understanding," it said.

"Please stay safe."

A crime scene has been set up and police are appealing for any shoppers or customers from the cafe who who witnessed the crash to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or www.crimestoppersvic.com.au.

World.title: Let your oven do the hard work with four of our favourite roast recipes
World.content:
Few dinners fill bellies and nourish souls as effortlessly as a good old-fashioned roast, so we thought we'd share four of our favourites.

From a slow-roasted lamb shoulder to upside-down roast chicken and pork with perfect crackling, these dishes make the oven do the heavy lifting.

Roasting the chicken upside down helps get the skin crispy skin and stops the breast from overcooking. (ABC News: David Sier)

This easy recipe turns the traditional roast chook on its head.

Placing the bird in a roasting tin, breast side down, protects the delicate meat and also exposes the parson's nose — the fleshy tail stump — to give it a golden, crunchy texture.

It's topped off with a delicious, creamy, herb and garlic-infused lemon gravy.

The secrets to a crispy crackling are scoring and adding spices to the pork, then leaving in the fridge for at least six hours to dry the skin out. (ABC TV)

One of the biggest challenges when trying to make the perfect pork roast is nailing the crackling.

For this recipe, chef and cookbook author Hayden Quinn teamed up with comedian Matt Okine to share some tips about how to get it just right.

It takes a few hours of prep, but it’s worth it – and it pairs perfectly with the green apple slaw, which is quite tart and cuts through the fat.

Rub the seasoning into your lamb before searing the fat to help release the flavours. (ABC TV: Wesley Mitton)

This is another recipe that requires a little pre-planning, as it needs a few hours in the oven.

However, it is simple to prepare, and the result is a tender, succulent, fall-apart lamb roast that’s bursting with flavour — and the oven does all the heavy lifting.

This whole roasted cauliflower with turmeric coconut sauce is an impressive vegetarian and vegan main that's perfect a special event or Sunday roast. (ABC News: Hetty Lui McKinnon)

Whole roasted cauliflower is versatile if you're looking for a meat-free option for the dinner table and there are plenty of flavour possibilities in this recipe from Hetty Lui McKinnon.

Hetty suggests smothering it under a lemony tahini sauce and topping with black olives, balsamic-soaked raisins and parsley, or serving on a bed of romesco sauce, scattered with roasted chickpeas and baby spinach.

World.title: Zak Butters informs Port Adelaide he will depart club
World.content:
Port Adelaide's three-time best and fairest winner Zak Butters has requested to leave the club via free agency and return home to Victoria.

The 25-year-old dual All-Australian's future has dominated headlines all season with reports of offers of up to $18 million over eight years from Richmond, Geelong, Collingwood and the Western Bulldogs.

"I've made a decision to head home. It's obviously been one that I've wrestled with for a while now," he said.

"It's been a tough decision and one that I haven't taken lightly.

"Although I've loved my time in Adelaide … I'm probably at a stage in my life where I'd like to get back around some family and friends and enjoy some more time with them.

"There are so many special memories I'll take with me and hold with me forever … I'll be forever in debt to the football club for drafting a skinny club from Darley."

Butters said he would "always be a Port Adelaide person" and would "always value this club and what it's done for me".

"The supporters have been everything, they've always got around since day one of being drafted, even this year they've been awesome and showed nothing but love and support," he said.

"I feel like I've always tried to repay them in the right way and play football in the right way."

Zak Butters is a dual all-Australian. (Supplied: Port Adelaide Football Club)

In a club statement, the Power said they would now work to facilitate his request whilst securing the best outcome for the club.

"Port Adelaide has been informed by Zak Butters and his management that he intends to exercise his rights as a restricted free agent and explore a return home to Victoria," the statement said.

"Zak has been an outstanding servant to the football club since debuting in 2019.

"He is a three-time John Cahill Medallist and dual All-Australian and we thank him for everything he has given to Port Adelaide."

ABC Sport reported Zak Butters had informed some teammates in July of his decision to move to Victoria; a story that was denied by the club at the time.

Butters played 17 games this season before a syndesmosis injury in Round 18 prematurely ended his campaign, with coach Josh Carr admitting the star midfielder was likely departing after their 10-point win over Essendon on the weekend.

Port Adelaide has been adamant all season they would match any bid on Butters and force a trade to try maximise their draft capital.

Speaking to ABC Sport in May, chief executive Matthew Richardson said the club would focus on their best interests.

"There will be offers that we can match and we will match. It does give the club a fair bit of control in what happens," he said.

World.title: Business leaders urge governments to act as smelter power deadline looms
World.content:
Rio Tinto's deadline for a new power deal for its Bell Bay Aluminium smelter in Tasmania's north is just one week away, as business leaders step up pressure on the state and federal governments to help secure the smelter's future.

The smelter, which directly employs about 550 people, is one of the biggest companies connected to Tasmania's power grid.

Last year Rio Tinto signed a one-year power deal with Hydro Tasmania. That deal is due to expire at the end of the year.

Green energy funding snub for renewable-powered aluminium smelter Further doubt has been cast over the future of an aluminium smelter in Tasmania's north-east after a federal MP said it would not be eligible for a green energy scheme.

Last month, federal Bass MP Jess Teesdale said she understood Rio Tinto had set a deadline for the end of this month to secure a new power deal, with a "very high risk the smelter would close" if the deadline is not met.

State-owned power company Hydro Tasmania has continued to negotiate a power deal with Rio Tinto, which was offering $60 million less than what Hydro Tasmania was asking for.

Uncertainty over the deal and the smelter's future has prompted 13 northern Tasmanian industry and community leaders to write open letters to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Premier Jeremy Rockliff, calling for urgent federal and state action to secure the smelter's future.

Bell Bay Aluminium is one of the biggest power users connected to the Tasmanian grid. (ABC News: Mitchell Woolnough)

Industry, community leaders demand action

Among the signatories were Bell Bay Advanced Manufacturing Zone chief executive Susie Bower and Tasmanian Minerals, Manufacturing and Energy Council chief executive Ray Mostogl.

The letter to Mr Rockliff urged a new 10-year power agreement be signed as soon as possible.

"In 2025, the smelter paid almost $76 million in salaries, invested $40 million in capital works and spent approximately $262 million with around 180 Tasmanian suppliers," the letter reads.

Speaking at Bell Bay this morning, Ms Bower said the outcome of negotiations was critical to Tasmania's future.

"We want to have the voices here of industry, unions and community, come together with business to say to our governments, 'this is critically important that you work together, you get a solution, and you get it done now'," Ms Bower said.

"Hydro [Tasmania] is owned by the state government, so that is the critical negotiation that needs to occur.

"But if there is a gap then the state government needs to be putting that on the table for the federal government to be able to come to a solution together."

Susie Bower says community and business stakeholders have come together to call on the state and federal governments to act. (ABC News: Kelsey Reid)

George Town Mayor Greg Kieser said if the smelter were to close, the impact on the George Town community, and Tasmania more broadly, would be "huge".

"Both from the personal side and families who rely on that income, to the supply chain who rely on the business that keeps them viable," Councillor Kieser said.

"You really just can't understate the impact that [Bell Bay's closure] will have on this immediate community.

"So if you just looked at rateable revenue, the hole that it would leave in my community's finances would be massive," he said.

Government minister Jo Palmer said Hydro Tasmania had put a "very good" power deal on the table for Rio Tinto to consider.

"Now we need the federal government to step in, just as it's done in New South Wales and in Queensland to actually bridge that gap between what Rio is saying it needs and what Hydro Tasmania is able to put on the table," Ms Palmer said.

Jo Palmer says Hydro Tasmania has put a "very good" offer on the table. (ABC News: Ebony ten Broeke)

Asked if Hydro Tasmania would be willing to bridge the $60 million gap to secure a deal, Ms Palmer said that was not Hydro Tasmania's responsibility.

A spokesperson for federal Industry Minister Tim Ayres said the Tasmanian government had "complete control" over the "supply of low-cost, renewable electricity for Tasmanian industry".

"We encourage the Tasmanian government to use all the levers at its disposal to support its industrial base," the spokesperson said.

Deputy Tasmanian Labor leader Janie Finlay said the state government needed to secure a fair and competitive deal.

"Once that deal is done, Premier Rockliff needs to take a clear package to Canberra and seek Commonwealth support," Ms Finlay said.

According to its website, the Bell Bay Aluminium smelter produces roughly 190,000 tonnes of aluminium annually.

World.title: Orbit drilling set to grow 1.7Moz NSW polymetallic resource
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Orbit drilling set to grow 1.7Moz NSW polymetallic resource Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 24, 2026 — 4:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Orbit Resources has fired up the drill rig for a new campaign at its 1.7-million-ounce gold equivalent, gold-silver-base metals, Lewis Ponds project in New South Wales. The company is targeting resource expansion after a fresh batch of assays confirmed a significant mineralised zone sitting outside the current deposit. Orbit, formerly known as Godolphin Resources, is using a track-mounted diamond drill rig to test high-priority targets at the 148-square-kilometre project 15 km east of Orange. The program comes amid a backdrop of renewed interest in NSW’s Lachlan Fold Belt, where the likes of Regis Resources and C29 are chasing precious and polymetallic base metal systems. A track-mounted diamond drill rig has arrived at Orbit Resources’ Lewis Ponds gold-silver-base metals project in New South Wales. The company’s new program will test several key targets, including a specific off-hole electromagnetic conductor in the footwall of the main deposit, which Orbit believes represents a concealed accumulation of sulphides. The rods will also be turning at Tom’s Lode in the south of the company’s project area to gather samples for metallurgical test work and to upgrade resource confidence levels. The move follows the receipt of all remaining assays from a five-hole, 1663m reverse circulation and diamond drilling program completed earlier this year.



‘Significant upside exists both within and beyond the current Lewis Ponds resource footprint.’ Orbit Resources managing director Jeneta Owens One of the most encouraging results came from a hole that intersected 27 metres at 0.97 grams per tonne (g/t) gold equivalent from 83m, including a higher-grade 10-metre section running 1.44g/t gold equivalent from 89m. Notably, the intercept hit the Quarry Lode, a zone of mineralisation that sits outside both the current mineral resource estimate and the proposed open pit defined in a February 2026 scoping study. The company says bringing Quarry Lode into the resource inventory could increase the project’s scale and support future mining studies. Orbit Resources managing director Jeneta Owens said: “The intersection of meaningful gold and base metal mineralisation within the Quarry Lode is particularly important given its location outside the current Mineral Resource Estimate and proposed open pit. The results demonstrate the potential for this area to contribute additional mineralisation and support future mining studies aimed at evaluating open pit expansion opportunities.” The latest assays also include a full breakdown from the impressive Cousin Jack prospect discovery hole, announced in June. The hole hit two broad sulphide zones, with the upper zone returning 79 metres running at 1.3 per cent zinc equivalent from 311m and a lower zone delivering a hefty 104 metres grading 1.3 per cent zinc equivalent from 527m.



Within those broad zones were multiple higher-grade slices, including 15m at 2.8 per cent zinc equivalent, 11m at 4.4 per cent zinc equivalent and an impressive 1.7m intercept grading an eye-catching 13.1 per cent zinc equivalent. Orbit says downhole electromagnetic surveys have confirmed the Cousin Jack mineralisation is strongly conductive, with readings up to 1500 Siemens. Management believes this validates its exploration model and provides a powerful targeting tool for higher-grade mineralised centres. A 1.6-kilometre-long induced polarisation trend will now be screened with a ground electromagnetic survey in the fourth quarter, while a drone magnetic survey is planned for next month- The Lewis Ponds project already boasts a formidable JORC-compliant resource of 17.52 million tonnes grading 1.12g/t gold, 53.34g/t silver, 2.06 per cent zinc, 1.1 per cent lead and 0.14 per cent copper for a combined 1.7 million ounces of gold equivalent, including 630,000 ounces of gold and 30.1 million ounces of silver. Beyond its flagship project, Orbit has plenty waiting in the wings across almost 1700 square kilometres of gold-copper ground around Lewis Ponds in the broader Orange region, spanning established resources, drill-ready targets and greenfields opportunities. The company’s Mt Aubrey prospect,35km northeast of Parkes, has some runs on the board with an inferred 1.21Mt at 1.61g/t gold for 62,400 ounces within a 6km gold corridor. Meanwhile, Orbit’s Copper Hill East target offers a different prize, the hunt for a bigger porphyry system. Sitting 30km north of Molong, its 8km copper-gold corridor is less than 10km north of Golden Cross Resources’ Copper Hill porphyry deposit, which contains 280,000 tonnes of copper and 750,000 ounces of gold, with fieldwork now dialling in targets for drilling.



Behind those front-runners, the company’s Three Rivers prospect carries a 550-metre copper trend with historical samples up to a hefty 12.6 per cent copper, while its Calula target is a potential Lewis Ponds analogue across an 8km mineralised trend. Orbit’s Lyons, Auri and Sorrento targets add further pipeline depth. The porphyry hunt runs deeper too. The company’s never-drilled CM1 hotspot provides another greenfield shot, while 70km northwest of Orange, Orbit retains exposure to the 290-square-kilometre Yeoval-Goodrich copper-gold joint venture. Great Plains Metals has earned 51 per cent and is spending towards 70 per cent, giving the company another porphyry play without footing the entire exploration bill. With a new drill program underway aimed at growing an already significant figure, a new mineralised lode knocking on the door of the resource and a powerful geophysical tool lighting up a recent discovery, Orbit appears to have a full dance card as it looks to build on its solid foundation in a well-regarded Australian mining district. World.title: I love my boring little suburb but it does have some downsides
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Growing up in Cheltenham, we used to complain to my parents that it was boring, no one had heard of it, there were no shops and nothing ever happened. Little did we know that these things are what makes Cheltenham special. You probably have not heard of Cheltenham. We like it this way! Nestled between Beecroft and Epping in the north-west of Sydney, 22 kilometres from the CBD, it is not a suburb that seeks attention. There are no glittering skylines, fashionable restaurant precincts or crowds of tourists. It rarely makes headlines, and perhaps that is its greatest strength. A Sydney tailor, William Chorley, founded Cheltenham in 1890 and named it after his hometown in England. Chorley was the biggest landowner in the area and wanted to maintain the peace and quiet and so placed multiple covenants on land that he sold. Some covenants prevented pubs opening – even today the only place you can get a beer is at the Cheltenham Recreation Club. Even more covenants prevented commercial activity in the suburb, and as Chorley owned most of the land around the railway, Cheltenham Station today remains free of commercial development. We used to joke that the only shop in Cheltenham was the canteen at Cheltenham Girls’ High School, which consistently ranks as one of the highest achieving comprehensive schools in NSW. Every day, hundreds of girls in their distinctive pink uniforms make the march from the station to the school. Cheltenham represents something increasingly precious in modern Sydney – a suburb where nature still shapes daily life, where quiet streets remain genuinely quiet, and where the bush is not simply something viewed from a distance but an integral part of the community. As Sydney grows, we should ask an important question: what should never be sacrificed?



Cheltenham provides one answer. Two women walk along Cheltenham Road, in a suburb where quiet streets remain genuinely quiet. Audrey Richardson Bordered by magnificent bushland and the valleys of the Lane Cove National Park, Cheltenham offers something that cannot be recreated once it is lost. Towering eucalypts, sandstone gullies and native bush form an attractive backdrop. Federation homes, a welcoming recreation club and a very popular oval add to this suburban utopia. The only shop is the ticket office at the railway station. We even have two post boxes! These things create a living environment that shapes the suburb’s identity and the wellbeing of everyone fortunate enough to live here. Cheltenham residents living in the vicinity of Devlins Creek are surrounded by bushland. Sitthixay Ditthavong The Hut of Happy Omen is a historic open-air meditation and sleeping hut built in 1949 and managed by the NSW National Trust. Sitthixay Ditthavong The benefits are obvious every morning. Residents wake not to the constant roar of traffic but to the calls of kookaburras, lorikeets and cockatoos. Bush tracks begin only minutes from front doors. Children grow up knowing the sounds of native birds rather than endless construction. Even an evening walk allows you to reconnect with nature rather than escape from congestion.



Rainbow lorikeet on Cobran Road. Sitthixay Ditthavong Galahs on the grass verges. Audrey Richardson This isn’t simply sentimentality. Access to mature trees and bushland reduces stress, improves physical health, supports biodiversity and strengthens mental wellbeing. Green space is not a luxury reserved for national parks and weekend holidays. It is an essential ingredient of healthy communities. There are, of course, negatives to our little suburb. The cockatoos have advanced demolition skills and consider timber verandas and window frames to be little more than chew toys. Brush turkeys believe every carefully landscaped garden is a construction project requiring a large mound of leaves. And if you’ve ever wondered where all Sydney’s spiders retire after a long career, many seem to have chosen Cheltenham! But the beauty of the abundant wildlife more than makes up for some minor inconveniences. One of the most prized things about living in Cheltenham is the peace and quiet. While I complained about this in my youth, I now recognise this as a real asset. All over Sydney, everyday life is dominated by heavy traffic, construction, aircraft and constant activity. Genuine silence has become almost unfamiliar.



Cheltenham offers something different. Its streets remain calm. Traffic is largely local. Mature gardens soften the landscape. Federation homes line many of the streets. The bush absorbs much of the surrounding noise. There is room to pause, to think and simply to enjoy being outdoors. That quality matters. A peaceful neighbourhood like Cheltenham contributes to stronger communities. People walk more often. They know their neighbours. Children ride bicycles. Families spend time outdoors rather than behind closed doors. Growing up, we had wonderful neighbours who became lifelong friends. Community is built not only through organised events but through daily encounters made possible by a suburb that encourages people to slow down. Cheltenham Girls’ High students in their distinctive pink uniforms. Brook Mitchell Federation homes line many of the streets. Sitthixay Ditthavong Perhaps this explains why so many families remain in Cheltenham for decades. Some who grew up there eventually return to raise their own children. Some never leave in the first place. That continuity creates a genuine sense of belonging.



Growth is inevitable. Cities evolve. Housing demand is real and must be addressed. But not every suburb should become denser simply because it can. Places like Cheltenham perform an important role within the Sydney metropolitan region. They preserve mature tree canopies that help cool the city. They protect wildlife corridors connecting significant bushland. They provide environmental resilience during hot summers. Once those qualities disappear, they cannot simply be replanted. A peaceful neighbourhood character built over generations can be lost surprisingly quickly. Sydney’s future should not be measured solely by the number of apartments constructed. Success should also be measured by what we choose to preserve. Thoughtful planning can accommodate growth while respecting the environmental and community values that make places unique. Protecting established bushland and heritage homes and preserving neighbourhood character are investments in the city’s future, not obstacles to it. Cheltenham offers much to its residents. The opportunity to walk beneath gums after work. To hear birds instead of traffic. To let children explore bush tracks safely. To enjoy cool shade on a summer afternoon beneath trees planted generations ago. These experiences enrich life in ways that statistics rarely capture, and developers rarely comprehend, but residents deeply understand. The balls used for real tennis are painstakingly made by hand at the Cheltenham Recreation Club. Sitthixay Ditthavong

World.title: Beetaloo taps infrastructure giant for 750km NT gas pipeline push
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Beetaloo taps infrastructure giant for 750km NT gas pipeline push Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Penny Taylor August 24, 2026 — 4:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beetaloo Energy Australia has tapped one of the nation’s biggest gas infrastructure players to map out a 750-kilometre pipeline that could become the critical midstream link between its Carpentaria shale gas project and its ambitious Beetaloo Digital development near Darwin. Under a non-binding memorandum of understanding (MOU), Australian Gas Infrastructure Group (AGIG) intends to lead the design and planning of the pipeline and associated infrastructure needed to connect Carpentaria with future demand centres around Darwin. Conceptual aerial view of Beetaloo Energy Australia’s proposed Beetaloo Digital AI data centre campus at Waddell, near Darwin in the Northern Territory. The pipeline is intended to sit within the Northern Territory Government’s Territory Energy Link common-user infrastructure corridor, which Beetaloo believes could streamline approvals and development. At one end sits more than 1.6 trillion cubic feet of gas (Tcf) in previously reported 2C contingent resources. At the other, Beetaloo has secured NT Government exclusivity over 185 hectares at its Waddell site for Beetaloo Digital, its wholly owned subsidiary developing a proposed vertically integrated gas-to-power AI data centre campus.



‘This MOU with AGIG complements our upstream gas development capabilities as we continue to advance the Beetaloo Digital opportunity.’ Beetaloo Energy Australia managing director Alex Underwood Beetaloo’s footprint stretches across 28.9 million acres in the McArthur and Beetaloo sub-basins, including 80 per cent of the Eastern depositional Trough of the McArthur Basin. The company describes the trough as having enormous conventional and unconventional hydrocarbon potential. At the same time, industry activity is ramping up to appraise discoveries across the wider basin. AGIG brings serious infrastructure muscle to the party. It owns and operates more than 40,000km of gas pipelines serving more than 2.1 million customers, as well as gas storage infrastructure. It can also finance, build, own, operate and maintain major gas transmission infrastructure. Craig de Laine, chief executive of AGIG, said the basin could play an important role in the Territory’s future, with the group looking to develop practical infrastructure solutions to support that opportunity and long-term growth. The latest deal brings a second industry heavyweight into Beetaloo’s corner, following its recent collaboration with global oilfield services group Halliburton. Halliburton brings upstream development expertise and exposure to modular gas-fired power through its partnership with US distributed power specialist VoltaGrid, while AGIG potentially fills the midstream gap.



The parties will jointly assess the gas transport, processing and other facilities required to support Beetaloo Digital, ultimately targeting a future final investment decision. Beetaloo Energy Australia managing director Alex Underwood said: “Together we will assess the infrastructure required to connect our gas resources with the proposed development and continue progressing the integrated project towards future commercialisation.” The immediate next step is to develop an integrated project plan. The MOU does not commit either party to a future transaction. Any development also remains subject to technical studies, commercial agreements, regulatory approvals and relevant board approvals. Carpentaria provides the upstream starting point for that bigger ambition and is already moving towards initial production. Flagship C-5H previously averaged 6.9 terajoules (TJ) per day during a 30-day production test, while the initial gas plant is designed for 25TJ/d. The development is intended to establish an early production base from which Beetaloo can progressively scale its shale gas resources as demand grows. With its hyperscale AI data centre campus taking centre stage at Waddell, Beetaloo Digital could provide Carpentaria with an enormous new market. Beetaloo has previously estimated one gigawatt of computing capacity could consume up to 200TJ/d – eight times the initial Carpentaria plant capacity – while its broader concept envisages up to 2GW across two campuses. Management believes that scale of around-the-clock demand could help drive development of its vast gas resource over time.



Beetaloo says the gas delivered from Carpentaria could provide the firm power to underpin the development. Down the track, solar and batteries could shoulder more of the load, while surplus generation could also feed into the Territory’s grid. Waddell has geography firmly in its favour. The site sits near the proposed Darwin Energy Hub and close to Darwin’s subsea fibre-optic infrastructure, while Darwin is little more than 25 milliseconds in data-transfer time from major Southeast Asian markets. With a commanding resource footprint, control of the Waddell opportunity and heavyweights Halliburton and AGIG in the tent, Beetaloo is assembling a formidable gas-to-digital chain. If the 750km pipeline gets the green light, it could become the steel artery connecting its basin-scale gas with a potentially enormous new AI-energy market near Darwin. World.title: Accused killer’s third bid for freedom after allegedly dumping body in river
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts Accused killer’s third bid for freedom after allegedly dumping body in river Cloe Read August 24, 2026 — 4:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Queensland man accused of killing his former partner before dumping her body in the Brisbane River has made a third bid for freedom. Jesse Wahlen Beale allegedly murdered mother-of-two Crystal Beale after they went out to dinner in Sunnybank in Brisbane’s south in 2025. Jesse Beale was arrested and charged over the alleged murder of his former wife Crystal Beale. Facebook She was said to have been dropped off by Mr Beale on Ryan Street in West End about 9.30pm. She was allegedly murdered that evening, and her body taken to the river near Orleigh Park in West End. Mr Beale allegedly killed the 49-year-old after she threatened him over alleged images he had kept of Ms Beale being sexually assaulted while unconscious.



Mr Beale has so far made two unsuccessful bail applications and hired top barrister Saul Holt KC to represent him for an appeal relating to his most recent refusal, which related to a report by defence expert witness Professor John Duflou. Holt relied on the report, which found drowning could not be excluded as a cause of death, for the second application for bail. This was also combined with claims of her self-harm, substance abuse and threats of suicide, which had significantly weakened the allegations. Crystal Beale was last seen alive on February 21, 2025. Queensland Police He said the new evidence “dramatically changes the picture” for the prosecution case. The bail application was ultimately refused by Justice Patrick McAfferty.



“That contested issue opens up questions of causation, opens up questions of time, and especially in circumstances where the evidence is that … [Mr Beale] was in company with [Ms Beale] about 9.55pm, and the body of the deceased is found … around 5.30am,” Holt told the Court of Appeal on Monday. Related Article Courts Accused killer kept photos of unconscious ex-wife on device, court hears Holt said the only reason Beale was refused bail was because of his flight risk. Deputy Director of Public Prosecutions Caroline Marco said the report did not detract from the conclusion that Mr Beale allegedly caused Ms Beale’s neck injuries, and put her body in the water. She said the judge who ruled on Mr Beale’s bail application was not compelled by the report to find that there had been a material change of circumstances.



Marco said the allegation Mr Beale caused the significant neck injuries to Ms Beale had always been a fundamental premise of the prosecution case. “Those neck injuries may not be able to be proved irrefutably to have caused death, but notwithstanding, it cannot be denied they were seriously life-threatening,” she said. She said a pathologist’s report before the court did not provide any explanation to suggest the injuries could have been self-inflicted. Crystal Beale’s body was pulled from the Brisbane RIver. Facebook Marco said the judge found in the second bail application that the Duflou report simply added to an evidentiary foundation that had already been considered in the first application.



“That is, that the death could have resulted from drowning. But it didn’t detract from the possibility that [Mr Beale] may have caused the life-threatening injuries, and that was, with respect, correct.” She said the report would not have altered the court to grant bail, given the first judge concluded that the prosecution case was reasonably strong. Marco said the two judges, and the Court of Appeal judges, would have evidence before them that included that Mr Beale was the last person in Ms Beale’s company, the CCTV did not show any person leaving the vehicle at the time Mr Beale claimed Ms Beale left, and searches on Mr Beale’s device relating to tide times, VPN hiding search history, and CCTV cameras. Beale’s appeal remains before the Court of Appeal. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Trump’s weight is starting to worry doctors
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaDonald Trump Trump’s weight is starting to worry doctors Dan Diamond August 24, 2026 — 4:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US President Donald Trump has faced scrutiny for bruising on his hands, swelling in his ankles and apparent drowsiness, among other questions about his health. Some doctors say they’re worried about another risk: the 23 pounds (10 kilograms) that Trump may have gained since his last campaign for president. In August 2023, when he was charged in Georgia in an election interference case, Trump’s booking record listed his weight as 215 pounds (98 kilos). He weighed 238 pounds (108 kilos) in May of this year, according to a medical report released by the White House that month. The US president has repeatedly invoked weight – his own and others’ – in public remarks. AP That would leave him about 0.8 kilos shy of being classified as “obese”, as he was in 2019 and 2020, given his height of 190.5 centimetres. Trump’s medical measurements have long been dissected, and it’s unclear where the 2023 weight figure came from. But the president has appeared heavier in photos than he did during his campaign, and the administration said he gained 14 pounds (6 kilos) between his most recent annual medical checkups.



White House physicians have said they’ve advised Trump – who has made little secret of his love for fast food and his distaste for intense exercise – to focus on weight loss, improving his diet and sustained physical activity. Outside doctors put it more directly: The 80-year-old president would be safer if he reduced his waistline. “We know that obesity is a strong risk factor for numerous health issues – as well as premature disability and death,” said Scott Kahan, a George Washington University physician and director for the National Center for Weight and Wellness. Trump maintains that he has never taken a GLP-1 anti-obesity drug. Getty Images “Addressing obesity to protect the president’s health should be a priority similar to ensuring Secret Service protections for his life.” The White House did not directly respond to questions about Trump’s weight, pointing instead to his energy and stamina.



Trump has demonstrated signs of healthy ageing. His weekly White House schedule frequently includes intense periods of meetings, press events and public remarks; he spends many weekends playing golf. His physicians have repeatedly said that they’ve been impressed by his energy, cognitive fitness and other positive markers. “I told him he could do a better job with his diet, and he would be a little healthier if he exercised and lost some weight, but other than that, he was in outstanding shape for his age,” Ronny Jackson, who served as Trump’s physician in his first term, wrote in a 2022 memoir. But Trump’s weight is a risk factor, medical experts have said, acknowledging that many Americans struggle with similar challenges. More than 40 per cent of adult Americans are obese, and an additional 30 per cent-plus are overweight, according to federal data. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy jnr and other senior officials have said that helping reduce Americans’ weight should be a priority as part of their campaign to “Make America Healthy Again” and help people live longer lives. The president has also repeatedly invoked weight – his own and others’ – in public remarks. It is a favourite taunt he uses against opponents such as Democratic Illinois Governor J.B. Pritzker and his former adviser Chris Christie.



“I would never call anybody fat,” Trump said in a speech at last month’s White House correspondents’ dinner, where he mocked the idea of Christie and Democratic New York Congressman Jerry Nadler fighting over a cheesecake. “I have my own problems, you know?” Related Article Donald Trump Trump in ‘excellent health’ and ‘fully fit’ to serve, his physician says Trump has sometimes quipped about his own appearance, saying he hasn’t wanted to wear bulletproof vests because they could make him look fat. He has also jokingly defended his diet. “Maybe junk food is good and the other food is no good,” Trump said in the Oval Office in May. “I know many, many people that all they do is watch their weight, their this, their that, and they kicked the bucket, and here we are. I feel great.” In a statement, the White House praised Trump’s fitness and contrasted him with predecessor Joe Biden.



“President Trump’s sharpness, unmatched energy, relentless work ethic and historic accessibility stand in stark contrast to what we saw during the last administration, when Democrats and the legacy media intentionally covered up Joe Biden’s serious mental and physical decline from the American people,” spokesman Davis Ingle said in a statement. “President Trump is the sharpest and most accessible president in American history who is working non-stop to solve problems and deliver on his promises.” The White House did not respond to other questions about the president’s health, including physicians’ recommendation this year that Trump address his weight and whether he has ever taken a GLP-1 anti-obesity drug. Trump has said he has never taken a GLP-1 drug. Trump’s diet and weight have been scrutinised across his political career, with his love for McDonald’s a staple. Pressed by interviewer Barbara Walters in 2015 on whether there was anything they would change about their father, Trump’s children eventually conceded that they didn’t like his diet.



“I want him to eat healthier,” Ivanka Trump told Walters. Trump also discussed his weight in a September 2016 appearance on The Dr Oz Show. A letter released by Trump’s personal physician that month said he weighed 236 pounds. “The one thing I would like to do is be able to drop 15, 20 pounds,” Trump told Mehmet Oz, the show’s host – now the Medicare and Medicaid chief in Trump’s administration – saying that it was difficult because of his lifestyle. Trump has since joked about the experience. “I went on his show and he determined that I should lose weight,” the president said earlier this year, reflecting on his conversation with Oz. “He said, ‘I think you should lose weight.’ I said, ‘I don’t need you saying that in front of millions of people. You don’t have to tell me that.’”



Contrary to his goal, Trump grew heavier during his first term as president. Jackson in January 2018 said that Trump weighed 239 pounds, about a pound shy of being classified as obese under body-mass index (BMI) calculations. Related Article US politics Trump’s diagnosis revealed after ‘swollen leg’ photos trigger alarm “I think a reasonable goal, over the next year or so, is to lose 10-15 pounds,” Jackson told reporters that month. “We talked about diet and exercise a lot. He’s more enthusiastic about the diet part than the exercise part, but we’re going to do both.” It is unclear whether Trump adopted any changes to his diet or began more exercise during his first term, and spokespeople for the White House and Jackson did not respond to questions about it. Sean Conley, Jackson’s successor, said in February 2019 that Trump weighed 243 pounds, making him technically obese. Conley in June 2020 said Trump weighed 244 pounds.



Four months later, Trump contracted a serious case of COVID-19, the impact of which is linked with obesity, physicians have found. The president received a then experimental antibody cocktail, produced by Regeneron, that he credited with helping save his life. He left office in January 2021. Trump was noticeably thinner as he announced another campaign for president in 2023. A doctor’s note released by the campaign in November said that he had “reduced his weight through an improved diet and continued daily physical activity”. Loading Trump has continued to face questions in his second term about his weight. Those questions were renewed recently after Stat News reported that the administration had worked with Eli Lilly to expedite access to a new weight-loss medication for an unnamed patient who was 79 at the time. The White House has denied that Trump received the drug, Retatrutide, which is more powerful than traditional GLP-1 medications. Eli Lilly said it could not comment on any individual patient’s medical prescription, including whether Trump had ever been prescribed Retatrutide, a GLP-1 or other drugs.



Some doctors, who declined to comment specifically on Trump, disagreed on how to interpret a hypothetical 80-year-old patient with a BMI of 30. “BMI is a great screening tool, but it’s not everything,” said Gitanjali Srivastava, a physician who specialises in obesity. Srivastava, who said she has treated patients in their 70s and 80s with obesity, said that weight could be a secondary issue to other markers of health. Related Article Cardiovascular health The four visible signs of heart problems “At that age, it’s less about a number, but more about, what is the per cent body fat? What are we trying to improve including overall health, function, body fat?” she said. David Kessler, who served as head of the Food and Drug Administration under presidents George Bush snr and Bill Clinton, said that he was deeply concerned about Americans’ excess body fat, which he said contributes to premature death.



“That fat around the midsection – that visceral adiposity – is fat around our liver, pancreas, our heart where it doesn’t belong,” Kessler said. For his part, Trump has said he was wary of growing heavier, invoking former president William Howard Taft, who weighed more than 300 pounds. “He was our heaviest president, and I have to be careful because I don’t want to supersede his record,” Trump told second lady Usha Vance in a podcast posted last month. “And a thing like that would be possible if I allowed it to happen.” Washington Post Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Orbit drilling set to grow 1.7Moz NSW polymetallic resource
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Orbit drilling set to grow 1.7Moz NSW polymetallic resource Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Murray Ward August 24, 2026 — 4:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Orbit Resources has fired up the drill rig for a new campaign at its 1.7-million-ounce gold equivalent, gold-silver-base metals, Lewis Ponds project in New South Wales. The company is targeting resource expansion after a fresh batch of assays confirmed a significant mineralised zone sitting outside the current deposit. Orbit, formerly known as Godolphin Resources, is using a track-mounted diamond drill rig to test high-priority targets at the 148-square-kilometre project 15 km east of Orange. The program comes amid a backdrop of renewed interest in NSW’s Lachlan Fold Belt, where the likes of Regis Resources and C29 are chasing precious and polymetallic base metal systems. A track-mounted diamond drill rig has arrived at Orbit Resources’ Lewis Ponds gold-silver-base metals project in New South Wales. The company’s new program will test several key targets, including a specific off-hole electromagnetic conductor in the footwall of the main deposit, which Orbit believes represents a concealed accumulation of sulphides. The rods will also be turning at Tom’s Lode in the south of the company’s project area to gather samples for metallurgical test work and to upgrade resource confidence levels. The move follows the receipt of all remaining assays from a five-hole, 1663m reverse circulation and diamond drilling program completed earlier this year.



‘Significant upside exists both within and beyond the current Lewis Ponds resource footprint.’ Orbit Resources managing director Jeneta Owens One of the most encouraging results came from a hole that intersected 27 metres at 0.97 grams per tonne (g/t) gold equivalent from 83m, including a higher-grade 10-metre section running 1.44g/t gold equivalent from 89m. Notably, the intercept hit the Quarry Lode, a zone of mineralisation that sits outside both the current mineral resource estimate and the proposed open pit defined in a February 2026 scoping study. The company says bringing Quarry Lode into the resource inventory could increase the project’s scale and support future mining studies. Orbit Resources managing director Jeneta Owens said: “The intersection of meaningful gold and base metal mineralisation within the Quarry Lode is particularly important given its location outside the current Mineral Resource Estimate and proposed open pit. The results demonstrate the potential for this area to contribute additional mineralisation and support future mining studies aimed at evaluating open pit expansion opportunities.” The latest assays also include a full breakdown from the impressive Cousin Jack prospect discovery hole, announced in June. The hole hit two broad sulphide zones, with the upper zone returning 79 metres running at 1.3 per cent zinc equivalent from 311m and a lower zone delivering a hefty 104 metres grading 1.3 per cent zinc equivalent from 527m.



Within those broad zones were multiple higher-grade slices, including 15m at 2.8 per cent zinc equivalent, 11m at 4.4 per cent zinc equivalent and an impressive 1.7m intercept grading an eye-catching 13.1 per cent zinc equivalent. Orbit says downhole electromagnetic surveys have confirmed the Cousin Jack mineralisation is strongly conductive, with readings up to 1500 Siemens. Management believes this validates its exploration model and provides a powerful targeting tool for higher-grade mineralised centres. A 1.6-kilometre-long induced polarisation trend will now be screened with a ground electromagnetic survey in the fourth quarter, while a drone magnetic survey is planned for next month- The Lewis Ponds project already boasts a formidable JORC-compliant resource of 17.52 million tonnes grading 1.12g/t gold, 53.34g/t silver, 2.06 per cent zinc, 1.1 per cent lead and 0.14 per cent copper for a combined 1.7 million ounces of gold equivalent, including 630,000 ounces of gold and 30.1 million ounces of silver. Beyond its flagship project, Orbit has plenty waiting in the wings across almost 1700 square kilometres of gold-copper ground around Lewis Ponds in the broader Orange region, spanning established resources, drill-ready targets and greenfields opportunities. The company’s Mt Aubrey prospect,35km northeast of Parkes, has some runs on the board with an inferred 1.21Mt at 1.61g/t gold for 62,400 ounces within a 6km gold corridor. Meanwhile, Orbit’s Copper Hill East target offers a different prize, the hunt for a bigger porphyry system. Sitting 30km north of Molong, its 8km copper-gold corridor is less than 10km north of Golden Cross Resources’ Copper Hill porphyry deposit, which contains 280,000 tonnes of copper and 750,000 ounces of gold, with fieldwork now dialling in targets for drilling.



Behind those front-runners, the company’s Three Rivers prospect carries a 550-metre copper trend with historical samples up to a hefty 12.6 per cent copper, while its Calula target is a potential Lewis Ponds analogue across an 8km mineralised trend. Orbit’s Lyons, Auri and Sorrento targets add further pipeline depth. The porphyry hunt runs deeper too. The company’s never-drilled CM1 hotspot provides another greenfield shot, while 70km northwest of Orange, Orbit retains exposure to the 290-square-kilometre Yeoval-Goodrich copper-gold joint venture. Great Plains Metals has earned 51 per cent and is spending towards 70 per cent, giving the company another porphyry play without footing the entire exploration bill. With a new drill program underway aimed at growing an already significant figure, a new mineralised lode knocking on the door of the resource and a powerful geophysical tool lighting up a recent discovery, Orbit appears to have a full dance card as it looks to build on its solid foundation in a well-regarded Australian mining district.
