World.title: I love my boring little suburb but it does have some downsides
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Growing up in Cheltenham, we used to complain to my parents that it was boring, no one had heard of it, there were no shops and nothing ever happened. Little did we know that these things are what makes Cheltenham special. You probably have not heard of Cheltenham. We like it this way! Nestled between Beecroft and Epping in the north-west of Sydney, 22 kilometres from the CBD, it is not a suburb that seeks attention. There are no glittering skylines, fashionable restaurant precincts or crowds of tourists. It rarely makes headlines, and perhaps that is its greatest strength. A Sydney tailor, William Chorley, founded Cheltenham in 1890 and named it after his hometown in England. Chorley was the biggest landowner in the area and wanted to maintain the peace and quiet and so placed multiple covenants on land that he sold. Some covenants prevented pubs opening – even today the only place you can get a beer is at the Cheltenham Recreation Club. Even more covenants prevented commercial activity in the suburb, and as Chorley owned most of the land around the railway, Cheltenham Station today remains free of commercial development. We used to joke that the only shop in Cheltenham was the canteen at Cheltenham Girls’ High School, which consistently ranks as one of the highest achieving comprehensive schools in NSW. Every day, hundreds of girls in their distinctive pink uniforms make the march from the station to the school. Cheltenham represents something increasingly precious in modern Sydney – a suburb where nature still shapes daily life, where quiet streets remain genuinely quiet, and where the bush is not simply something viewed from a distance but an integral part of the community. As Sydney grows, we should ask an important question: what should never be sacrificed?



Cheltenham provides one answer. Two women walk along Cheltenham Road, in a suburb where quiet streets remain genuinely quiet. Audrey Richardson Bordered by magnificent bushland and the valleys of the Lane Cove National Park, Cheltenham offers something that cannot be recreated once it is lost. Towering eucalypts, sandstone gullies and native bush form an attractive backdrop. Federation homes, a welcoming recreation club and a very popular oval add to this suburban utopia. The only shop is the ticket office at the railway station. We even have two post boxes! These things create a living environment that shapes the suburb’s identity and the wellbeing of everyone fortunate enough to live here. Cheltenham residents living in the vicinity of Devlins Creek are surrounded by bushland. Sitthixay Ditthavong The Hut of Happy Omen is a historic open-air meditation and sleeping hut built in 1949 and managed by the NSW National Trust. Sitthixay Ditthavong The benefits are obvious every morning. Residents wake not to the constant roar of traffic but to the calls of kookaburras, lorikeets and cockatoos. Bush tracks begin only minutes from front doors. Children grow up knowing the sounds of native birds rather than endless construction. Even an evening walk allows you to reconnect with nature rather than escape from congestion.



Rainbow lorikeet on Cobran Road. Sitthixay Ditthavong Galahs on the grass verges. Audrey Richardson This isn’t simply sentimentality. Access to mature trees and bushland reduces stress, improves physical health, supports biodiversity and strengthens mental wellbeing. Green space is not a luxury reserved for national parks and weekend holidays. It is an essential ingredient of healthy communities. There are, of course, negatives to our little suburb. The cockatoos have advanced demolition skills and consider timber verandas and window frames to be little more than chew toys. Brush turkeys believe every carefully landscaped garden is a construction project requiring a large mound of leaves. And if you’ve ever wondered where all Sydney’s spiders retire after a long career, many seem to have chosen Cheltenham! But the beauty of the abundant wildlife more than makes up for some minor inconveniences. One of the most prized things about living in Cheltenham is the peace and quiet. While I complained about this in my youth, I now recognise this as a real asset. All over Sydney, everyday life is dominated by heavy traffic, construction, aircraft and constant activity. Genuine silence has become almost unfamiliar.



Cheltenham offers something different. Its streets remain calm. Traffic is largely local. Mature gardens soften the landscape. Federation homes line many of the streets. The bush absorbs much of the surrounding noise. There is room to pause, to think and simply to enjoy being outdoors. That quality matters. A peaceful neighbourhood like Cheltenham contributes to stronger communities. People walk more often. They know their neighbours. Children ride bicycles. Families spend time outdoors rather than behind closed doors. Growing up, we had wonderful neighbours who became lifelong friends. Community is built not only through organised events but through daily encounters made possible by a suburb that encourages people to slow down. Cheltenham Girls’ High students in their distinctive pink uniforms. Brook Mitchell Federation homes line many of the streets. Sitthixay Ditthavong Perhaps this explains why so many families remain in Cheltenham for decades. Some who grew up there eventually return to raise their own children. Some never leave in the first place. That continuity creates a genuine sense of belonging.



Growth is inevitable. Cities evolve. Housing demand is real and must be addressed. But not every suburb should become denser simply because it can. Places like Cheltenham perform an important role within the Sydney metropolitan region. They preserve mature tree canopies that help cool the city. They protect wildlife corridors connecting significant bushland. They provide environmental resilience during hot summers. Once those qualities disappear, they cannot simply be replanted. A peaceful neighbourhood character built over generations can be lost surprisingly quickly. Sydney’s future should not be measured solely by the number of apartments constructed. Success should also be measured by what we choose to preserve. Thoughtful planning can accommodate growth while respecting the environmental and community values that make places unique. Protecting established bushland and heritage homes and preserving neighbourhood character are investments in the city’s future, not obstacles to it. Cheltenham offers much to its residents. The opportunity to walk beneath gums after work. To hear birds instead of traffic. To let children explore bush tracks safely. To enjoy cool shade on a summer afternoon beneath trees planted generations ago. These experiences enrich life in ways that statistics rarely capture, and developers rarely comprehend, but residents deeply understand. The balls used for real tennis are painstakingly made by hand at the Cheltenham Recreation Club. Sitthixay Ditthavong

World.title: Beetaloo taps infrastructure giant for 750km NT gas pipeline push
World.content:
Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears Beetaloo taps infrastructure giant for 750km NT gas pipeline push Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Penny Taylor August 24, 2026 — 4:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Beetaloo Energy Australia has tapped one of the nation’s biggest gas infrastructure players to map out a 750-kilometre pipeline that could become the critical midstream link between its Carpentaria shale gas project and its ambitious Beetaloo Digital development near Darwin. Under a non-binding memorandum of understanding (MOU), Australian Gas Infrastructure Group (AGIG) intends to lead the design and planning of the pipeline and associated infrastructure needed to connect Carpentaria with future demand centres around Darwin. Conceptual aerial view of Beetaloo Energy Australia’s proposed Beetaloo Digital AI data centre campus at Waddell, near Darwin in the Northern Territory. The pipeline is intended to sit within the Northern Territory Government’s Territory Energy Link common-user infrastructure corridor, which Beetaloo believes could streamline approvals and development. At one end sits more than 1.6 trillion cubic feet of gas (Tcf) in previously reported 2C contingent resources. At the other, Beetaloo has secured NT Government exclusivity over 185 hectares at its Waddell site for Beetaloo Digital, its wholly owned subsidiary developing a proposed vertically integrated gas-to-power AI data centre campus.



‘This MOU with AGIG complements our upstream gas development capabilities as we continue to advance the Beetaloo Digital opportunity.’ Beetaloo Energy Australia managing director Alex Underwood Beetaloo’s footprint stretches across 28.9 million acres in the McArthur and Beetaloo sub-basins, including 80 per cent of the Eastern depositional Trough of the McArthur Basin. The company describes the trough as having enormous conventional and unconventional hydrocarbon potential. At the same time, industry activity is ramping up to appraise discoveries across the wider basin. AGIG brings serious infrastructure muscle to the party. It owns and operates more than 40,000km of gas pipelines serving more than 2.1 million customers, as well as gas storage infrastructure. It can also finance, build, own, operate and maintain major gas transmission infrastructure. Craig de Laine, chief executive of AGIG, said the basin could play an important role in the Territory’s future, with the group looking to develop practical infrastructure solutions to support that opportunity and long-term growth. The latest deal brings a second industry heavyweight into Beetaloo’s corner, following its recent collaboration with global oilfield services group Halliburton. Halliburton brings upstream development expertise and exposure to modular gas-fired power through its partnership with US distributed power specialist VoltaGrid, while AGIG potentially fills the midstream gap.



The parties will jointly assess the gas transport, processing and other facilities required to support Beetaloo Digital, ultimately targeting a future final investment decision. Beetaloo Energy Australia managing director Alex Underwood said: “Together we will assess the infrastructure required to connect our gas resources with the proposed development and continue progressing the integrated project towards future commercialisation.” The immediate next step is to develop an integrated project plan. The MOU does not commit either party to a future transaction. Any development also remains subject to technical studies, commercial agreements, regulatory approvals and relevant board approvals. Carpentaria provides the upstream starting point for that bigger ambition and is already moving towards initial production. Flagship C-5H previously averaged 6.9 terajoules (TJ) per day during a 30-day production test, while the initial gas plant is designed for 25TJ/d. The development is intended to establish an early production base from which Beetaloo can progressively scale its shale gas resources as demand grows. With its hyperscale AI data centre campus taking centre stage at Waddell, Beetaloo Digital could provide Carpentaria with an enormous new market. Beetaloo has previously estimated one gigawatt of computing capacity could consume up to 200TJ/d – eight times the initial Carpentaria plant capacity – while its broader concept envisages up to 2GW across two campuses. Management believes that scale of around-the-clock demand could help drive development of its vast gas resource over time.



Beetaloo says the gas delivered from Carpentaria could provide the firm power to underpin the development. Down the track, solar and batteries could shoulder more of the load, while surplus generation could also feed into the Territory’s grid. Waddell has geography firmly in its favour. The site sits near the proposed Darwin Energy Hub and close to Darwin’s subsea fibre-optic infrastructure, while Darwin is little more than 25 milliseconds in data-transfer time from major Southeast Asian markets. With a commanding resource footprint, control of the Waddell opportunity and heavyweights Halliburton and AGIG in the tent, Beetaloo is assembling a formidable gas-to-digital chain. If the 750km pipeline gets the green light, it could become the steel artery connecting its basin-scale gas with a potentially enormous new AI-energy market near Darwin. World.title: Accused killer’s third bid for freedom after allegedly dumping body in river
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts Accused killer’s third bid for freedom after allegedly dumping body in river Cloe Read August 24, 2026 — 4:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A Queensland man accused of killing his former partner before dumping her body in the Brisbane River has made a third bid for freedom. Jesse Wahlen Beale allegedly murdered mother-of-two Crystal Beale after they went out to dinner in Sunnybank in Brisbane’s south in 2025. Jesse Beale was arrested and charged over the alleged murder of his former wife Crystal Beale. Facebook She was said to have been dropped off by Mr Beale on Ryan Street in West End about 9.30pm. She was allegedly murdered that evening, and her body taken to the river near Orleigh Park in West End. Mr Beale allegedly killed the 49-year-old after she threatened him over alleged images he had kept of Ms Beale being sexually assaulted while unconscious.



Mr Beale has so far made two unsuccessful bail applications and hired top barrister Saul Holt KC to represent him for an appeal relating to his most recent refusal, which related to a report by defence expert witness Professor John Duflou. Holt relied on the report, which found drowning could not be excluded as a cause of death, for the second application for bail. This was also combined with claims of her self-harm, substance abuse and threats of suicide, which had significantly weakened the allegations. Crystal Beale was last seen alive on February 21, 2025. Queensland Police He said the new evidence “dramatically changes the picture” for the prosecution case. The bail application was ultimately refused by Justice Patrick McAfferty.



“That contested issue opens up questions of causation, opens up questions of time, and especially in circumstances where the evidence is that … [Mr Beale] was in company with [Ms Beale] about 9.55pm, and the body of the deceased is found … around 5.30am,” Holt told the Court of Appeal on Monday. Related Article Courts Accused killer kept photos of unconscious ex-wife on device, court hears Holt said the only reason Beale was refused bail was because of his flight risk. Deputy Director of Public Prosecutions Caroline Marco said the report did not detract from the conclusion that Mr Beale allegedly caused Ms Beale’s neck injuries, and put her body in the water. She said the judge who ruled on Mr Beale’s bail application was not compelled by the report to find that there had been a material change of circumstances.



Marco said the allegation Mr Beale caused the significant neck injuries to Ms Beale had always been a fundamental premise of the prosecution case. “Those neck injuries may not be able to be proved irrefutably to have caused death, but notwithstanding, it cannot be denied they were seriously life-threatening,” she said. She said a pathologist’s report before the court did not provide any explanation to suggest the injuries could have been self-inflicted. Crystal Beale’s body was pulled from the Brisbane RIver. Facebook Marco said the judge found in the second bail application that the Duflou report simply added to an evidentiary foundation that had already been considered in the first application.



“That is, that the death could have resulted from drowning. But it didn’t detract from the possibility that [Mr Beale] may have caused the life-threatening injuries, and that was, with respect, correct.” She said the report would not have altered the court to grant bail, given the first judge concluded that the prosecution case was reasonably strong. Marco said the two judges, and the Court of Appeal judges, would have evidence before them that included that Mr Beale was the last person in Ms Beale’s company, the CCTV did not show any person leaving the vehicle at the time Mr Beale claimed Ms Beale left, and searches on Mr Beale’s device relating to tide times, VPN hiding search history, and CCTV cameras. Beale’s appeal remains before the Court of Appeal. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Trump’s weight is starting to worry doctors
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaDonald Trump Trump’s weight is starting to worry doctors Dan Diamond August 24, 2026 — 4:11pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

US President Donald Trump has faced scrutiny for bruising on his hands, swelling in his ankles and apparent drowsiness, among other questions about his health. Some doctors say they’re worried about another risk: the 23 pounds (10 kilograms) that Trump may have gained since his last campaign for president. In August 2023, when he was charged in Georgia in an election interference case, Trump’s booking record listed his weight as 215 pounds (98 kilos). He weighed 238 pounds (108 kilos) in May of this year, according to a medical report released by the White House that month. The US president has repeatedly invoked weight – his own and others’ – in public remarks. AP That would leave him about 0.8 kilos shy of being classified as “obese”, as he was in 2019 and 2020, given his height of 190.5 centimetres. Trump’s medical measurements have long been dissected, and it’s unclear where the 2023 weight figure came from. But the president has appeared heavier in photos than he did during his campaign, and the administration said he gained 14 pounds (6 kilos) between his most recent annual medical checkups.



White House physicians have said they’ve advised Trump – who has made little secret of his love for fast food and his distaste for intense exercise – to focus on weight loss, improving his diet and sustained physical activity. Outside doctors put it more directly: The 80-year-old president would be safer if he reduced his waistline. “We know that obesity is a strong risk factor for numerous health issues – as well as premature disability and death,” said Scott Kahan, a George Washington University physician and director for the National Center for Weight and Wellness. Trump maintains that he has never taken a GLP-1 anti-obesity drug. Getty Images “Addressing obesity to protect the president’s health should be a priority similar to ensuring Secret Service protections for his life.” The White House did not directly respond to questions about Trump’s weight, pointing instead to his energy and stamina.



Trump has demonstrated signs of healthy ageing. His weekly White House schedule frequently includes intense periods of meetings, press events and public remarks; he spends many weekends playing golf. His physicians have repeatedly said that they’ve been impressed by his energy, cognitive fitness and other positive markers. “I told him he could do a better job with his diet, and he would be a little healthier if he exercised and lost some weight, but other than that, he was in outstanding shape for his age,” Ronny Jackson, who served as Trump’s physician in his first term, wrote in a 2022 memoir. But Trump’s weight is a risk factor, medical experts have said, acknowledging that many Americans struggle with similar challenges. More than 40 per cent of adult Americans are obese, and an additional 30 per cent-plus are overweight, according to federal data. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy jnr and other senior officials have said that helping reduce Americans’ weight should be a priority as part of their campaign to “Make America Healthy Again” and help people live longer lives. The president has also repeatedly invoked weight – his own and others’ – in public remarks. It is a favourite taunt he uses against opponents such as Democratic Illinois Governor J.B. Pritzker and his former adviser Chris Christie.



“I would never call anybody fat,” Trump said in a speech at last month’s White House correspondents’ dinner, where he mocked the idea of Christie and Democratic New York Congressman Jerry Nadler fighting over a cheesecake. “I have my own problems, you know?” Related Article Donald Trump Trump in ‘excellent health’ and ‘fully fit’ to serve, his physician says Trump has sometimes quipped about his own appearance, saying he hasn’t wanted to wear bulletproof vests because they could make him look fat. He has also jokingly defended his diet. “Maybe junk food is good and the other food is no good,” Trump said in the Oval Office in May. “I know many, many people that all they do is watch their weight, their this, their that, and they kicked the bucket, and here we are. I feel great.” In a statement, the White House praised Trump’s fitness and contrasted him with predecessor Joe Biden.



“President Trump’s sharpness, unmatched energy, relentless work ethic and historic accessibility stand in stark contrast to what we saw during the last administration, when Democrats and the legacy media intentionally covered up Joe Biden’s serious mental and physical decline from the American people,” spokesman Davis Ingle said in a statement. “President Trump is the sharpest and most accessible president in American history who is working non-stop to solve problems and deliver on his promises.” The White House did not respond to other questions about the president’s health, including physicians’ recommendation this year that Trump address his weight and whether he has ever taken a GLP-1 anti-obesity drug. Trump has said he has never taken a GLP-1 drug. Trump’s diet and weight have been scrutinised across his political career, with his love for McDonald’s a staple. Pressed by interviewer Barbara Walters in 2015 on whether there was anything they would change about their father, Trump’s children eventually conceded that they didn’t like his diet.



“I want him to eat healthier,” Ivanka Trump told Walters. Trump also discussed his weight in a September 2016 appearance on The Dr Oz Show. A letter released by Trump’s personal physician that month said he weighed 236 pounds. “The one thing I would like to do is be able to drop 15, 20 pounds,” Trump told Mehmet Oz, the show’s host – now the Medicare and Medicaid chief in Trump’s administration – saying that it was difficult because of his lifestyle. Trump has since joked about the experience. “I went on his show and he determined that I should lose weight,” the president said earlier this year, reflecting on his conversation with Oz. “He said, ‘I think you should lose weight.’ I said, ‘I don’t need you saying that in front of millions of people. You don’t have to tell me that.’”



Contrary to his goal, Trump grew heavier during his first term as president. Jackson in January 2018 said that Trump weighed 239 pounds, about a pound shy of being classified as obese under body-mass index (BMI) calculations. Related Article US politics Trump’s diagnosis revealed after ‘swollen leg’ photos trigger alarm “I think a reasonable goal, over the next year or so, is to lose 10-15 pounds,” Jackson told reporters that month. “We talked about diet and exercise a lot. He’s more enthusiastic about the diet part than the exercise part, but we’re going to do both.” It is unclear whether Trump adopted any changes to his diet or began more exercise during his first term, and spokespeople for the White House and Jackson did not respond to questions about it. Sean Conley, Jackson’s successor, said in February 2019 that Trump weighed 243 pounds, making him technically obese. Conley in June 2020 said Trump weighed 244 pounds.



Four months later, Trump contracted a serious case of COVID-19, the impact of which is linked with obesity, physicians have found. The president received a then experimental antibody cocktail, produced by Regeneron, that he credited with helping save his life. He left office in January 2021. Trump was noticeably thinner as he announced another campaign for president in 2023. A doctor’s note released by the campaign in November said that he had “reduced his weight through an improved diet and continued daily physical activity”. Loading Trump has continued to face questions in his second term about his weight. Those questions were renewed recently after Stat News reported that the administration had worked with Eli Lilly to expedite access to a new weight-loss medication for an unnamed patient who was 79 at the time. The White House has denied that Trump received the drug, Retatrutide, which is more powerful than traditional GLP-1 medications. Eli Lilly said it could not comment on any individual patient’s medical prescription, including whether Trump had ever been prescribed Retatrutide, a GLP-1 or other drugs.



Some doctors, who declined to comment specifically on Trump, disagreed on how to interpret a hypothetical 80-year-old patient with a BMI of 30. “BMI is a great screening tool, but it’s not everything,” said Gitanjali Srivastava, a physician who specialises in obesity. Srivastava, who said she has treated patients in their 70s and 80s with obesity, said that weight could be a secondary issue to other markers of health. Related Article Cardiovascular health The four visible signs of heart problems “At that age, it’s less about a number, but more about, what is the per cent body fat? What are we trying to improve including overall health, function, body fat?” she said. David Kessler, who served as head of the Food and Drug Administration under presidents George Bush snr and Bill Clinton, said that he was deeply concerned about Americans’ excess body fat, which he said contributes to premature death.



“That fat around the midsection – that visceral adiposity – is fat around our liver, pancreas, our heart where it doesn’t belong,” Kessler said. For his part, Trump has said he was wary of growing heavier, invoking former president William Howard Taft, who weighed more than 300 pounds. “He was our heaviest president, and I have to be careful because I don’t want to supersede his record,” Trump told second lady Usha Vance in a podcast posted last month. “And a thing like that would be possible if I allowed it to happen.” Washington Post Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Free-range hens likely to go in and out of lockdown as bird flu cases continue to emerge
World.content:
Hundreds of thousands of hens in lockdown Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

While the threat of bird flu still hangs over the egg industry, the Egg producers Federation says it's likely free-range chickens will be going in and out of lockdown in coming months.

Hundreds of thousands of hens have been in lockdown as the third case of bird flu was confirmed in a wild bird in Aotearoa.

But chairperson of the Egg Producers Federation and Mainland Poultry chief executive, John McKay told Checkpoint they would let half a million of their hens back outside on Wednesday.

McKay said there was now good data out there for farmers to decide the risk level for their birds and whether to let their hens out of temporary lockdown.

Many egg suppliers that have the ability to do so have put their hens into lockdown, restricting their roaming as a precaution to protect them from bird flu, meaning free-ranging was not always possible.

The most recent data McKay had seen showed there was a low risk for chickens, he said, even with the third detection.

"It's in a petrel and it's likely we will continue to find those ocean going birds occasionally washed up on our shores.

He said Mainland Poultry had decided to prepare its farms on Tuesday for the hens to be let outside on Wednesday morning.

"This is an evolving situation so we will continue to look at it and judge the risk - the welfare of our birds is paramount and the risk is likely to change in the future. As the risk level changes it might be time to bring those birds back in again."

McKay warned it might be something Aotearoa had to get used to with free-range farming going forward.

"We are free-range farmers because we want our birds roaming outside and we value that highly and people who buy free-range eggs care deeply about welfare.

For consumers who were worried about whether their eggs were still free-range, McKay said stickers would be be put on Mainland Poultry cartons, next time the birds went into lockdown, alerting potential buyers to the fact the birds were temporarily kept inside.

He said the stickers would very clearly state the eggs had been laid by birds temporarily housed for their own welfare.

World.title: Travellers who already booked Fiji holidays could pay more, travel groups warn
World.content:
The Fiji government's new five percent Tourism Services Tax (TST) has been criticised by international travel associations.

The Australian Travel Industry Association (ATIA) and the Travel Agents' Association of New Zealand (TAANZ) say the tax will penalise visitors who have already booked their travels to Fiji.

ATIA and TAANZ have called on the Fijian government to withhold implementing the new tax, scheduled to take effect from 1 September.

ATIA chief executive Dean Long said the tax would mean a Fiji holiday could become more expensive for Aussie travellers.

The new tax will be in place for large-scale tourism operators and travel industry experts are warning the costs are likely to be passed on to customers.

"The design and rollout reflect a complete lack of understanding of how the travel booking ecosystem works, and it is travellers and travel businesses who will pay the price for that failure," Long said in a statement.

"Retrospective application is an absolute no-go. Once a customer has paid, that price is locked in. Sending a fresh bill after the fact is not tax collection, it is a broken promise dressed up as policy."

He said many travellers are being asked to find extra money for a holiday they thought was settled months ago.

"That is not how you treat people who chose Fiji in good faith," he said.

Fiji remains a popular travel destination for Aussies and New Zealanders, but a new tax could threaten that.

TAANZ chief executive Julie White said travel was routinely booked, contracted and paid for many months in advance and the sudden announcement puts all that into chaos.

"Our concern is simple: travellers who booked and agreed a price before 1 September should not be hit with an additional tax simply because they are travelling after that date," White said.

"There is a significant volume of existing Fiji bookings where the price has already been agreed, and in many cases the customer has paid in full. Those travellers have every reasonable expectation that their holiday is paid for.

"They should not suddenly be faced with an additional cost because a new tax has been introduced after they made their booking."

White said the timing is particularly concerning as it comes immediately before the busy September and October school holiday travel period.

"Families have planned and budgeted for these holidays months in advance. There are also group, wedding, corporate and other large bookings where contracts and pricing have already been finalised," White stated.

"Reopening those arrangements creates uncertainty for travellers. Travel agents, wholesalers and tour operators are stuck in the middle. They are being asked to explain and potentially administer a cost they did not create, could not have anticipated and have no control over.

"At the same time, basic practicalities remain unclear, including who is responsible for collecting the tax, how it applies to net rates and existing contracts, and where a supplier ends and an agent begins. These questions need clarity not only for existing bookings, but for new bookings from 1 September as well."

TAANZ said the issue is compounded by a lack of clarity around the practical implementation of the tax, including how it will be treated across different types of bookings and existing contractual arrangements

The new tax will apply to tourism operators, including hotels, tour operators and cruise businesses, with an annual turnover above FJ$2 million (NZ$1.4m).

Fiji's Minister for Finance Esrom Immanuel said the Tourism Services Tax was introduced as part of the coalition government's broader efforts to support Fiji Airways. RNZI/Sally Round

Local concerns

The new tax has also raised concerns locally, with members of the business community also voicing their disappointment.

J Hunter Pearls boss Justin Hunter said the government's decision showed a lack of understanding.

"One really has to question the economic brain trust behind this," he said in a Facebook comment on the issue.

"It shows remarkably little understanding of how the international tourism wholesale mechanism actually works. Product is contracted, priced and sold months in advance. You cannot simply change the cost retrospectively and assume somebody in the supply chain will absorb it.

"Fiji doesn't have that sort of leverage. If Fiji becomes too expensive, unpredictable or difficult for wholesalers to sell, they won't argue with us forever. They'll simply remove Fiji from the menu."

Tony Whitton, the managing director at Rosie Holidays and Ahura Resorts Fiji, said they had been in discussions with government line ministries about repealing or delaying the tax to cover those bookings made later in the year.

"The tourism industry (hotels, tour operators, activity companies, marine) have been in discussion with our line Ministry and the tax office for over 6 weeks to either repeal or at least apply the new tax to only new bookings made after 01 September 2026, warning that retroactively applying a tax on an existing contract that is already in place is a breach and there will be push back," Whitton said.

"So here we are 10 days before implementation."

Businessman Grahame Southwick questioned the tax idea.

"One wonders if these economic " super brains " in Govt even realize that this 5% tax on GROSS turnover can easily represent 20-50% of the profit ??? Am I missing something here?

"What that can translate to is closing the doors for properties than are currently marginal. As for retro charging.. are they serious ??

"Words fail me."

The Fiji Hotel and Tourism Association (FHTA) said businesses remained unclear about how the new TST would work, with concerns that taxing turnover rather than profit could significantly increase the tax burden on tourism operators, particularly those with smaller profit margins.

FHTA chief executive Fantasha Lockington told fjivillage.com they continue to receive thousands of questions from businesses in Fiji and abroad about how the levy would apply to existing bookings, deposits and transactions through wholesalers and agents.

She said that a resort in the Yasawas had asked whether a booking paid in full in April for travel in October would be subject to the new levy, while a Sydney-based wholesaler wanted to know whether it needed to return to clients who paid deposits months ago and ask for an additional 5 percent.

"The concern is not simply about the additional cost, but how the tax is calculated," she told fijivillage.com.

Lockington explained that a business retaining 25 percent of its revenue as profit would see the 5 percent turnover tax take a significant share of its actual profit when combined with the existing 25 percent corporate income tax, while an operator retaining 15 percent of revenue as profit, the 5 percent turnover tax would consume a third of its profit, resulting in a total tax burden equivalent to 58 percent of its income.

Government stand

In a statement, Finance Minister Esrom Immanuel said the government was concerned by the continued delaying tactics being employed by the FHTA and a number of industry players in relation to the implementation of the tax.

He said government had engaged with the FHTA and key tourism industry stakeholders since June to discuss the introduction, application and implementation of the new tax.

According to the government, it had also provided the industry with additional time to prepare for the new measure, with the implementation date adjusted from 1 July, to 1 August, and subsequently to 1 September.

"These extensions were provided in good faith to allow the industry sufficient time to prepare its systems, communicate with customers and ensure compliance. Despite this, government is concerned that some industry players, with the support of the FHTA, continue to create negative publicity around the TST and its implementation," he said.

He said the industry should recognise that protecting Fiji Airways meant protecting the connectivity on which hotels, resorts, tour operators, restaurants, transport operators, cruise services and thousands of other tourism-related businesses depend.

He added, for many years, the tourism industry had benefited from significant tax holidays, duty concessions and other incentives designed to encourage investment and support the development of the sector.

"Many hotels and tourism service providers have received tax holidays ranging from 13 to 20 years, together with various duty concessions and other forms of government support.

"The industry also benefits from taxpayer-funded tourism marketing and other public investments that help promote Fiji as a destination and support visitor arrivals.

"Today, the entire tourism industry contributes only around 5 percent of the total corporate taxes collected by government. The other 95 percent is paid by non-tourism sectors.

"Government recognises the importance of tourism and the investment that the industry brings to Fiji. However, the industry must also recognise that it has a responsibility to contribute to the wider national effort when the country and its critical tourism infrastructure require support."

He also claimed that under the previous Government, the tourism sector was subject to a combined 16 percent turnover-based tax through the 10 percent ECAL and 6 percent STT, which remained in place for a number of years.

World.title: New rules for the Dunedin's alcohol licences don't go far enough - councillor
World.content:
A Dunedin councillor wants the public to get involved in changes to the city's alcohol laws, saying proposed changes do not go far enough.

Consultation begins this week on new rules for the city's alcohol licences, including capping the number of off-licences in high depravation areas - including the student quarter - and reducing alcohol trading and delivery hours.

City councillor Russell Lund told Checkpoint that Invercargill had a ban on supermarket sales of alcohol, and there were nearly half the level of alcohol-related emergency department admissions there than were seen in Dunedin.

"[In Dunedin] one in 25 visits is alcohol related harm. So if we want to be serious about it we've got to start having a good hard look at the idea that we should allow supermarkets to devote a huge amount of floor-space to selling alcohol," Lund said.

Lund said the council should not be "threatened" by supermarket opposition to restricting alcohol sales.

He said he also strongly opposed any scheme to allow alcohol purchases to be made under buy now-pay later schemes.

"No. 1000 percent no. It's not a necessity. It defies any sort of logic or common sense to me," Lund said.

Lund said capping the number of new off-licences in high depravation areas would be a useful tool to limit the extent of alcohol related harm about the city.

"If you want to control behaviours or try and get better results for society you have to put subtle barriers - you have to make it essentially a little bit harder and less convenient - and that's just one obvious things you can do," Lund said.

He appealed to the public to get involved and make submissions to the consultation process.

World.title: Final emergency services test underway as opening date for Auckland's City Rail Link draws near
World.content:
More than 75 actors have been helping Auckland's emergency services test their responses to a range of scenarios ahead of the city's underground train network opening next month.

The City Rail Link (CRL), would open in three weeks on Sunday, September 13.

The last emergency exercise was taking place this week, simulating a fire on a train near one of the main stations.

In total, 15 emergency exercises have tested police, paramedics and fire fighters' responses to a range of scenarios including train derailments, station fires and mass evacuations.

These have each involved more than 300 volunteer passengers and also, actors, to help bring the scenario to life.

CRL Karanga-a-Hape Station on open day. (File photo) RNZ / Lucy Xia

The volunteers reflected the diversity of Auckland's daily commuters including older people, those with health conditions, people with limited English, and those with hearing, visual or mobility needs.

Auckland Transport (AT) General Manager Rail Services, Mark Lambert, said the testing programme has provided confidence the CRL was ready to welcome Aucklanders when it opened.

"The City Rail Link is unlike anything else in New Zealand's rail network, so it has been vital for everyone involved to practise how we would respond in a range of different situations. The strong collaboration between emergency services and our rail partners has helped build confidence that Aucklanders will be well supported should an incident ever occur."

The tests were comprehensive and looked at frontline responses through to the supporting systems behind the scenes, including ventilation and smoke extraction, alarms, communications, CCTV, lighting and control room operations.

Hato Hone St John Area Operations Manager, Kim Moser, said these realistic exercises help ensure emergency services were well prepared to respond safely and effectively if they were needed once the CRL opens.

"For Hato Hone St John, this testing has been an important opportunity for our ambulance personnel to build familiarity with the CRL's new underground environment and practise coordinated responses alongside our emergency service and transport partners."

The exercise builds on an extensive emergency testing programme completed last month, which involved more than 1400 volunteer passengers.

KiwiRail leads and coordinates emergency response to incidents in the CRL tunnels via its Auckland Rail Operations Centre. Auckland One Rail responds to unplanned events on trains and in the CRL stations - with the assistance of emergency services as needed.

City Rail Link chief executive Patrick Brockie said it was a unique environment.

"The City Rail Link's underground environment, with tunnels more than 40 metres below ground in some parts, presents unique challenges around access, evacuation and communication, requiring specialist planning and coordination."

Fire and Emergency New Zealand region manager Ron Devlin said they were carrying out site visits and additional training in the weeks leading up to opening.

"People may have seen our fire trucks parked outside the stations at all hours of the day," he said.

World.title: Marsden Point dry dock seeks fast-track consent, but funding uncertain
World.content:
A proposed dry dock at Northland's Marsden Point would be a game changer for New Zealand's maritime industry, says the regional development minister, as it will allow large ships to be repaired and serviced at home instead of having to go overseas.

A fast-track consent application for the shipyard and dry dock was lodged on Friday.

Minister Shane Jones said the facility would be built just west of Northport in Whangārei Harbour.

It would reduce reliance on overseas dry docks, save ship owners hefty transit costs, improve vessel availability, and reduce emissions.

Large ships such as navy frigates or inter-island ferries currently had much of their maintenance done in Australia and Singapore.

The project would need to be largely privately funded.

Jones conceded funders were not yet lined up, but said potential investors had made it clear they would not put their hands in their pockets until all the consents had been obtained.

For that reason, the government was funding the project through the consenting stages and had set aside $100 million-plus as a construction co-investment from the Regional Infrastructure Fund.

Regional Development Minister Shane Jones. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

He estimated the total cost would be $400-500m, which meant about $300m would have to be secured from the private sector.

"There is a need for us to service our fishing fleet, the ferries, our naval vessels, but unless we create the statutory consent and attract the private sector, blended with some prior public sector money, we're never going to build this facility," he said.

Jones said he wanted the dry dock built at Northland's Marsden Point because it had a suitable deep-water harbour plus the facilities and expertise of neighbouring Northport.

He said the dock would have to be "bog standard model that's fit for purpose" and not a "Taj Mahal or a Club Riviera model".

"We are not an inordinately wealthy country, and unless the cost of the dry dock comes in at around $400 or $500 million, it's never going to be blessed by my good self."

Jones said the public-private partnership plan had been floated with investors in Japan, Singapore and the US.

"But everyone has said, well, let's see whether or not the actual project can be legally consented first, because there is a view overseas that Kiwis often hawk ideas, but it takes forever and a day for the regulatory framework to consent things."

Jones said securing the consents alone would likely cost several million dollars.

But enabling more marine maintenance to be carried out in New Zealand would be a "win-win", because it would support the domestic economy and help deepen the country's skills and supplier base.

A fast-tracked consent application has already been lodged to expand Northport, the deepwater port at the entrance to Whangārei Harbour. Supplied

Previous modelling had indicated the project could boost the economy by $1.05 billion over 38 years.

It was also estimated an average of 1700 jobs a year would be created during the three-year construction phase and 450 jobs during operation.

Jones was optimistic the dry dock would be built - but said he was also a realist, because it would depend on the shape of the next government and Kiwis' many competing demands for infrastructure, such as roads and hospitals.

Progressing work on the Northland Shipyard and Dry Dock was part of the National-NZ First coalition agreement.

The project was listed in Schedule 2 of the Fast-Track Approval Act which meant it did not have to go through the initial phase of applying for fast-track consideration.

World.title: Blaze breaks out in North Canterbury in terrain too rough for ground firefighters
World.content:
Helicopters are battling a wildfire on three fronts in North Canterbury.

FENZ says the terrain on Karaka Road, south of the Hurunui River, is too rugged for firefighters to access it from the ground.

The fire was earlier estimated at about 100 hectares, but FENZ now believes the fire covers about 50 hectares.

World.title: Govt pushes ahead with social media ban for under-16s
World.content:
The government is pressing ahead with its ban on social media for under-16 year olds, with the legislation set to be introduced on Monday.

But ACT and New Zealand First will not support the bill.

The bill puts the pressure on social media companies to comply, establishing an online safety regulator and setting up a penalty regime.

Watch the prime minister answer questions about the ban:

Education Minister Erica Stanford, who had been tasked with leading the work on the ban, said the bill would bring New Zealand into line with other countries that were placing greater responsibility on tech companies to protect children online.

"The bill places legal obligations on platforms. No penalties are proposed for children, their parents or caregivers," Stanford said.

"It doesn't just introduce a minimum age requirement. It creates an enduring framework that can evolve alongside technology and holds platforms responsible for understanding and reducing the risks they create for children."

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon admitted it was unlikely the bill would have its first reading before the end of this Parliamentary term, and it would take some time to get the legislation through Parliament and set the regulator up.

"That'll be something we have to pick up on the other side of the election, but I hope that many other parties will look at the bill and say 'that's a really sensible proposal.'"

Watch the government announcement here:

But ACT and New Zealand First have invoked the 'agree to disagree clause', meaning National will need Labour's support to get the bill past its first reading.

ACT leader David Seymour said protecting children online was serious, but disagreed with National's approach.

"The National Party wanted to put this out before the election. It's their right, I wish them luck, but the country does need a more serious solution to this problem."

Seymour poured scorn on an idea to impose financial penalties on companies that fail to comply of up to 10 percent of their global revenue.

"You just have to look at the idea that the New Zealand government is going to fine a company like Meta 10 percent of its global revenue. That would be $33 billion, which would be great, I mean, the government would be in a massive surplus, but I don't think they're going to pay, and that small fact alone shows this is not a serious solution."

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters called an impromptu media conference at Parliament to respond, saying Luxon should have been more upfront with voters.

"To call it a government bill is a falsity," he said.

"It is from the National Party, and that should have been explained to you."

Peters said he intended to investigate how much taxpayers' money has been spent on the legislation and the "propagandising" around it.

"No matter if the old parties Tweedledum and Tweedledee do it, it's not fair game if they fail at the taxpayers' expense," he said.

"They're spending packets of money on it when it's already failed in another country."

He said such a ban would result in New Zealanders losing "all sorts of freedoms" through the use of digital ID.

But even Labour has indicated it may not support the bill, releasing a letter written by its science and technology spokesperson Reuben Davidson to Stanford.

The letter - which Davidson wrote on Friday - said there were still some matters Labour wanted addressed before it could offer its support.

"I want to be clear that we take this legislation very seriously. The safety of young people in Aotearoa New Zealand is at stake, and the risks they face in increasingly complex online environments are significant. It is critically important that this legislation is in the best possible shape at first reading to ensure it provides a robust safety net for those who need it most," he wrote.

Among the 79 things Labour was asking were the extent of consultation with children and young people on the bill, how a social media operator could show it has complied, whether the government would publish a full privacy impact assessment, and how the penalties would be enforced.

Davidson also wanted the whole Labour caucus to have access to the bill before deciding whether it could support it.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins said the party was yet to hear back from Stanford on its concerns.

"We'll just continue to engage with them in good faith on it," he said.

The Greens also criticised the bill. Its media and communications spokesperson Hūhana Lyndon said it did not solve the problem of platforms "churning out harmful and dangerous content" in the first place.

"We need to regulate social media platforms for all users so these platforms are free from harmful content, rather than just trying to limit access for young people while others continue to engage with harmful algorithms," she said.

"The government needs evidence-based solutions for reducing online harm. We need a government that will take on the dangerous algorithms that fuel division, damage democracy and expose people to extreme misogyny, racism, and hatred."

What's in the bill - and what's not

The bill would require "high risk" platforms, such as Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube, X, and Facebook, to take "reasonable steps" to check users were over the age of 16.

The reasonable steps included using existing account information, facial age estimation, digital ID services, and formal ID.

Messaging apps such as WhatsApp or Discord, and online games like Roblox, are not included in the bill.

AI chatbots that are primarily for productivity, such as ChatGPT and Gemini, are also out of scope, but social AI companions are covered by the ban.

File photo. AFP / Jonathan Raa

Platforms would also be required to regularly assess the risks they posed, and report on how those risks were being identified and reduced.

A factsheet released by the government said those risks included included illegal content, harmful content (such as grooming, cyberbullying, harassment, and AI deepfakes), advertising and behavioural profiling, and service design and function.

The regulator, which will be established within the Department of Internal Affairs, will be able to monitor, investigate and enforce compliance.

Its tools would range from simply gathering information or auditing the age assurance technology used by tech companies, all the way up to geo-blocking or criminal penalties.

The penalties for companies that fail to comply could cost up to 10 percent of their global revenue.

Despite the scepticism from Seymour that the companies would pay up, Stanford said New Zealand was in "lockstep" with other countries, which would be key to the bill's success.

She believed social media companies would pay up, if it came to it.

"They don't give a damn about our kids, and they will pay, which is why it was so important to have that percentage of global profits, and we are in lockstep with other countries on that."

A ban on VPNs is not in the legislation.

Luxon said parents did have a role to play in monitoring what social media platform their children were on, but so did social media companies.

"Social media is exposing them to harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to deal with and it's affecting their family life, mental health, sleep, and education," he said.

Parents heard 'loud and clear' - Luxon

Despite opposition from his coalition partners, Luxon said the National was pressing ahead as it had heard "loud and clear" from parents and principals around the country that they wanted an intervention.

"We think this is the right thing to be doing, and it's the right thing to be doing to protect our kids," he said.

"I appreciate political parties will form their own views about it, but we've introduced it to the Parliament, we'll get to go through the election process. People can come back and and weigh it all up, and we'll go through a normal process."

Asked whether banning children from one platform could push them towards other more harmful platforms not covered in the legislation, Stanford said there would always be an argument around a slippery slope, but children were already being exposed to harm.

She indicated the government could look at other harms online, given the bill would establish age verification for YouTube but not to things like pornography.

"This bill sets a framework where we can include other things in the future, but the most important thing is, the only reason that young people know about those other platforms is because of the social media they're on in the first place," she said.

World.title: Family of toddler who drowned in pool hopes inquest into his death will save lives
World.content:
A "beautiful boy" wandered into a pool in 2023, he died in his mother's arms 12 days later.

Now, River Albert-Wihone's family is hoping his story can save lives.

The Coroner's inquest into the toddlers death is underway in Auckland District Court, and has heard emotional statements from his family.

Albert-Wihone was just over a year old when he was found in the pool at his family home and was taken to Starship Children's Hospital, where he later died.

River's parents addressed the Coroner through tears on Monday morning at the beginning of the inquest before Coroner Alison Mills.

A number of family members watched from the back of the courtroom, clad in All Blacks jerseys - River's favourite team.

His father, Matthew, spoke about the immense pain of his loss.

"Losing a child changes you in ways you can't describe," he said.

"I always worried if my kids would be okay if I died, I never once imagined losing one of them."

He described the feeling as numb, while at the same time the worst pain imaginable.

"The last almost three years have been the hardest of my life, but I stand here today, like you all, in hopes that our experience, our pain and grief, can help make changes so that no other family has to experience it also," Albert-Wihone said.

"That's how we can honour our boy."

River's mother, Lauren, spoke about the things that could have been that they never get to share with their son.

"Him saying I love you for the first time, him meeting his little sisters, his first day of kindy, school, Christmases, his first All Blacks or Warriors game, birthdays," she said.

"He would be four this year, I would give anything in the world for the life we were supposed to have."

River Albert-Wihone's family at the inquest into his death. RNZ / Finn Blackwell

Part of the inquest will look at issues with the pool fence and gate at the property.

River's grandmother, Christine Robinson, told the inquest she had raised concerns prior to her grandson's death.

"I first raised concerns to, firstly, the builder, about January, I think it was the 20th of January 2022," she said.

Robinson described it as an intermittent fault in the pool gate, some times closing on the second try, others taking a number of attempts before properly closing.

Her pleas for a fix fell on deaf ears, Robinson said.

"I was frustrated," she said.

"I was hoping that the council could step in and do something, I was frustrated at that stage."

Robinson said she tried to manage the issue by locking the gate and keeping people away from the pool.

The inquest was set to hear from the property's landlord as well as the property manager on Tuesday.

A fencing expert told the inquest he believed Albert-Wihone's death was preventable.

The coroner later that afternoon heard from Alexander Silver, who runs a fencing company, and had a look at the gate and fence at the rental property.

Silver said the drowning could have been avoided had the gates been installed using better quality hinges and latches.

"There were a lot of basic mistakes," he said.

"The way they attached the post into the concrete rather than into the actual brick, that wasn't done by a professional."

'He's left a big hole'

Speaking to RNZ, Robinson remembered her grandson's "beautiful" hair.

"He loved the All Blacks," she said.

"He was 14 months, but he's left a big hole."

Robinson was hoping for more accountability from landlords, but had been left wondering if she could have done more.

"I thought I did enough to get the gate repaired, I thought managing it, it would be fine," she said.

World.title: Ex-NBA player who says he identifies as woman ejected from WNBA game
World.content:
Former NBA centre Enes Kanter Freedom has been ejected from an Indiana-Chicago WNBA game after Sky guard Natasha Cloud yelled and pointed in his direction late in the third quarter.

Freedom was sitting along the baseline on Sunday night (Monday AEST). He had on a black shirt that read "WOMAN noun. adult human female".

The Fever called for a timeout after Cloud scored with 1:22 left in the third. Cloud then went to confront Kanter, who held his arms out and took one step on the court. Security and a handful of Sky players stepped in between the two before the dispute escalated.

Freedom was then escorted from the court area. He displayed his shirt as he walked toward the lobby. He had a conversation with a group of police officers before departing Wintrust Arena.

Sky coach Tyler Marsh said the team had rallied around Cloud.

"Tash didn't wanna feel like she was a distraction and I told her she wasn't," he said.

"I told her that we all embrace her as someone that protects our team and protects people that need to be protected. Tash is always going to stand on that, and we stand for Tash."

Freedom and Royce White, another former NBA player, declared themselves eligible for the WNBA draft this month, saying they identified as women.

The argument that's hijacking the WNBA Sophie Cunningham insists she wants to protect the sanctity of women's sport, but her comments have opened her league up to an unprecedented attack.

"I'm transgender. I'm a woman … I identify as sometimes identifying as a woman for purposes of … professional basketball," White previously said.

"I think I'd be unstoppable."

Freedom said he and his team had reviewed the WNBA's eligibility criteria and its approach to self-identification and inclusion, and argued that if declaring an identity were sufficient, then he met the requirements to compete.

The confrontation came in a game that Indiana star Sophie Cunningham was playing in. Cunningham previously voiced support for barring transgender girls and women from girls' and women's sports in an extensive ESPN profile.

"I got a lot of negative feedback about me hating trans," Cunningham said.

"And I'm like, 'I never once said that.' I think that I am here to extend love.

"But I also think with that love is truth, being honest. And I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn't have to go against biological men."

Protesters from both sides of the argument have gathered outside a number of WNBA games, with fans at the Sky-Fever game calling out Kanter as he entered the arena.

Sophie Cunningham (left) has been at the centre of the controversy, highlighted by Enes Kanter's (right) stunt. (Getty Images: Michael Reaves)

One was heard telling the former NBA centre to get his "bitch ass out of Chicago", while another said "I'm not touching him I'm just saying f*** you, bitch".

"Knowing that rallies are happening on both sides shows the platform that the W has and the stunts for attention are just continuing to try and ride the wave that we have,” New York Liberty star Breanna Stewart said.

"I want Liberty fans and even Indy fans that are going to come here tonight to be able to have this arena be a safe space."

There has never been a transgender woman player in the WNBA.

Commissioner Cathy Engelbert last week denounced people she said were trying to "sow divisiveness" over the issue.

Engelbert's comments in a pre-game gathering before a Fever-Wings game in Dallas were her first public remarks since the league called out what it said were bad faith efforts to use the debate to "demean or marginalise others".

"People are trying to use the league to sow divisiveness," Engelbert said.

"We're being the centre of political football for people who have never watched the WNBA, never have written about the WNBA or reported on the WNBA."

The league's collective bargaining agreement states that "only players who are women are eligible to play in the WNBA", but it does not include any more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth.

Engelbert sent a memo this month to team presidents and general managers saying the league would discuss the subject of transgender women in women's basketball.

"There's always going to be haters out there and we denounce it," Engelbert said last week.

"But that's what happens when you have made it as a legitimate sports media and entertainment product."

World.title: AFL boss says suspended Swans will not be invited to Brownlow ceremony
World.content:
AFL boss Andrew Dillon has spoken to the media about the Sydney Swans scandal, saying "the actions of a few don't define the actions of the entire industry".

Dillon was at the launch of the men's AFL finals series and the first-ever wildcard round but was mainly asked about the AFL's handling of the Sydney Swans scandal, as well as details on allegations of drug use by the players.

Players Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon have been stood down by the Sydney Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late after last Sunday's win over Essendon in Melbourne.

Police from Victoria's sexual crimes squad are separately investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a player allegedly touching a woman without her consent.

A police investigation is still underway, but no charges have been laid or arrests made.

Dillon and the AFL released a statement on Tuesday evening, the day after the story emerged, but today marked the first time Dillon or any of the league's higher-ups had fronted the media on the matter.

Chief executive Dillon said it was fair to say the scandal had "overshadowed" the start of the finals, but that he hoped football could bring people together, as evidenced by the emotional scenes after the Swans' men's and women's double header at the SCG on Sunday.

Swans fans descend on SCG amid club scandal Sydney Swans fans react to an emotional week, where a scandal continues to engulf the club, as they prepare to watch a historic double header at the SCG.

"The actions of a few do not take away from the thousands of people involved in football at all different levels who do great things all the time," he said.

"But what we do know is that we can do things better and we will continue to do that and we will continue to learn to be better.

"I think the actions of a few don't define the actions of the entire industry."

Dillon said the five suspended players would not be invited to the Brownlow Medal ceremony, held on the Monday before the grand final, but remained eligible for the award.

Dillon said the league would not conduct its own enquiries into the incident until after the police investigation was finished.

On Saturday, police provided an update about the investigation being undertaken by detectives from the Sexual Crimes Squad.

"The exact circumstances of the matter are still being established, and a number of people have been spoken to," the statement read.

"As the investigation remains active and ongoing, we will not be commenting further, including providing information on the specific circumstances of the matter, movements of detectives and any statements or interviews taken."

In a statement, the Sydney Swans said the club "supports the action taken by Victoria Police in releasing today's statement regarding the investigation".

The club's statement also addressed comments relating to other men, beyond the five players identified by the club, being present in the hotel room at the centre of the allegations.

"The Sydney Swans categorically confirms that no member of staff is involved in the investigation. This includes being in the hotel room central to the police investigation," it read.

"The club reiterates that no player has been interviewed by police at this stage."

Live Moment Look back at how ABC readers and other Australians responded to this live moment. That's the end of the press conference 'It is a privilege to play AFL': Dillon Dillon is asked a follow up whether the five named players relating to the scandal have been held accountable. "There's been accountability for those players," he says. "It is a privilege to play AFL and with that comes responsibilities." AFL has reviewed illicit drugs policy Dillon is asked whether the alleged drug use that has created part of the story around the Swans scandal has prompted a rethink over the league's illicit drugs policy. "We've just undergone an extensive review of the illicit drugs policy," Dillon says. "That will be taking effect from this off season. "There's accountability for the players and there will continue to be." Show more

World.title: Runner smashes half-marathon record, heads straight to the football
World.content:
Yomif Kejelcha has smashed the half-marathon world record, running a staggering 56 minutes and 51 seconds at the Media Maratón Ciudad de Buenos Aires in Argentina on Sunday.

The Ethiopian shaved 29 seconds off the previous mark of 57:20, which had been set by Uganda's Jacob Kiplimo in Lisbon in March.

Kejelcha's time and that of the record he just beat are still subject to ratification by World Athletics.

The Media Maratón Ciudad de Buenos Aires is a World Athletics Label road race and took place under favourable conditions of 6 degrees Celsius and with a slight breeze.

As ever, the super shoe gets plenty of post-race love from Yomif Kejelcha. (Instagram: @maratondebuenosaires)

Tadese Worku (59:20) and Bereket Nega (1:00:20) of Ethiopia completed the podium.

"I'm over the moon," Kejelcha told World Athletics.

"I'm super happy and right now I don't feel any tiredness. The travel from Ethiopia was too long and I was tired the first days here, but later I felt better and today I was full of beans.

"I had planned to run conservatively over the early stages, but I felt good and decided to give it my all.

"This time is unbelievable. I can't describe it with words.

"I now hope to try the Argentinian meat, which has a very good reputation, and this afternoon I have been invited to watch the River Plate-Vélez football match. I'm very grateful."

At the historic Estadio Monumental, Kejelcha showed off his new record on a new River Plate shirt, although would have been disappointed as Vélez Sarsfield came from 2-0 down to draw 2-2 in their Argentine Primera División clash.

Clearly Los Millonarios don't share Kejelcha's stamina.

Yomif Kejelcha showed off his record on a new River Plate kit at at the Estadio Monumental. (Instagram: @maratondebuenosaires)

Kejelcha's time allowed him to reclaim the record, which he previously held with a 57:30 in Valencia in October 2024.

The time is slower than that recorded by Kiplimo in Barcelona last year, when he ran what he described as "the perfect race" to stop the clock in 56:42.

But World Athletics did not ratify that time because race conditions did not comply with their regulations.

Kejelcha ran the race at an average pace of 2 minutes and 42 seconds per kilometre — which would give you a 5km parkrun time of 13 minutes and 28 seconds.

However, as was the case when he became the second man to run an official race marathon in less than two hours in London last year, he negative split the race, running the second half faster than the first.

Super shoes won't be banned despite 'technological doping' claims Lord Sebastian Coe says World Athletics has a duty to "enable" super shoe development despite concerns.

He set out behind two pacemakers, going through the first 5km at 13:45, while the second 5km was run in 13:34.

His subsequent 5km split was a remarkable 13:22, with the Ethiopian holding that pace through the next 5km, running it in 13:23.

Last April at the London Marathon, the 29-year-old two-time Olympian ran 1:59:41, finishing second behind Kenya's Sabastian Sawe, who set the world record with a 1:59:30.

In the women's race, Ethiopia's Fotyen Tesfay stormed to victory in 1:03:57, comfortably beating her two Kenyan rivals Nelvin Jepkemboi (1:05:06) and Catherine Amanang'ole (1:05:11).

World.title: 'Disappointed' Hird congratulates McVeigh ahead of Bombers coach call
World.content:
Mark McVeigh appears set to be unveiled as Essendon's next senior coach, with fellow applicant James Hird congratulating his former teammate on the impending appointment.

Bombers legend Hird had been vocal in expressing his desire to return for another stint as coach, after Brad Scott was sacked in May.

Fremantle assistant Jaymie Graham and Adelaide assistant Murray Davis were also in the mix.

But McVeigh, an assistant to Dean Cox at Sydney, is reportedly on the verge of being appointed, with an announcement expected as soon as tomorrow.

Mark McVeigh is in the box seat to be offered the Bombers job. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Interim coach Dean Solomon hands over the reins after the Bombers (2-21) completed the worst season in club history with a 10-point defeat to Port Adelaide on Sunday.

"Firstly, congratulations to Mark. He's a great friend of mine and I'm very proud of him that he's going to be named the coach, so good on him," Hird said on Nine yesterday night.

"From a personal point of view, it's very disappointing. I'm disappointed. I put my heart and soul into the effort, but obviously fell short and that's the way it goes."

Hird indicated he was yet to hear an official decision from Essendon, but said "maybe that's coming".

The 53-year-old ruled out returning to the Bombers in a different role, but said he still had the passion to coach.

James Hird, Dean Solomon and Mark McVeigh together in 2022 when they were all at the Giants. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Hird is director of coaching with VFL club Port Melbourne.

"We have a finals series to play," Hird said.

"We'll see what plays out at the end of the year with some other clubs who have contacted me and we'll see what happens."

McVeigh is reportedly set to present to the Essendon board again today, with an announcement imminent.

The 45-year-old played 232 games for Essendon and was one of the 34 players suspended over the club's devastating drugs saga, when Hird was coach.

McVeigh currently serves as Sydney's defensive coach, but could leave the club immediately to play a role in the Bombers' end-of-season exit meetings and list management decisions.

The second-placed Swans are preparing for a finals campaign while bracing for more fallout from the scandal that has rocked the club.

"That's one thing this football club's done well for a long period of time … be ready for the unexpected or if something does arise," Sydney coach Cox said last week about the potential of losing McVeigh to the Bombers.

"We've had those meetings [and] discussions. We're really clear on what will happen if he was or wasn't to get the [Essendon] position."

Two-time Essendon premiership champion and former captain Hird first took over as Bombers coach in 2010.

He was suspended for the 2014 season amid the fallout from the drugs saga, returned as coach in 2015 and resigned in August that year.

Hird had garnered plenty of support from Bombers fans in his latest bid to return as coach, after he narrowly missed out when Scott was appointed in 2022.

World.title: Former Roosters premiership star unveiled as PNG Chiefs' '007' signing
World.content:
Joey Manu has been unveiled as the much-hyped PNG Chief 007, with the two-time premiership winner to return to the NRL in 2028.

The Chiefs officially confirmed today the former Sydney Roosters utility signed a two-year deal with the club, which now boasts a backline that will be the envy of the NRL.

PNG had long hyped their seventh signing, with speculation Penrith superstar Nathan Cleary was bound for the club as their inaugural halfback.

But with a staircase at their home base showing each of their signings and "007" listed as "reserved", that honour will now go to code-hopper Manu ahead of the 2028 season.

Loading Instagram content

"We're thrilled to add Joey to our squad moving forward," Chiefs general manager Michael Chammas said.

"He is a world-class footballer with versatility across several positions and can change a game in a single moment with the skills he possesses.

"His experience and demonstrated success at the highest level will be a great benefit to our team and we can't wait to see him have a significant impact in the Chiefs jersey."

Manu joins a list that already includes Jarome Luai, Alex Johnston, Connor Watson, Zac Lomax, Brian To'o and Englishman Matty Lees.

But the move appears likely to have ended the 30-year-old's boyhood dream of representing the All Blacks.

To'o is still just the beginning for PNG Brian To'o is the fourth player to sign for Papua New Guinea who has played State of Origin in the past two years. It's a sign of things to come, with the NRL's richest club yet to truly enter free agency.

Manu left the NRL for an overseas rugby union career after the 2024 season, starting in Japan before a move to French team Racing 92 last year.

But his French rugby deal runs to the end of 2027, and New Zealand Rugby only selects players for the All Blacks if they play domestically.

Manu will be 33 by the time his Chiefs deal finishes.

Manu became one of the NRL's most prized utility players across 181 games, including the 2018 and 2019 premiership wins, with the Roosters.

He was named Dally M centre of the year in 2022 and won the Golden Boot award as the sport's best international player later that year.

The athletic New Zealand representative is equally adept in the centres and at fullback, and can also capably slot into the halves in a pinch.

On leaving the NRL after the Roosters' 2024 finals campaign, Manu offered no guarantees of ever returning to the 13-man code.

But any possible comeback had widely been expected to come with the Roosters, who scouted him as a teenager.

Instead, Manu becomes the latest jewel in the crown of the NRL's forthcoming 19th team, which can offer lucrative tax-free salaries to its signings.

PNG will be able to officially hit the market on November 1, with Cleary headlining a list of players who could still become free agents at that time.

The club has also been linked to Gold Coast utility AJ Brimson and Canberra second-rower Hudson Young, both of whom are State of Origin players, in recent weeks.

Isaah Yeo, Latrell Mitchell and Bradman Best are among other household names without deals beyond the 2027 season.
